questions.short_title: UNCLOS Pollution Definition, Coastal State Obligations, and the Three Compensation Tiers
questions.text_verbatim: A. One of the objectives of UNCLOS is protection of marine environment and prevention of pollution. Define pollution as per UNCLOS and discuss the key features of obligations of coastal states in this regard. B. State the 3 main tiers of the oil pollution damage compensation conventions of the IMO. In each case elaborate one who is responsible for payment of compensation. Also, state the source of funds as well as certification required by ship under each tier.

State the 3 main tiers of the oil pollution damage compensation conventions of the IMO; in each case who is responsible for payment of compensation, the source of funds, and the certification required by the ship under each tier.

blocks.h: 1. The Convention's definition of pollution, and what makes it unusually wide

blocks.p: The stem asks for the definition as per UNCLOS, so it must be the Convention's own, and not a general description of dirty water. It is given at article 1, paragraph 1(4):

"Pollution of the marine environment" means the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results or is likely to result in such deleterious effects as harm to living resources and marine life, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine activities, including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea, impairment of quality for use of sea water and reduction of amenities.
The marks are in taking that definition apart, because four separate elements in it are each wider than a candidate expects:

rows: "by man, directly or indirectly"
Human agency is required, so a natural seep is not pollution - but indirect introduction is caught, so a river carrying industrial waste to the sea is within the definition
"substances OR ENERGY"

The most under-used word in the definition. Heat, noise and radiation are pollution. Thermal discharge from a power station and underwater noise from shipping both fall within it, without any substance being discharged at all
"results OR IS LIKELY TO RESULT"
No damage need have occurred. Likelihood of deleterious effect is enough, which is what makes the definition capable of supporting preventive obligations rather than only remedial ones
The five deleterious effects

Harm to living resources and marine life; hazards to human health; hindrance to marine activities, including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea; impairment of quality for use of sea water; and reduction of amenities. The last two are economic and even aesthetic, not merely ecological

blocks.p: Two further points are worth a line each. The definition expressly includes estuaries, so it reaches inland of the coastline. And it is source-neutral: nothing in it is about ships. Ships are one source among several, which is exactly how Part XII goes on to treat them.

blocks.h: 2. The general obligation, and why it is not confined to any zone

blocks.p: The stem's own opening - that one of the objectives of UNCLOS is protection of the marine environment - is answered by article 192, which is one sentence long and is the foundation of the whole of Part XII: "States have the obligation to protect and preserve the marine environment."
Three features of that make it unusual, and they are what the second half of limb A is really about.

ul: It is free-standing and is not confined to any zone. The rest of the Convention allocates rights zone by zone - territorial sea, contiguous zone, exclusive economic zone, continental shelf, high seas. Article 192 imposes a duty, and it runs across all of them and beyond. A coastal State does not owe it only in its own waters.

It qualifies sovereignty itself. Article 193 confirms that States have the sovereign right to exploit their natural resources pursuant to their environmental policies and in accordance with their duty to protect and preserve the marine environment. The right to exploit is expressly made subject to the duty - which is the single most quoted proposition in this Part.

It is an obligation of conduct with a stated standard. Article 194 requires States to take all measures necessary to prevent, reduce and control pollution from any source, using the best practicable means at their disposal and in accordance with their capabilities. That formulation is deliberate: it does not demand the impossible of a developing State, and it does not excuse a capable one.

blocks.p: Article 194(2) adds a further duty that a good answer names: activities under a State's jurisdiction or control must be so conducted as not to cause damage by pollution to other States and their environment, and pollution arising from them must not spread beyond the areas where the State exercises sovereign rights. Article 195 is then a separate article in its own right - Duty not to transfer damage or hazards or transform one type of pollution into another - and it provides that in taking measures under this Part, States shall act so as not to transfer, directly or indirectly, damage or hazards from one area to another or transform one type of pollution into another. That is the provision an examiner will reach for if the answer strays into scrubber washwater or incineration, and it is worth citing by its own number rather than folding it into article 194.

blocks.h: 3. The coastal State's obligations - rule-making

blocks.p: The Convention deals with pollution source by source, and the coastal State's obligation differs with the source. The pattern is consistent and is worth showing as a pattern rather than as a list:

headers: What the coastal State must do
rows: Land-based sources
Adopt national laws and regulations, taking into account internationally agreed rules and standards. The weakest link in the chain, and the largest source of marine pollution
Dumping
Adopt national law; and dumping within the territorial sea, the EEZ or on the continental shelf requires the express prior approval of the coastal State
Pollution from vessels

Act through the competent international organization - IMO - and national laws must have at least the same effect as the generally accepted international rules and standards. In the territorial sea, laws must not hamper innocent passage; in the EEZ, they must conform to those international rules
From or through the atmosphere
Adopt laws applicable to the air space under its sovereignty and to vessels of its flag or registry

blocks.p: The discrimination that carries the mark is between article 207 and article 211. For land-based sources, which are entirely within a State's own territory, the Convention leaves it a wide discretion and asks only that it take international standards into account. For pollution from vessels, which is inherently international, it requires the State to act through IMO and forbids it from legislating below the international standard. A coastal State may be stricter than the international rules for its own ships; it may not be laxer, and it may not impose its own construction standards on foreign ships in innocent passage. That single sentence explains the entire architecture of ship-source pollution regulation.
The Convention also requires that these rules be re-examined from time to time as necessary, which is why the IMO instruments they refer to are amendable while UNCLOS itself is not.

blocks.h: 4. The coastal State's obligations - enforcement, and its limits

blocks.p: Enforcement under Part XII is divided three ways, and the coastal State holds one of the three - which is why an answer that treats the coastal State as the only actor misses the structure.

ul: The flag State (article 217) must ensure that vessels flying its flag comply, wherever the violation occurs, and must investigate and where appropriate institute proceedings. This is the primary duty and it does not go away.

The port State (article 218) may, where a vessel is voluntarily in its port, investigate and institute proceedings in respect of discharges that occurred outside its own waters - a remarkable extension of jurisdiction, and the treaty foundation of port State control as an environmental instrument.

The coastal State (article 220) may act in respect of violations within its territorial sea or exclusive economic zone, and the powers available are graded: information may be required where there are clear grounds for believing a violation occurred; physical inspection where the response is inadequate or manifestly at odds with the facts; and detention and proceedings only where there is clear objective evidence of a discharge causing or threatening major damage.

blocks.p: Two further coastal-State features complete the picture. Article 221 preserves the right to take and enforce measures beyond the territorial sea, proportionate to the actual or threatened damage, to protect the coastline from pollution following a maritime casualty. And article 235 makes States responsible for the fulfilment of their international obligations concerning the marine environment and liable in accordance with international law.

Article 235(2) is where limb A hands over to limb B, and saying so joins the question together: States must ensure that recourse is available in accordance with their legal systems for prompt and adequate compensation or other relief in respect of damage caused by pollution by natural or juridical persons under their jurisdiction, and must cooperate in developing the law of liability and compensation further. The three tiers in limb B are how that obligation is actually discharged for oil.

Finally, the coastal State's powers are not unqualified. Part XII, section 7 carries its own safeguards, articles 223 to 233, and they constrain every enforcement power described above. The ones that bear on a ship are: enforcement against foreign vessels may be exercised only by officials or warships and aircraft on government service (article 224); the powers must be exercised without endangering the safety of navigation or the vessel (article 225); a foreign vessel shall not be delayed longer than is essential for the investigation, and physical inspection is limited to an examination of certificates unless there are clear grounds to go further (article 226); there must be no discrimination against the vessels of any other State (article 227); only monetary penalties may be imposed for pollution violations by foreign vessels beyond the territorial sea, and the recognized rights of the accused are to be observed (article 230); the flag State must be promptly notified (article 231); and States are liable for damage or loss attributable to enforcement measures that are unlawful or exceed those reasonably required (article 232). Naming two or three of these is what separates an answer that knows the coastal State's obligations from one that knows only its powers.

blocks.h: 5. Why the oil pollution compensation regime has three tiers

blocks.p: Limb B asks for the three main tiers, who pays in each case, and the source of the funds. Before naming them it is worth one sentence on why the regime is layered at all, because it explains everything that follows.

A major tanker spill can cost far more than any shipowner or his insurer could reasonably be required to carry, and requiring unlimited liability would have made tankers uninsurable. But leaving victims uncompensated was unacceptable. The compromise was to make the shipowner strictly but limitedly liable, and then to place the balance on the cargo interest - the oil industry which benefits from the trade - through funds financed by those who receive the oil. The regime therefore shares the cost between the ship and the cargo, which is its defining idea.

blocks.h: 6. Tier one - the shipowner and his insurer

rows: Who is liable

The registered owner of the ship at the time of the incident. Liability is strict - no fault need be proved - and it is channelled to the registered owner, so claims may not ordinarily be brought against the master, crew, pilot, charterer, manager or salvor
Who actually pays

The registered owner, and in practice his liability insurer - normally a protection and indemnity club. Insurance or other financial security is compulsory for ships carrying persistent oil in bulk as cargo above a stated size, evidenced by a certificate carried on board, and the claimant has a right of direct action against the insurer
Source of the funds
The shipping side - the owner's own resources and his insurance, ultimately funded by the premiums of shipowners generally
The limit

The owner may limit his liability to an amount fixed by reference to the ship's tonnage, by constituting a fund with the competent court. No figure is given here - the limits are amended over time and MIW holds no text of the Convention
When the limit is lost

Where the damage resulted from the owner's personal act or omission, committed with intent to cause such damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result. A very high threshold, and deliberately so
Exceptions to liability

Narrow: act of war, hostilities or an exceptional natural phenomenon; damage wholly caused by a third party's intentional act; and negligence of an authority responsible for maintaining navigational aids. Contributory fault of the claimant may reduce the claim

blocks.p: The practical point for an engineer is the compulsory insurance certificate: it is a document carried on board, checked at port State control, and without it the ship does not trade.

blocks.h: 7. Tiers two and three - the Funds, and who actually provides the money

rows: When it responds
Where tier one gives no compensation - the owner is exempt, or cannot be identified - or where it is financially inadequate, including where the owner's limit is exhausted
Where tier two is itself insufficient to meet established claims in full
Who pays
The 1992 International Oil Pollution Compensation Fund, an intergovernmental organisation with its own legal personality
The Supplementary Fund, established by the 2003 Protocol
Source of the funds

Contributions levied on the receivers of contributing oil - crude oil and heavy fuel oil - received by sea in the territory of a Member State above a threshold quantity in a calendar year. The cargo interest pays, not the shipowner
The same mechanism, but levied only on receivers in the States that have opted into the Protocol. It is optional, and a State must be a party to the 1992 Fund Convention first
Who it is available to
Claimants in 1992 Fund Member States
Claimants in Supplementary Fund Member States only

blocks.p: Three features of the Fund tiers are worth stating expressly, because they are what the limb's second question is aimed at.

ol: The money comes from the cargo, not from the ship. Contributions are collected from oil receivers - refineries and terminals - and not from shipowners, charterers or governments. That is the structural answer to "who is responsible for payment", and it is the point most candidates miss.

The tiers are cumulative and sequential, not alternative. Tier two tops up tier one; tier three tops up tier two. Each has its own overall ceiling, and the third tier's ceiling is a total that includes the amounts payable under the first two.

Tier three is optional; tiers one and two are the standard regime. A State that has not joined the 2003 Protocol has two tiers, not three - so the compensation available for the same casualty depends on where it happens.

blocks.p: No monetary figure is given anywhere in this answer, and that is deliberate rather than evasive. The tonnage-band limits and the fund ceilings are amended by tacit acceptance over time, so any figure carries a date with it. MIW holds no text of the three instruments and does not assert their limits. The architecture - strict limited liability on the owner, then the cargo interest twice over - is what is stable and is what the question asks for.

blocks.h: 8. What the three tiers do NOT cover - and the trap

blocks.p: The limb says oil pollution damage, and the boundaries of the regime are where an examiner will press. Four exclusions are worth a line each:

ul: The regime is about persistent oil carried in bulk as cargo - the tanker case. It is not a general pollution compensation scheme.

Bunker oil from a non-tanker is a different regime. The Bunkers Convention 2001 covers pollution damage from a ship's own fuel, and it is a single tier, not three: liability rests on the shipowner in a wider sense, backed by compulsory insurance, with limitation under the general limitation convention - and there is no fund behind it. That is the sharpest available discrimination, and it is why a question comparing Bunkers with CLC is a different question from this one.
Hazardous and noxious substances are dealt with by their own convention, which was not in force at this sitting.
Geography matters. The tiers respond only in States party to the relevant instrument, and the third tier only in States that have opted into it.

blocks.p: And the closing observation, which returns the answer to limb A: the three tiers exist because UNCLOS article 235(2) requires States to ensure that recourse is available for prompt and adequate compensation. Limb A states the duty; limb B is the machinery by which, for oil, it is actually met.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Two limbs, no printed marks, so treat them as eight and eight. Limb A contains two separate instructions - define pollution as per UNCLOS, and discuss the key features of coastal-State obligations - and both must be answered explicitly. A candidate who writes generally about marine environmental protection has answered neither. Limb B contains three: name the tiers, say who pays in each case, and state the source of the funds. Answer all three for all three tiers and the limb is complete.
The strongest single move is to give the definition as a definition - close to the Convention's own words - and then take it apart. Paraphrasing it loosely throws away the easiest marks on the paper.

blocks.h: The definition, and the four things inside it

blocks.p: The introduction BY MAN, directly or indirectly, of substances OR ENERGY into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results OR IS LIKELY TO RESULT in deleterious effects - harm to living resources and marine life, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine activities including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea, impairment of quality for use of sea water, and reduction of amenities.

ul: "by man" - a natural seep is not pollution. But "indirectly" catches a river carrying waste to the sea.
"or energy" - heat, noise and radiation are pollution. The most under-used word in the definition and a reliable extra mark.
"or is likely to result" - no damage need have occurred. This is what lets the definition support preventive duties.
Five deleterious effects, and the last two - impairment of quality for use of sea water, and reduction of amenities - are economic and aesthetic, not merely ecological.

blocks.h: The three propositions that carry the coastal-State half

ol: Article 192 - the obligation to protect and preserve is free-standing and not confined to any zone. The zones allocate rights; this imposes a duty across all of them.
Article 193 - the sovereign right to exploit is expressly subject to that duty. Sovereignty is qualified by it.

Article 194 - all necessary measures from any source, by the best practicable means and in accordance with capabilities; no causing damage to other States; and no transferring damage from one area to another or transforming one type of pollution into another.

blocks.h: The rule-making discrimination worth a mark on its own

blocks.p: For land-based sources (207) a State need only take international standards into account - wide discretion. For vessel-source pollution (211) it must act through IMO and its national law must have at least the same effect as the international rules. So: a coastal State may be stricter than the international standard for its own ships; it may not be laxer, and it may not impose its own construction standards on foreign ships in innocent passage. That sentence explains the whole architecture of ship-source regulation.

blocks.h: Enforcement - three actors, not one

ul: Flag State (217) - compliance by its own ships, wherever the violation occurs.
Port State (218) - where the ship is voluntarily in port, may proceed for discharges outside its own waters.

Coastal State (220) - violations in its territorial sea or EEZ, with powers graded from requiring information, to physical inspection, to detention and proceedings on clear objective evidence of major damage.
Article 221 - measures beyond the territorial sea after a maritime casualty, proportionate to the damage threatened.
Article 235 - responsibility, liability, and the duty to ensure recourse for prompt and adequate compensation.

blocks.h: The sentence that joins the two limbs

blocks.p: Article 235(2) requires States to ensure recourse is available for prompt and adequate compensation - and the three tiers are how that duty is discharged for oil. Write it at the join and the answer reads as one argument. It is also the single best way to show you have understood why these two limbs are on the same question.

blocks.h: The three tiers, in the form the limb asks for

rows: One
The registered owner, strictly liable, and in practice his P&I club - with compulsory insurance and a right of direct action against the insurer
The shipping side - the owner's resources and his insurance
Two
Fund Convention 1992
The 1992 IOPC Fund, where tier one gives nothing or is inadequate
Contributions from receivers of contributing oil received by sea in Member States above a threshold quantity - the cargo interest
Three
Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003
The Supplementary Fund, where tier two is insufficient
The same levy, but only in the States that have opted in

blocks.p: The one-sentence answer to "who is responsible for payment": the ship pays first and the cargo pays afterwards - twice.

blocks.h: Quote no money

blocks.p: Give no limitation figure, fund ceiling or contribution threshold. The limits are amended by tacit acceptance, so every figure carries a date, and a remembered number from a textbook is very likely to be the wrong year's. Saying "limited by reference to tonnage, to an amount amended from time to time" is both safer and more accurate than a number.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Describing pollution loosely instead of giving the Convention's definition. The stem says 'as per UNCLOS'.
Omitting "or energy" and "or is likely to result" - the two phrases that make the definition wide.
Writing about the maritime zones. They are not asked for here, and article 192 is precisely not zone-limited.
Treating the coastal State as the only enforcement actor. There are three, and the flag State's duty is primary.
Missing the 207 against 211 discrimination between land-based and vessel-source rule-making.
Naming the wrong three tiers - for example putting Bunkers 2001 in as a tier. It is a separate, single-tier regime.
Saying the Fund is financed by governments or by shipowners. It is financed by receivers of contributing oil.
Forgetting that tier three is optional, so the same casualty attracts different compensation in different States.
Quoting monetary limits.
Answering only 'who pays' and never 'the source of the funds' - the stem asks for both, and they are different questions for tiers two and three.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Is underwater noise pollution under UNCLOS?" Yes - the definition covers substances or energy.
"Must damage have occurred?" No - 'results or is likely to result'.
"Is a natural oil seep pollution?" No - the introduction must be by man, directly or indirectly.
"Can India apply its own construction standards to a foreign ship in innocent passage?" No - vessel-source rules must be adopted through IMO and must not hamper innocent passage.
"Who may prosecute a discharge on the high seas?" The flag State always; and a port State where the ship comes voluntarily into its port.
"Who is liable under CLC?" The registered owner, strictly, with liability channelled to him - not the master, crew, charterer or salvor.
"When does the owner lose the right to limit?" His own personal act or omission, with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result.
"Who funds the IOPC Fund?" Receivers of contributing oil - the cargo interest - not shipowners and not governments.
"Your ship's bunkers pollute a beach. Which tier?" None of them - that is the Bunkers Convention 2001, a separate single-tier regime with no fund behind it.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which certificate on your ship proves compulsory insurance for oil pollution, and who checks it?
Your ship is a bulk carrier. Which liability regime covers a fuel oil spill from her?
What is 'channelling of liability' and why does it matter to you personally?
Give me an example of pollution by energy rather than by substance.
If a coastal State detained your ship after a discharge in its EEZ, what would it have to establish?
Who ultimately pays for a very large tanker spill?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb A - define, then duty, then rules, then enforcement. DEFINE (1): by man, directly or indirectly, substances or energy, results or is likely to result, five effects. DUTY (2): 192 free-standing, 193 sovereignty qualified, 194 best practicable means. RULES (3): 207 take into account, 211 through IMO and no less effective. ENFORCEMENT (4): 217 flag, 218 port, 220 coastal graded, 221 casualty, 235 compensation. Limb B - why, then one, then two and three, then what is outside. WHY (5): ship pays first, cargo pays after. ONE (6): owner strictly liable, insurer pays, direct action. TWO AND THREE (7): the Funds, financed by receivers of contributing oil; three is optional. OUTSIDE (8): bunkers, HNS, and geography.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: Limb A is the strongest evidential position on this paper and limb B is the weakest, and the contrast is worth stating. UNCLOS has been in force since 16 November 1994 and is unamended, so the text MIW holds is the text a candidate sat this examination on. There is no reversal of any kind to perform, and the definition and articles 192, 193, 194 and 235 were read verbatim at source for this answer. The remaining Part XII articles are cited by identity, with their substance carried from MIW's own verification of the same held text; and the Part XII safeguards at section 7 are referred to only in general terms, their individual articles not having been read.

By contrast, MIW holds no text of any of the three compensation instruments. Accordingly no convention text is quoted, no article number is asserted for any of the three, and NO MONETARY OR SPECIAL DRAWING RIGHT FIGURE APPEARS ANYWHERE - not a tonnage-band limit, not a fund ceiling, and not the contributing-oil threshold quantity. That is deliberate rather than evasive. The tonnage-band limits and the fund ceilings are amended by tacit acceptance, so every figure carries a date with it, and a figure learned for one year is wrong for another. Check the current values against the IOPC Funds' own published tables before quoting any of them in an answer. The architecture is what is stable, and the architecture is what the question asks for.

That discipline is right on the merits and not merely as a matter of evidence. The limitation amounts and fund ceilings are amended by tacit acceptance over time, so every figure carries a date with it, and a figure carried from a later source into a March 2023 answer would be wrong twice over. The architecture - strict limited liability on the registered owner, then the cargo interest twice - does not move, and it is what the printed limb actually asks about.

No list of parties is given and no claim is made about which States have opted into the third tier, because membership changes continuously. No claim is made about any State's declared maritime zones, including India's. The Indian statute giving effect to these conventions at this sitting is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; the 2025 Act is three years after this examination and is not cited.

DUTY (2): 192 free-standing, 193 sovereignty qualified, 194 best practicable means. RULES (3): 207 take into account, 211 through IMO and no less effective. questions.understand_first: Two quite different things are being asked, and the second one exists because of the first. Start with the definition, because it is much wider than an engineer's instinct. The Convention does not say pollution is oil in the water. It says it is the introduction by man - so a natural seep does not count - of substances or energy into the sea, which results or is likely to result in harm. Two things in that are easy to miss and both earn marks. Energy means heat and noise are pollution, with nothing spilt at all. And likely to result means nothing has to have gone wrong yet - which is precisely what allows the Convention to require States to prevent rather than merely to clean up. Then the obligations. The rest of UNCLOS is a map: it divides the sea into zones and says who may do what in each. Part XII is different, because the duty to protect the marine environment is not attached to a zone at all - it simply exists, everywhere, and it even qualifies a State's right to exploit its own resources. What a coastal State must actually do splits in two. It must make rules, and how much freedom it has depends on the source: for pollution from the land, which is its own business, it has wide discretion; for pollution from ships, which is everyone's business, it must work through IMO and may not set a lower standard than the international one. And it must enforce - but it is one of three enforcers, alongside the flag State, whose duty is primary, and the port State, which can prosecute a discharge that happened on the other side of an ocean. The last article of Part XII is the one that hands over to the second half of the question: States must make sure that somebody who suffers pollution damage can actually get paid. And the three tiers are how the world arranged that for oil. A tanker spill can cost more than any owner could ever insure, so the owner is made liable without proof of fault but only up to a limit, and everything above that comes from the industry that wanted the oil shipped in the first place - collected from the refineries and terminals that receive it. Ship first, cargo afterwards. That is the whole idea.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Limb A - the definition, UNCLOS article 1(1)(4). The introduction BY MAN, directly or indirectly, of SUBSTANCES OR ENERGY into the marine environment, including estuaries, which RESULTS OR IS LIKELY TO RESULT in such deleterious effects as harm to living resources and marine life, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine activities including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea, impairment of quality for use of sea water, and reduction of amenities. Energy = heat, noise, radiation. No damage need have occurred. Obligations. 192 - the duty to protect and preserve is free-standing and not zone-limited. 193 - the sovereign right to exploit is subject to it. 194 - all necessary measures from any source, by the best practicable means and in accordance with capabilities; no damage to other States; no transferring damage or transforming one type of pollution into another. Rule-making: 207 land-based, take international rules into account; 210 dumping, express prior approval; 211 vessels, act through IMO and national law must be no less effective; 212 atmosphere. Enforcement three ways: 217 flag State wherever the violation occurs; 218 port State for discharges outside its waters where the ship is voluntarily in port; 220 coastal State in territorial sea or EEZ, graded from information to inspection to detention on clear objective evidence of major damage; 221 measures after a casualty beyond the territorial sea; 235 responsibility, liability and recourse for prompt and adequate compensation. Limb B - the three tiers. ONE: CLC 1992 - the registered owner, strictly liable, liability channelled to him; compulsory insurance with a certificate on board and direct action against the insurer; limitation by tonnage, lost for his personal act with intent or recklessness. Source: the shipowner and his P&I club. TWO: 1992 IOPC Fund, where tier one gives nothing or is inadequate. THREE: Supplementary Fund (2003 Protocol), where tier two is insufficient - and it is optional. Source for both: contributions from RECEIVERS OF CONTRIBUTING OIL received by sea above a threshold quantity - the CARGO INTEREST, not shipowners and not governments. Bunker oil from a non-tanker is NOT one of the tiers - that is the Bunkers Convention 2001, single tier, no fund. Quote no monetary figures.
critical_numbers: UNCLOS in force 16 November 1994 and UNAMENDED - the held text is the sitting text
The definition is at article 1, paragraph 1(4), and lists FIVE deleterious effects
Enforcement is divided THREE ways - flag State 217, port State 218, coastal State 220
THREE tiers: CLC 1992, Fund Convention 1992, Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003
NO MONETARY OR SPECIAL DRAWING RIGHT FIGURE IS QUOTED ANYWHERE - the limits are amended by tacit acceptance and MIW holds no text of the three instruments
quick_revision.critical_regulation: UNCLOS article 1(1)(4): pollution of the marine environment means the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results or is likely to result in such deleterious effects as harm to living resources and marine life, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine activities including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea, impairment of quality for use of sea water and reduction of amenities. And article 235(2): States shall ensure that recourse is available in accordance with their legal systems for prompt and adequate compensation or other relief in respect of damage caused by pollution of the marine environment by natural or juridical persons under their jurisdiction - which is the obligation that the three-tier compensation regime discharges for oil.
quick_revision.major_trap: Writing about the maritime zones instead of about the obligations. The zones are not asked for, and article 192 is precisely not zone-limited - introducing them works against the point limb A is making. Second trap: paraphrasing the definition loosely and losing 'or energy' and 'or is likely to result', which are the two phrases that make it wide. Third: treating the coastal State as the only enforcement actor, when there are three and the flag State's duty is primary. Fourth, and the biggest on limb B: saying the Funds are financed by shipowners or by governments. They are financed by receivers of contributing oil - the cargo interest. Fifth: naming the Bunkers Convention 2001 as one of the three tiers; it is a separate, single-tier regime with no fund behind it. Sixth: forgetting that tier three is optional, so the same casualty attracts different compensation in different States. Seventh: quoting monetary limits, which are amended by tacit acceptance and therefore carry a date.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the UNCLOS pollution and compensation tiers question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb A: 1 the definition and the four elements that make it wide. 2 the general obligation - articles 192, 193, 194. 3 coastal-State rule-making, source by source. 4 enforcement three ways, closing on article 235 as the bridge. Limb B: 5 why the regime is layered. 6 tier one, the owner and his insurer. 7 tiers two and three, the Funds and the cargo levy. 8 what falls outside.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem contains five separate instructions and the commonest failure is to answer fewer than five.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define pollution of the marine environment as per UNCLOS.
retrieval_cards.answer: The introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results or is likely to result in such deleterious effects as harm to living resources and marine life, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine activities including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea, impairment of quality for use of sea water, and reduction of amenities. Article 1(1)(4).
retrieval_cards.why: The stem says 'as per UNCLOS', so the Convention's own words are the answer and a loose paraphrase loses the easiest marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is underwater noise pollution? Must damage have occurred?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes to the first: the definition covers the introduction of substances or energy, so heat, noise and radiation are all within it without any substance being discharged. No to the second: the phrase is 'results or is likely to result', so likelihood of a deleterious effect is enough - which is what allows the Convention to support preventive obligations rather than only remedial ones.
retrieval_cards.why: The two phrases that make the definition wide, and the two most often dropped in a paraphrase.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes the article 192 obligation unusual?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is free-standing and not confined to any zone - the rest of the Convention allocates rights zone by zone, while article 192 imposes a duty across all of them. Article 193 then makes the sovereign right to exploit natural resources expressly subject to that duty, and article 194 supplies the standard: all necessary measures against pollution from any source, by the best practicable means and in accordance with capabilities.
retrieval_cards.why: Three propositions that answer the 'key features of obligations' half of limb A.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the coastal State's rule-making duty differ between land-based and vessel-source pollution?
retrieval_cards.answer: For land-based sources (article 207) it adopts national law taking international rules into account - wide discretion. For pollution from vessels (article 211) it must act through the competent international organization, and its national law must have at least the same effect as the generally accepted international rules. So a coastal State may be stricter than the international standard for its own ships, may not be laxer, and may not impose its own construction standards on foreign ships in innocent passage.
retrieval_cards.why: This single discrimination explains the entire architecture of ship-source pollution regulation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who enforces Part XII, and what may a coastal State actually do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Three actors. The flag State (217) - compliance by its ships wherever the violation occurs, and its duty is primary. The port State (218) - where the ship is voluntarily in port, proceedings for discharges outside its own waters. The coastal State (220) - violations in its territorial sea or EEZ, with graded powers: require information, then physical inspection, then detention and proceedings on clear objective evidence of a discharge causing or threatening major damage. Article 221 adds measures beyond the territorial sea after a casualty.
retrieval_cards.why: Treating the coastal State as the only enforcer misses the structure the question is testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three tiers and, for each, who pays.
retrieval_cards.answer: Tier one - CLC 1992: the registered owner, strictly liable, and in practice his liability insurer, with compulsory insurance and a right of direct action. Tier two - the 1992 IOPC Fund, where tier one gives nothing or is inadequate. Tier three - the Supplementary Fund under the 2003 Protocol, where tier two is insufficient - and it is optional for States.
retrieval_cards.why: The limb asks for the tiers and for who pays in each case; both must be answered explicitly.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does the money in the two Funds actually come from?
retrieval_cards.answer: From contributions levied on the receivers of contributing oil - crude oil and heavy fuel oil received by sea in the territory of a Member State above a threshold quantity in a calendar year. The cargo interest pays - refineries and terminals - not shipowners and not governments. Tier three uses the same mechanism but levies only in States that have opted into the Protocol.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for the source of the funds, and this is the point most candidates get wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is channelling of liability, and when does the owner lose the right to limit?
retrieval_cards.answer: Channelling means liability is directed to the registered owner alone, so claims may not ordinarily be brought against the master, crew, pilot, charterer, manager or salvor - which is why the Chief Engineer is not personally exposed. The owner loses the right to limit where the damage resulted from his own personal act or omission, committed with intent to cause such damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result - a deliberately very high threshold.
retrieval_cards.why: Channelling is what protects you personally, and the loss-of-limitation test is a standard oral question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your bulk carrier spills fuel oil on a beach. Which tier responds?
retrieval_cards.answer: None of the three. The three-tier regime covers persistent oil carried in bulk as cargo - the tanker case. Bunker oil from a non-tanker falls under the Bunkers Convention 2001, which is a single tier: liability on the shipowner in a wider sense, backed by compulsory insurance and limitation under the general limitation convention, with no fund behind it.
retrieval_cards.why: The clearest available boundary of the regime, and the discrimination that separates this question from the Bunkers-versus-CLC ones.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The tier ceilings of CLC 1992, the Fund Convention 1992 and the Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003, and the contributing-oil threshold quantity.
reverify_before_publication.why: NO MONETARY OR SPECIAL DRAWING RIGHT FIGURE IS ASSERTED ANYWHERE IN THIS ANSWER, and none may be added without the date it belongs to. MIW holds no text of any of the three instruments - only verified status facts and status placeholders - and the corpus family log expressly declines to assert the limits. The ceilings are also amended by tacit acceptance over time, so a figure is a currency risk as well as an evidential one. Verify against the official compensation tables, AS AT MARCH 2023, before publication.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The architecture of the three-tier regime - strict channelled liability on the registered owner with compulsory insurance and direct action, then the 1992 Fund, then the Supplementary Fund, both financed by receivers of contributing oil.
reverify_before_publication.why: Carried as authoritative secondary. NO TEXT OF ANY OF THE THREE INSTRUMENTS IS HELD BY MIW, so NO ARTICLE NUMBER IS ASSERTED and no wording is quoted. The architecture is stable and is what the printed limb asks about, but it should be confirmed against the instruments themselves before publication, and no article reference should be added until they have been read.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The Part XII articles other than 1(1)(4), 192, 193, 194 and 235.
reverify_before_publication.why: Articles 207, 210, 211, 212, 217, 218, 220 and 221 are cited by identity, with their substance carried from MIW's own verification record for QP2309-Q8 where it was established against the same held text. The Part XII SECTION 7 SAFEGUARDS are referred to in general terms only and their individual articles were NOT read in this session - a limitation inherited from that record and restated here rather than dropped.

blocks.h: 1. What decarbonisation means in shipping

blocks.p: Decarbonisation is the progressive reduction, towards elimination, of the greenhouse gas emissions arising from the operation of ships - principally carbon dioxide from the combustion of fossil fuel, together with methane and nitrous oxide, and increasingly assessed across the whole life cycle of the fuel rather than only at the funnel.
Three distinctions belong at the start, because they decide what the rest of the answer is about:

ul: It is a climate measure, not an air-quality measure. Sulphur oxides, nitrogen oxides and particulate matter are local pollutants - they harm the place they are emitted. Carbon dioxide is a global problem and is harmless to breathe. That is why the two are regulated on entirely different principles, and why an emission control area makes sense for one and not for the other.

Carbon dioxide cannot be scrubbed out at the funnel in the way sulphur can. It is the intended product of burning a carbon fuel. So the only routes are to burn less fuel, to burn a fuel with less carbon in it, or to burn none at all - and that is the whole of the subject.

It is therefore an efficiency problem before it is a fuel problem. Every tonne of fuel not burned is an emission that requires no new technology, no new bunkering infrastructure and no new safety regime. The two short-term measures in this question both attack efficiency, and neither touches the fuel.

blocks.p: It is worth adding one sentence of scope. International shipping was excluded from the national commitments of the climate treaties, because emissions from a ship built in one country, owned in a second, flagged in a third and trading between a fourth and a fifth cannot sensibly be allocated to any of them. That is why IMO, rather than any national government, carries the mandate - and it is why the instruments in this answer are IMO instruments.

blocks.h: 2. The instrument that frames it at this sitting

blocks.p: IMO's decarbonisation policy is set out in a Strategy, which is not itself binding but which drives everything that becomes binding. The operative instrument at this sitting is the Initial IMO Strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships, resolution MEPC.304(72), adopted in 2018.
Two points about it are worth making explicitly, because they are what a strong answer knows:

ul: It is a strategy, not a regulation. Nothing in it binds a ship. What binds a ship is what is subsequently written into MARPOL Annex VI as a result of it - which is exactly what the two short-term measures in this question are.

It carries its own programme of follow-up actions, dividing candidate measures into short-term, mid-term and long-term. That programme is the 'pathway' the stem asks about, and it is the reason the two measures exist at all.

blocks.p: The relationship is confirmed by the measures' own founding instrument: the resolution that introduced EEXI and CII into Annex VI expressly recalls the Committee's adoption of the Initial Strategy in its preamble. The two short-term measures are, in terms, delivered under that Strategy.

blocks.h: 3. The levels of ambition

blocks.p: The Initial Strategy sets out three levels of ambition, all measured against a 2008 baseline. They should be given as three, and in this order:

headers: What kind of target it is
rows: One - peaking
GHG emissions from international shipping should peak as soon as possible, and be reduced thereafter
A turning point, with no date attached
Two - carbon intensity
The CO2 emissions per transport work of international shipping should fall by at least 40 per cent by 2030, pursuing efforts towards 70 per cent by 2050
Relative - per unit of work done, so it improves even if the fleet grows
Three - total GHG
Total annual GHG emissions from international shipping should be at least 50 per cent lower by 2050
Absolute - the actual tonnage emitted, whatever the fleet does

blocks.p: The Strategy also expresses the ambition to phase out GHG emissions from international shipping as soon as possible in this century, and states that its levels are to be pursued in a manner consistent with the temperature goals of the Paris Agreement.

The distinction between the second and third levels carries a mark on its own and is where most candidates are vague. Carbon intensity is a ratio and total emissions are a quantity. A fleet that becomes forty per cent more efficient per tonne-mile while carrying seventy per cent more cargo has met the second ambition and gone backwards on the third. Both are needed precisely because neither implies the other, and it is the reason the two short-term measures - which are both intensity measures - are described as a first step and not as an answer.

blocks.h: 4. The pathway - short-term, mid-term and long-term

blocks.p: The Strategy's programme of follow-up actions divides candidate measures into three phases. At this sitting the short-term measures are the only ones that have become law; the mid-term and long-term measures are candidate measures under consideration, and describing them as anything more would be wrong.

rows: Short-term
Agreed and in force. Technical and operational, applying to the existing fleet burning existing fuels
Strengthening the design index for new ships; the fuel oil consumption data collection system; and, as the two measures this question asks about, EEXI and CII with the enhanced SEEMP
Mid-term
Candidate measures under consideration. Nothing adopted

An implementation programme for the uptake of alternative low-carbon and zero-carbon fuels; further operational energy efficiency measures; new and innovative emission reduction mechanisms, possibly including market-based measures; research and development; technical cooperation and capacity building; and a feedback mechanism
Long-term
Directional. Beyond 2030
Pursuit of the development and provision of zero-carbon or fossil-free fuels, and encouragement of other new and innovative emission reduction mechanisms

blocks.p: Two supporting principles run through the whole programme and are worth naming: no more favourable treatment, so that measures apply to all ships regardless of flag; and the recognition of the impacts on States, particularly developing countries, small island developing States and least developed countries, which is assessed before a measure is adopted.

The honest position at March 2023 is that the mid-term measures are the argument, not the answer. Whether the emission reduction mechanism becomes a levy, a trading scheme, a fuel standard or some combination was, at this sitting, unresolved - and a candidate who says so is more accurate than one who describes a mechanism as settled.

blocks.h: 5. The first short-term measure - the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index

blocks.p: Both short-term measures were introduced into MARPOL Annex VI by resolution MEPC.328(76), which entered into force on 1 November 2022, with the requirements applying from 1 January 2023 - ten weeks before this examination. They are the first mandatory greenhouse gas measures ever applied to the existing fleet.

rows: What kind of measure
Technical, one-off, design-based. It extends to existing ships the discipline that the design index already imposed on new ones
What it measures

The ship's theoretical CO2 output per tonne-mile at a reference condition, computed from installed power, specific fuel consumption, deadweight and reference speed. It is a calculation, not a measurement of the ship in service
The test

The attained EEXI must not exceed the required EEXI, which is derived from the design-index reference line for the ship type and size with a reduction factor applied. No factor is quoted here - they are type and size specific
Who it applies to
Existing ships of and above the applicable size, in the ship types the design index covers - broadly the cargo-carrying fleet
When it is demonstrated
Once, at the first periodical survey on or after 1 January 2023, and endorsed on the International Energy Efficiency Certificate. Having passed, a ship does not repeat it

blocks.p: How a ship actually complies is the practical heart of the measure, and there are three routes:

ol: Limit the power. By far the commonest route, because it is the cheapest. Engine power limitation or shaft power limitation caps the maximum power available, which lowers the reference speed and therefore the attained index. The limitation must be verifiable and sealed, and it is accompanied by an overridable power reserve that the master may release in circumstances where the ship's safety requires full power - which is the provision every engineer should know about, and which must be recorded when used.

Improve the ship technically. Energy-saving devices, propeller and hull-form modification, waste heat recovery, hull coatings, air lubrication. Effective and expensive, and generally justified only where the ship has years of trading life ahead of her.
Change the fuel to one with a lower carbon factor, which changes the calculation directly.

blocks.p: The obvious criticism should be stated rather than avoided, because it is what an examiner is probing for. EEXI is a theoretical index calculated at a reference condition. A ship may pass it by limiting her power and then be operated inefficiently, and a ship may fail it while being operated extremely well. It says what the ship is capable of, not what she does. That gap is precisely why the second measure exists.

blocks.h: 6. The second short-term measure - the Carbon Intensity Indicator

rows: What kind of measure
Operational, annual, continuing. It measures what the ship actually did in the year
What it measures
The attained annual operational carbon intensity - the CO2 emitted in the calendar year, derived from the fuel actually consumed, divided by the ship's capacity and the distance actually sailed
Where the data comes from
The IMO fuel oil consumption data collection system, which the fleet had already been reporting into. The data existed before the measure did - which is why it could be introduced quickly
The test
The attained CII is compared with a required CII, obtained from a reference line for the ship type and size with an annual reduction factor that tightens each year
The result
A rating from A to E, A being the best. The rating is documented and is visible - to charterers, to financiers and to cargo interests, which is a large part of how the measure is expected to bite
Who it applies to
Cargo and cruise ships of and above the applicable size - a higher threshold than EEXI, so a ship may be caught by one and not the other
The consequence of a poor rating

A ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E for one year, must develop a plan of corrective actions in the SEEMP, which must be approved. This is the enforcement mechanism, and it is the reason the SEEMP was enhanced

blocks.p: The SEEMP is the third component and is not optional. From the same date, an enhanced Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan is required to contain the ship's implementation plan for achieving the required CII, the methodology for calculating and reporting the attained value, and, where the rating requires it, the plan of corrective actions. It is subject to verification, which is what converts the SEEMP from a document into a requirement.

How a ship actually improves her rating: speed optimisation and voyage planning - which dominates everything else, because the relationship between speed and power is steep; hull and propeller cleaning and coating condition; trim and draught optimisation; weather routeing; efficient port operations and reduced waiting at anchor; and use of shore power where it is available. The single most powerful lever an operator has is speed, and it costs nothing to install.

And the criticisms of the CII should be stated too, because they were live at this sitting. The metric divides by capacity and distance rather than by cargo actually carried, so a ship can improve her rating by sailing further, and a ship waiting fully loaded at anchor is penalised while a ship steaming empty is not. Certain trades - short sea, offshore support, ships with long idle periods - are treated poorly by a metric designed around laden voyages. The regulation itself provides for the arrangement to be reviewed, which is the correct answer to the criticism: it is a first attempt, and it is designed to be corrected.

blocks.h: 7. The guidelines that make the two measures operable

blocks.p: The stem asks for the measures with their guidelines, and this is where a strong answer separates itself, because the regulation does not contain the arithmetic. The guidelines carry it, and without them neither measure could be applied to a single ship.
For the CII, the set is known as G1 to G5, and all five were in place at this sitting:

rows: The method of calculating the attained annual operational CII - what counts as fuel, capacity and distance
The reference lines against which each ship type and size is measured
The reduction factors, which tighten the required value year by year
The rating boundaries - where A ends and B begins, and so on
The interim correction factors and voyage adjustments - what a ship may legitimately deduct from the CII calculation, and for which ship types and voyage conditions

blocks.p: For the EEXI, a corresponding set governs the method of calculating the attained EEXI, the survey and certification of it, and the limitation of shaft or engine power including the operation and recording of the overridable power reserve. Those guidelines are named here by function rather than by resolution number, deliberately: their numbers were not established for this answer and inventing one to match the symmetry of the CII table would be worse than leaving the gap visible.

And the SEEMP guidelines operative at this sitting are the 2022 set, resolution MEPC.346(78), which govern the content and verification of the enhanced plan. A later edition exists; it is not this one, and a candidate answering for this year should not reach for it.

The general point is worth stating in the answer: IMO regulates by putting the requirement in the Annex and the method in a guideline, so that the arithmetic can be revised as experience accumulates without amending the Convention. Recognising that structure is worth more than memorising the resolution numbers.

blocks.h: 8. What the two measures do and do not achieve

blocks.p: The stem's opening asks what decarbonisation is, so the answer should close by saying honestly where these measures sit within it.

ul: They are the first mandatory GHG measures applied to the existing fleet, and that is a genuine achievement. Everything before them applied to ships not yet built.

They are both intensity measures. They improve emissions per unit of transport work. Neither caps the total tonnage emitted, and the third level of ambition is an absolute one - so on the Strategy's own terms these two measures cannot deliver it.

They do not touch the fuel. They make a ship burning fossil fuel burn less of it. Decarbonisation in the full sense requires fuels that are not carbon-based, and that belongs to the mid-term and long-term measures.

They are administratively light and were achievable quickly, which is why they came first: the data collection system already existed, and the design index already existed. That is also their limitation - they are what could be agreed, rather than what would be sufficient.

They shift commercial pressure onto the operator. A published rating changes chartering behaviour faster than a regulation changes engineering, and much of the intended effect is expected to arrive through the charter market rather than through enforcement.

blocks.p: The fair conclusion at this sitting is that the short-term measures are a floor and not a destination. They were adopted under a Strategy that was itself under revision, they are explicitly subject to review, and the decisive questions - what the mid-term measure will be, and where zero-carbon fuel will come from - remained open. An answer that says so, and says why, is a better answer than one that presents the two measures as the solution to the problem the stem opened with.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Three instructions in one stem, and they are of different sizes. Define decarbonisation - a short paragraph. Discuss the ambitions and pathways with focus on short, mid and long-term goals - about a third of the answer. Explain the two short-term measures with their guidelines - about half. The last two words of the stem are the ones candidates skip, and they are worth real marks: the guidelines are where the arithmetic lives.
Note also that the stem prints "long tern goals". It is a printing error for 'long term' and is reproduced as printed in the transcribed question. Nothing turns on it.

blocks.h: Open with the three distinctions

ul: Climate, not air quality. SOx, NOx and particulates are local; CO2 is global. Different problems, different regulatory logic - which is why there are emission control areas for one and not for the other.
CO2 cannot be scrubbed out. It is the intended product of burning carbon. So: burn less, burn less carbon, or burn none. That sentence is the whole subject.
Efficiency before fuel. Fuel not burned needs no new technology and no new infrastructure - which is exactly why the two short-term measures are both efficiency measures.

blocks.h: The three levels of ambition, and the distinction inside them

ol: Peak GHG emissions from international shipping as soon as possible.
Carbon intensity - CO2 per transport work - down at least 40 per cent by 2030, pursuing 70 per cent by 2050.
Total annual GHG down at least 50 per cent by 2050.

blocks.p: All against a 2008 baseline, with phase-out as soon as possible in this century, consistent with the Paris temperature goals. And the distinction that earns the mark: level two is a RATIO, level three is a QUANTITY. A fleet can meet the intensity ambition and go backwards on the absolute one by simply carrying more. That is why both exist - and it is why the two short-term measures, which are both intensity measures, cannot deliver the third ambition.

blocks.h: The pathway - and the word that keeps it accurate

blocks.p: Short-term = agreed and in force. Mid-term and long-term = CANDIDATE MEASURES under consideration. Use the word 'candidate' and the whole limb becomes accurate. Mid-term: an implementation programme for alternative low-carbon and zero-carbon fuels; further operational efficiency measures; new and innovative emission reduction mechanisms, possibly including market-based measures; research and development; capacity building. Long-term: zero-carbon or fossil-free fuels, and further innovative mechanisms. Add the two running principles: no more favourable treatment, and assessment of impacts on States.

blocks.h: The two measures in one comparison

rows: Type
Technical, design-based
Operational
Frequency
One-off - pass it once

What it tells you
What the ship could do
What the ship actually did

Calculated from design particulars at a reference condition

blocks.p: The sentence that ties them together: EEXI says what the ship is capable of; CII says what she does. The second exists because the first can be passed and then ignored.

blocks.h: The guidelines - the part most candidates omit

blocks.p: The regulation states the requirement; the guidelines carry the arithmetic. For the CII the set runs G1 to G5: G1 calculation method, G2 reference lines, G3 reduction factors, G4 rating boundaries, G5 correction factors and voyage adjustments. If you can name the five functions you have the mark, whether or not you can recite the resolution numbers. For the EEXI there is a corresponding set on calculation, survey and certification, and shaft or engine power limitation. And the enhanced SEEMP has its own guidelines governing content and verification.

Say why it is structured that way: the requirement goes in the Annex and the method goes in a guideline, so that the arithmetic can be revised without amending the Convention. That is a structural insight and it is worth more than the numbers.

blocks.h: The criticisms - state them, do not avoid them

ul: EEXI is theoretical. A ship can pass it by limiting power and then be run badly. It measures capability, not conduct.
CII divides by capacity and distance, not by cargo carried. So sailing further can improve the rating, and a fully loaded ship waiting at anchor is penalised while an empty ship steaming is not.
Certain trades are treated poorly - short sea, offshore, ships with long idle periods.
Both are intensity measures, so neither caps total emissions - which is the Strategy's own third ambition.
Neither touches the fuel.
And the fair answer to all of it: the arrangement is expressly subject to review. It is a first attempt designed to be corrected.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Treating CO2 like SOx - proposing a scrubber, or an emission control area for carbon.
Giving two levels of ambition instead of three, or omitting the 2008 baseline.
Confusing the intensity ambition with the absolute one. They are a ratio and a quantity.
Describing mid-term measures as though they were adopted. They are candidate measures.
Naming the wrong two short-term measures - EEDI is the measure for new ships and was already there; the two asked for are EEXI and CII.
Saying EEXI is calculated annually. It is one-off.
Saying CII is a design calculation. It is operational, from actual fuel and actual distance.
Forgetting the D-three-years-or-E-once trigger, which is the whole enforcement mechanism.
Forgetting the SEEMP, which is where the corrective action plan lives.
Ignoring the guidelines, when the stem asks for them in terms.
Quoting reduction factors, reference-line values or rating boundaries as though they were general - they are ship-type and size specific.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Can you scrub CO2 out of your exhaust the way you do sulphur?" No - it is the intended product of combustion. Burn less, burn less carbon, or burn none.
"Which two short-term measures?" EEXI and CII - not EEDI, which applies to new ships and came earlier.
"How often do you calculate your EEXI?" Once. It is demonstrated at a survey and endorsed on the certificate.
"Your ship is rated E. What happens?" A plan of corrective actions in the SEEMP, which must be approved. Also D for three consecutive years.
"You limited engine power for EEXI. What if you need full power in heavy weather?" The overridable power reserve may be released where the ship's safety requires it - and its use must be recorded.
"What is the fastest way to improve your CII?" Speed. The relationship between speed and power is steep, and it costs nothing to install.
"Does CII measure cargo carried?" No - it divides by capacity and distance, which is the metric's principal criticism.
"Will these two measures achieve the total-emissions ambition?" No - both are intensity measures, and the third level of ambition is absolute.
"Where do the reduction factors and rating boundaries come from?" The guidelines, not the regulation - which is what lets them be revised without amending the Convention.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: What is your ship's CII rating this year, and what did you do about it?
Show me your SEEMP and tell me what is in each part of it.
How was your EEXI compliance achieved, and is there a power limitation fitted?
How is your fuel consumption data collected and reported, and by whom is it verified?
What would you tell the charterer who wants an extra half knot?
What difference does a foul hull make to your carbon intensity, and how would you show it?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Define, frame, three ambitions, three phases, two measures, five guidelines. DEFINE (1): climate not air quality; burn less, less carbon, or none. FRAME (2): the Initial Strategy - a strategy binds nobody; the Annex does. AMBITIONS (3): peak; intensity -40% by 2030 pursuing -70% by 2050; total GHG -50% by 2050, all on 2008. PHASES (4): short-term in force, mid and long-term candidates. MEASURES: EEXI technical and one-off - what she could do (5); CII operational and annual, rated A to E - what she did (6). GUIDELINES (7): calculation, reference lines, reduction factors, rating boundaries, corrective action. LIMITS (8): both are intensity measures, and neither touches the fuel.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: This is the most date-sensitive question on the paper, and almost everything a reader will recognise from later material is wrong for it. IMO adopted a revised greenhouse gas strategy four months after this examination, and that revision replaced the levels of ambition wholesale - introducing a net-zero formulation, intermediate checkpoints for 2030 and 2040, and a vocabulary that did not exist at this sitting. None of it appears in this answer, and none of it may be added. The instrument in force here is the Initial Strategy of 2018, and its three levels of ambition are the ones stated. A reviewer reading this after July 2023 must not 'update' it.

MIW holds no copy of the Initial Strategy itself, and the way round that is worth knowing because it is a technique you can use. The resolution that introduced the two short-term measures into MARPOL Annex VI - MEPC.328(76) - expressly recalls, in its preamble, the Committee's adoption of the Initial Strategy. So the Strategy's identity, and its relationship to the two measures, are established from the instrument that created them: an IMO resolution's preamble names the policy it is delivering, which is the strongest evidence available that the two sit together at this date. The levels of ambition themselves are stated as the Strategy's levels and are not attributed to any numbered paragraph, because the document was not read directly.

The entry-into-force date is the single fact this whole question stands on, and it was taken from the resolution itself. Resolution MEPC.328(76) records deemed acceptance on 1 May 2022 at its operative paragraph 2 and entry into force on 1 NOVEMBER 2022 at its operative paragraph 3, with the requirements applying from 1 January 2023. Secondary summaries of this amendment circulate with the year wrong; if a date a year later is met anywhere, it would place both measures after this examination and make the question unanswerable, which is the quickest way to know it is wrong. Go to the resolution's operative paragraphs.

Two instruments are easy to get the wrong way round at this sitting. The 2022 SEEMP guidelines, MEPC.346(78), are the operative set here even though a later edition exists; their 2024 replacement is two years future and must not be substituted. And no provision of MARPOL Annex VI is quoted anywhere: MIW's licensed copy may be cited but not reproduced, so the measures are described in substance. No numeric reduction factor, reference-line value or rating boundary is asserted anywhere, all being ship-type and size specific; the EEXI guidelines are named by function only because their resolution numbers were not established for this answer, and inventing one to match the CII table would have been worse than showing the gap.

THE SINGLE SHARPEST TRAP: RESOLUTION MEPC.377(80), THE 2023 IMO GHG STRATEGY, WAS ADOPTED ON 7 JULY 2023 - FOUR MONTHS AFTER THIS EXAMINATION. IT APPEARS NOWHERE IN THIS OBJECT. The corpus HOLDS it and marks it current, which is exactly inverted for a March 2023 paper; direction was checked on every consumption. Removed with it: net-zero 'by or around 2050'; the 20 per cent striving 30 per cent by 2030 and 70 per cent striving 80 per cent by 2040 checkpoints; and the term 'indicative checkpoints', which had not been coined at this sitting and does not appear.

THE OPERATIVE POLICY INSTRUMENT IS THE INITIAL IMO STRATEGY, RESOLUTION MEPC.304(72) OF 2018, and its three levels of ambition are stated: peak as soon as possible; carbon intensity at least 40 per cent lower by 2030 pursuing 70 per cent by 2050; and total annual GHG at least 50 per cent lower by 2050, all against 2008.

THE IDENTITY OF THE INITIAL STRATEGY IS PRIMARY-VERIFIED FROM THE MEASURES' OWN FOUNDING INSTRUMENT, WHICH IS THE STRONGEST TEMPORAL ANCHOR AVAILABLE ON THIS QUESTION. The preamble to MEPC.328(76) RECALLS FURTHER that the Committee at its seventy-second session adopted resolution MEPC.304(72) on the Initial IMO Strategy. That was read at source in this session. The instrument that created EEXI and CII names the Initial Strategy as the frame they sit under, and at March 2023 that relationship is current.

MEPC.304(72) IS NOT HELD AS A DOCUMENT. Its identity is primary-verified as above; its SUBSTANTIVE LEVELS are graded P2 authoritative secondary, stated as the Strategy's levels of ambition, NOT attributed to a quoted paragraph, and flagged in reverify_before_publication.

THE CORPUS AMENDMENT REGISTER IS WRONG BY ONE YEAR ON THE INSTRUMENT THIS QUESTION DEPENDS ON, AND THE ERROR WOULD HAVE MADE THE QUESTION UNANSWERABLE. It records MEPC.328(76) as entering into force 2023-11-01. THE RESOLUTION'S OWN OPERATIVE PARAGRAPHS WERE READ AT SOURCE: paragraph 2, deemed acceptance 1 MAY 2022; paragraph 3, entry into force 1 NOVEMBER 2022. Taken at face value the register would put both short-term measures eight months after this examination. The defect is raised as a TRUE_SOURCE_CORRECTION_REQUEST in the anchor at section 2.3 and NOTHING WAS WRITTEN BACK TO THE CORPUS FROM THIS BRANCH.

THE TWO SHORT-TERM MEASURES ARE THE STABLE CORE AND ARE SQUARELY OPERATIVE. EEXI and CII were introduced by MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022, with the requirements applying from 1 January 2023 - ten weeks before this sitting. The enhanced SEEMP requirement dates from the same day.
THE CII GUIDELINE SET IS SITTING-CORRECT AND IS CITED BY NUMBER: MEPC.352(78), MEPC.353(78), MEPC.338(76), MEPC.354(78), MEPC.355(78). All are 2021 to 2022.

THE EEXI GUIDELINES ARE CITED BY FUNCTION ONLY AND NO RESOLUTION NUMBER IS ASSERTED.
