steps.title: What decarbonisation means in shipping
points: The progressive reduction, towards elimination, of greenhouse gas emissions from the operation of ships
Principally CO2, with methane and nitrous oxide, increasingly assessed across the whole fuel life cycle
A climate measure, not an air-quality measure - SOx and NOx are local, CO2 is global
CO2 cannot be scrubbed out - it is the intended product of burning carbon
So the only routes are burn less, burn less carbon, or burn none
An efficiency problem before it is a fuel problem - which is why both short-term measures are efficiency measures
International shipping was excluded from national commitments, which is why IMO carries the mandate

steps.title: The instrument that frames it at this sitting
points: The Initial IMO Strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships, resolution MEPC.304(72), adopted 2018
A strategy, not a regulation - nothing in it binds a ship
What binds a ship is what is written into MARPOL Annex VI as a result of it
It carries its own programme of follow-up actions - short-term, mid-term and long-term
The measures' own founding resolution expressly recalls the adoption of the Initial Strategy in its preamble
So the two short-term measures are, in terms, delivered under that Strategy

steps.title: The levels of ambition
points: Three levels, all against a 2008 baseline
One - peaking: GHG emissions should peak as soon as possible and decline thereafter
Two - carbon intensity: CO2 per transport work down at least 40 per cent by 2030, pursuing 70 per cent by 2050
Three - total annual GHG: at least 50 per cent lower by 2050
Phase-out as soon as possible in this century, consistent with the Paris temperature goals
Level two is a RATIO; level three is a QUANTITY
A fleet can meet the intensity ambition and go backwards on the absolute one by carrying more

steps.title: The pathway - short-term, mid-term and long-term
points: Short-term - agreed and in force: the design index, the data collection system, and EEXI and CII with the enhanced SEEMP
Mid-term - CANDIDATE measures under consideration, nothing adopted at this sitting
An implementation programme for alternative low-carbon and zero-carbon fuels
Further operational efficiency measures; new and innovative emission reduction mechanisms, possibly including market-based measures; R&D and capacity building
Long-term - directional: zero-carbon or fossil-free fuels, and further innovative mechanisms
Two running principles: no more favourable treatment, and assessment of impacts on States
The honest position: the mid-term mechanism was unresolved at this sitting

steps.title: The first short-term measure - the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index
points: Both measures were introduced by MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022, applying from 1 January 2023
Technical, one-off, design-based - it extends the new-ship design discipline to existing ships
It computes the ship's theoretical CO2 per tonne-mile at a reference condition - a calculation, not a measurement
Attained EEXI must not exceed required EEXI, derived from the reference line with a reduction factor. No factor quoted
Demonstrated once, at the first periodical survey on or after 1 January 2023, endorsed on the IEEC
Compliance route one: engine or shaft power limitation, sealed and verifiable, with an overridable power reserve the master may release for safety, recorded when used
Route two: technical improvement - energy-saving devices, propeller and hull work, waste heat recovery. Route three: a lower-carbon fuel
The honest criticism: it says what the ship is CAPABLE of, not what she does

steps.title: The second short-term measure - the Carbon Intensity Indicator
points: Operational, annual, continuing - it measures what the ship actually did
The attained annual operational CII: CO2 from fuel actually consumed, over capacity and distance actually sailed
The data comes from the fuel oil consumption data collection system, which already existed
Compared with a required CII from a reference line with an annual reduction factor that tightens each year
Result: a rating A to E, documented and visible to charterers and financiers
D for three consecutive years, or E for one year - a plan of corrective actions in the SEEMP, approved
The enhanced SEEMP carries the implementation plan, the calculation methodology and the corrective action plan, and is verified
Improving it: speed above all, then hull and propeller condition, trim, weather routeing, port efficiency, shore power
The honest criticism: it divides by capacity and distance, not by cargo carried - and the regulation provides for review

steps.title: The guidelines that make the two measures operable
points: The regulation states the requirement; the guidelines carry the arithmetic
G1 - MEPC.352(78): the method of calculating the attained annual operational CII
G2 - MEPC.353(78): the reference lines. G3 - MEPC.338(76): the reduction factors
G4 - MEPC.354(78): the rating boundaries. G5 - MEPC.355(78): the interim correction factors and voyage adjustments
The EEXI set - calculation, survey and certification, and shaft or engine power limitation - named by function only; no resolution number asserted
The 2022 SEEMP guidelines, MEPC.346(78), govern the enhanced plan at this sitting
Why it is structured that way: the method can be revised without amending the Convention

steps.title: What the two measures do and do not achieve
points: The first mandatory GHG measures applied to the EXISTING fleet - everything earlier applied to ships not yet built
Both are intensity measures - neither caps total emissions, and the third ambition is absolute
Neither touches the fuel - they make a ship burning fossil fuel burn less of it
They were administratively light and quickly achievable, because the data and the index already existed
Which is also their limitation - what could be agreed, not what would be sufficient
They shift commercial pressure onto the operator through a visible rating
A floor, not a destination - adopted under a Strategy itself under revision, and expressly subject to review

questions.memory_cue: Define, frame, three ambitions, three phases, two measures, five guidelines, limits. DEFINE (1): climate not air quality - burn less, less carbon, or none. FRAME (2): the Initial Strategy; a strategy binds nobody, the Annex does. AMBITIONS (3): peak; intensity -40% by 2030 pursuing -70% by 2050; total GHG -50% by 2050, all on 2008. PHASES (4): short-term in force, mid and long-term candidates. MEASURES: EEXI technical, one-off, what she could do (5); CII operational, annual, A to E, what she did (6). GUIDELINES (7): calculation, reference lines, reduction factors, rating boundaries, corrective action. LIMITS (8): both intensity, neither touches the fuel.
questions.understand_first: The reason this subject is hard is that carbon dioxide is not like the other things that come out of a funnel. Sulphur and nitrogen oxides and soot are local problems - they damage the air where the ship happens to be, which is why the rules for them are geographical and why you can fit a scrubber and remove them. Carbon dioxide harms nobody standing next to it, and it cannot be removed at the funnel at all, because it is what burning a carbon fuel produces. Take the carbon out of the exhaust and you have taken it out of the fuel. So there are only three things anyone can do: burn less fuel, burn a fuel with less carbon in it, or burn none. Everything in this question is one of those three. IMO's plan for getting there is set out in a Strategy - which is worth understanding for what it is, because it binds nobody. It is a statement of what the Organization intends, with targets attached, and the targets only become real when somebody writes a regulation into MARPOL Annex VI to deliver them. At the time of this examination that plan had three ambitions: emissions should stop rising, the amount of carbon per tonne of cargo carried a mile should fall a long way by 2030, and the total emitted should be halved by 2050. Notice the difference between the last two, because it is the point of the whole thing: the second is a ratio and the third is a quantity, and improving the ratio while the fleet grows can leave the quantity higher than before. And then the two measures. The first, EEXI, is a piece of arithmetic done once on paper: given her engine, her hull and her design speed, how much carbon would this ship emit per tonne-mile? If the answer is too high she must be improved - and in practice most ships were made compliant simply by capping the engine power, which lowers the design speed and therefore the number. Which raises the obvious objection: a sum done on paper says nothing about how the ship is actually run. That is exactly why the second measure exists. CII looks at what she really burned and how far she really went over a whole year, and gives her a grade from A to E - a grade that charterers can see. Do badly for long enough and you must write a plan and have it approved. One measures what the ship could do; the other measures what she did.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Decarbonisation = progressive reduction towards elimination of GHG from ship operation - mainly CO2, increasingly on a life-cycle basis. A climate measure, not air quality: SOx and NOx are local, CO2 is global and cannot be scrubbed out, because it is the product of burning carbon. So: burn less, burn less carbon, or burn none. Frame: the Initial IMO Strategy, MEPC.304(72) of 2018 - a strategy, not a regulation; what binds is MARPOL Annex VI. Three levels of ambition, all against 2008: peak as soon as possible; carbon intensity at least -40% by 2030, pursuing -70% by 2050; total annual GHG at least -50% by 2050; phase out as soon as possible this century, consistent with Paris. Level two is a ratio, level three a quantity. Pathway: short-term in force; mid-term and long-term are CANDIDATE measures - alternative low- and zero-carbon fuels, further operational efficiency, new and innovative mechanisms possibly including market-based measures, R&D and capacity building; long-term zero-carbon or fossil-free fuels. Principles: no more favourable treatment and assessment of impacts on States. The two short-term measures, introduced by MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022 and applying from 1 January 2023: EEXI - technical, one-off, theoretical CO2 per tonne-mile at a reference condition; attained must not exceed required; demonstrated once at survey and endorsed on the IEEC; complied with by engine or shaft power limitation (with an overridable power reserve), technical improvement, or a lower-carbon fuel. CII - operational, annual, from actual fuel and actual distance via the data collection system; rated A to E; D for three years or E for one requires an approved plan of corrective actions in the SEEMP; improved chiefly by speed. Guidelines G1-G5: MEPC.352(78) calculation, MEPC.353(78) reference lines, MEPC.338(76) reduction factors, MEPC.354(78) rating boundaries, MEPC.355(78) correction factors and voyage adjustments. SEEMP guidelines MEPC.346(78). Both are intensity measures; neither touches the fuel.
critical_numbers: THREE levels of ambition, all against a 2008 baseline
Carbon intensity at least 40 per cent lower by 2030, pursuing efforts towards 70 per cent by 2050
Total annual GHG at least 50 per cent lower by 2050
Both short-term measures introduced by MEPC.328(76): in force 1 NOVEMBER 2022, requirements applying from 1 JANUARY 2023
CII rating runs A to E; D for THREE consecutive years or E for ONE year triggers a plan of corrective actions
CII guidelines G1 to G5: MEPC.352(78), MEPC.353(78), MEPC.338(76), MEPC.354(78), MEPC.355(78)
NO reduction factor, reference-line value or rating boundary is quoted - all are ship-type and size specific
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4, as introduced by resolution MEPC.328(76), which entered into force on 1 November 2022 with the requirements applying from 1 January 2023. It carries the two short-term measures: the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index, a one-off technical requirement under which a ship's attained EEXI must not exceed the required EEXI derived from the design-index reference line with a reduction factor; and the Carbon Intensity Indicator, an annual operational requirement under which the attained annual operational CII is compared with a required value and the ship rated A to E, a rating of D for three consecutive years or E for one year requiring a plan of corrective actions in an enhanced SEEMP. The policy frame is the Initial IMO Strategy, resolution MEPC.304(72) of 2018. No provision of Annex VI is quoted here and no numeric factor is asserted.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering on the wrong Strategy. IMO replaced its greenhouse gas strategy four months after this examination, and nearly every source a candidate will have seen is written on the later one - with a net-zero formulation and 2030 and 2040 checkpoints that did not exist at this sitting. The operative instrument here is the Initial Strategy of 2018, with its three levels of ambition against a 2008 baseline. Second trap: naming EEDI as one of the two short-term measures. EEDI is the pre-existing measure for new ships; the two asked for are EEXI and CII. Third: describing mid-term measures as agreed - they are candidate measures. Fourth: saying EEXI is annual (it is one-off) or that CII is a design calculation (it is operational, from actual fuel and distance). Fifth: forgetting the D-three-years-or-E-once trigger and the SEEMP corrective action plan, which together are the entire enforcement mechanism. Sixth: ignoring the guidelines, when the stem asks for them in terms - the regulation states the requirement and the guidelines carry the arithmetic. Seventh: confusing the intensity ambition with the absolute one, and so failing to see that neither short-term measure can deliver the third level of ambition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the decarbonisation question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 what decarbonisation is, and the three distinctions. 2 the framing instrument - a strategy, not a regulation. 3 the three levels of ambition against 2008. 4 the three-phase pathway, with mid and long-term as candidates. 5 EEXI - technical and one-off. 6 CII - operational and annual. 7 the guidelines that carry the arithmetic. 8 what the measures do not achieve.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem carries three instructions of unequal size, and the last two words - 'with their guidelines' - are worth about a quarter of the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can carbon dioxide not be treated the way sulphur is?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because SOx, NOx and particulates are local pollutants that harm the air where they are emitted, while CO2 is a global one that is harmless to breathe - so geographic controls make no sense for it. And CO2 cannot be scrubbed out: it is the intended product of burning a carbon fuel. The only routes are therefore to burn less fuel, burn a fuel with less carbon, or burn none.
retrieval_cards.why: This distinction is the whole logic of the subject and explains why both short-term measures are efficiency measures.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the levels of ambition, and the baseline.
retrieval_cards.answer: Three, all against 2008. One: GHG emissions from international shipping should peak as soon as possible and decline thereafter. Two: carbon intensity - CO2 per transport work - down at least 40 per cent by 2030, pursuing efforts towards 70 per cent by 2050. Three: total annual GHG emissions at least 50 per cent lower by 2050. With phase-out as soon as possible in this century, consistent with the Paris temperature goals.
retrieval_cards.why: Three levels and the 2008 baseline are the core of the ambitions limb, and candidates routinely give only two.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between the carbon intensity ambition and the total GHG ambition?
retrieval_cards.answer: Carbon intensity is a RATIO - emissions per unit of transport work - so it improves as ships get more efficient even if the fleet grows. Total annual GHG is a QUANTITY - the actual tonnage emitted. A fleet forty per cent more efficient per tonne-mile while carrying seventy per cent more cargo has met the intensity ambition and gone backwards on the absolute one. Both short-term measures are intensity measures, so neither can deliver the third ambition.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the sharpest analytical point available in the question and it explains the limits of the two measures.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the two short-term measures - and say what EEDI is.
retrieval_cards.answer: EEXI - the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index - and CII - the Carbon Intensity Indicator - both introduced by resolution MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022 and applying from 1 January 2023, with an enhanced SEEMP alongside them. EEDI is NOT one of them: it is the pre-existing design index for new ships, and it supplies the reference line from which the required EEXI is derived.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming EEDI as one of the two is the commonest factual error in this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain EEXI, and how a ship complies.
retrieval_cards.answer: A technical, one-off requirement: the ship's theoretical CO2 per tonne-mile at a reference condition, calculated from installed power, specific fuel consumption, deadweight and reference speed. The attained EEXI must not exceed the required value, derived from the design-index reference line with a reduction factor. Demonstrated once at the first periodical survey on or after 1 January 2023 and endorsed on the IEEC. Compliance by engine or shaft power limitation (sealed, with an overridable power reserve for safety), by technical improvement, or by a lower-carbon fuel.
retrieval_cards.why: One-off, theoretical and power-limitation are the three things that must be right, and the power reserve is the engineer's part of it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain CII, and what happens to a poor rating.
retrieval_cards.answer: An operational, annual requirement: the attained annual operational CII is the CO2 from the fuel actually consumed over the capacity and the distance actually sailed, taken from the fuel oil consumption data collection system, and compared with a required value that tightens each year. The ship is rated A to E. A rating of D for three consecutive years, or E for one year, requires a plan of corrective actions in the SEEMP, which must be approved.
retrieval_cards.why: The D-three-or-E-once trigger and the SEEMP plan together are the entire enforcement mechanism of the measure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What do the CII guidelines G1 to G5 supply?
retrieval_cards.answer: G1 the method of calculating the attained annual operational CII; G2 the reference lines; G3 the reduction factors; G4 the rating boundaries; G5 the interim correction factors and voyage adjustments. In resolution terms: MEPC.352(78), MEPC.353(78), MEPC.338(76), MEPC.354(78), MEPC.355(78). The regulation states the requirement and the guidelines carry the arithmetic, so the method can be revised without amending the Convention.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for the measures 'with their guidelines', and naming the five functions earns the mark even without the numbers.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the principal criticism of the CII metric?
retrieval_cards.answer: It divides by capacity and distance, not by cargo actually carried. So a ship can improve her rating by sailing further, a fully loaded ship waiting at anchor is penalised while an empty ship steaming is not, and short-sea, offshore and long-idling trades are treated poorly. The fair answer is that the arrangement is expressly subject to review - it is a first attempt designed to be corrected.
retrieval_cards.why: Stating the criticism with the review provision is more accurate than presenting the measure as settled, and examiners probe for it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Will EEXI and CII achieve IMO's decarbonisation ambitions?
retrieval_cards.answer: No, and they were never expected to. They are the first mandatory GHG measures applied to the existing fleet, which is a real achievement - but both are intensity measures, so neither caps the total tonnage emitted, and the third level of ambition is an absolute one. Neither touches the fuel. They are a floor rather than a destination, adopted quickly because the data and the index already existed, and they are expressly subject to review.
retrieval_cards.why: The honest limit is the closing mark, and it ties the measures back to the ambitions the stem opened with.

questions.short_title: Perils of the Sea, Cover for Uninsured Perils, and Due Diligence
questions.text_verbatim: What are the perils of the sea which are covered in a Marine Insurance contract? What can an insured do to cover a peril other than an insured peril of the sea? Explain with examples. Also enumerate the perils which are covered under a marine insurance contract, but the onus of proof is upon the insurers to prove the assured's want of "due diligence" to avoid the claim.

blocks.h: 1. What 'perils of the sea' actually means

blocks.p: The phrase has a narrow legal meaning, and almost every mark in the first part of this question turns on knowing that it is narrow. It is not "anything bad that happens at sea". The Rules for Construction of Policy in the Schedule to the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 define perils of the seas as fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas, and expressly exclude the ordinary action of the winds and waves.
Two tests come out of that definition, and applying them in order is the whole technique:

ul: Test one - fortuity. Was the loss accidental? A loss that is inevitable, or that is the natural and expected consequence of sending a ship to sea, is not fortuitous and is not covered. Rust is not a peril of the sea. Neither is a hull that was always going to leak.

Test two - of the sea, not merely at sea. The sea must be the cause, not the location. A cargo that spoils in the hold because it was loaded wet has not been damaged by a peril of the sea, however far from land the spoiling happened.

headers: Covered as a peril of the sea
NOT a peril of the sea
rows: Stranding, grounding, sinking and foundering
Wear and tear, and ordinary leakage and breakage
Collision, and striking a submerged object or wreck
Inherent vice - the goods' own tendency to deteriorate
Heavy weather damage of an extraordinary kind
The ordinary action of the winds and waves
Accidental entry of seawater through a hull opening or fitting
Corrosion, and damage by vermin
Capsizing, and loss of the vessel in a casualty
Machinery damage not proximately caused by a maritime peril

blocks.p: The last line of the right-hand column is the one that matters most to an engineer, and it is the reason the whole of section 4 below exists. A broken crankshaft is not a peril of the sea. If it is covered at all, it is covered by a different provision of the policy - and that provision comes with the due-diligence qualification the question is ultimately asking about.

blocks.h: 2. The maritime perils that are covered but are NOT perils of the sea

blocks.p: Candidates lose marks here by assuming that "perils of the sea" is the whole of the cover. It is not. It is only the first item in the perils clause of a hull and machinery policy. Everything else in that clause is listed separately precisely because the sea did not cause it, and would otherwise be uninsured:

ul: Fire and explosion. Listed on its own, because fire is not a casualty of the sea at all.
Violent theft by persons from outside the vessel - which is theft with violence by outsiders, not pilferage and not theft by the crew.
Jettison - the deliberate throwing overboard of property to save the adventure.
Piracy.
Contact with land conveyance, dock or harbour equipment or installation - the ship struck by a crane or a gangway, or striking a quay fitting.
Earthquake, volcanic eruption or lightning.
Accidents in loading, discharging or shifting cargo or fuel - a cargo unit dropped into a hold, a bunker transfer that goes wrong.

blocks.p: So the correct shape of an answer to the first two sentences of the stem is: here is the narrow class of perils of the seas; here is the wider class of maritime perils that the policy also names; and here is what to do about everything outside both.

blocks.h: 3. How an insured covers a peril that is not an insured peril - with examples

blocks.p: This is the middle limb of the question, and it wants practical answers with examples, not theory. There are four routes, and they are not alternatives to each other - a well-covered owner uses all four at once.

rows: Extend the existing policy
Agree an additional clause with the underwriter for an additional premium, widening what the same policy responds to

Additional perils cover, which extends latent-defect protection to pay for the defective part itself and not only the damage it caused - the single most valuable extension an engineering department can ask for
Buy a separate policy
The risk is written on its own contract, because it is priced and underwritten quite differently
War and strikes cover, which is excluded from the ordinary hull policy; loss of hire; increased value and hull interest; and freight insurance
Cover it mutually through a P&I club
Third-party liabilities are pooled among shipowner members rather than bought from a commercial underwriter

Pollution liability, cargo claims, crew injury and repatriation, wreck removal, and damage to fixed and floating objects. None of these is a hull risk at all - the hull policy insures the ship, the club insures what the ship does to others
Adjust the terms rather than the perils
The peril is already covered; what is inadequate is the amount or the condition attached to it
Raise the sum insured, lower the deductible, or negotiate removal of a restrictive warranty such as a trading or lay-up warranty

blocks.p: And two limits must be stated, because an examiner will test them:

ul: An inevitable loss is not insurable at all. Insurance transfers risk, and where there is no fortuity there is no risk to transfer - only a certainty, which is a cost.

A known existing defect is a repair bill, not a risk. If the owner knows the shaft is cracked, no underwriter will insure the crack. And the duty of disclosure under section 20 of the 1963 Act means concealing it puts the whole policy in jeopardy, not merely that claim.

blocks.h: 4. The perils whose cover is qualified by due diligence - the Inchmaree group

blocks.p: This is the third limb, and it is the one the printed question is really driving at. The market's answer to the problem identified at the end of section 1 - that machinery casualties are not perils of the sea - is a clause the market itself calls the Inchmaree clause, after the case in which a donkey-engine casualty was held not to be a peril of the seas. The clause exists to insure exactly the losses that the narrow definition leaves out.
The perils it adds are these, and they are the direct answer to the stem's final sentence:

ol: Bursting of boilers.
Breakage of shafts.
Latent defect in the machinery or hull.
Negligence of Master, Officers, Crew or Pilots.
Negligence of repairers or charterers, provided they are not an assured under the policy.
Barratry of master, officers or crew - a wilful wrongful act done to the prejudice of the owner.

blocks.p: And every one of them is subject to a single proviso: that the loss has not resulted from want of due diligence by the assured, owners, managers or superintendents, or any of their onshore management. Three features of that proviso carry marks on their own:

ul: The Master, Officers and Crew are NOT in the diligence list. That is deliberate and it is the heart of the clause. Their negligence is the insured peril - it is what is being covered. It would be incoherent to insure crew negligence and then defeat the claim because the crew were negligent.

Latent defect cover pays the resulting damage, not the renewal of the defective part. If a defective bolt fails and wrecks the gearing, the gearing is paid for and the bolt is not - unless additional perils cover has been bought, as in section 3.

A latent defect is a defect not discoverable by the exercise of reasonable care. A defect that a proper survey or a proper inspection would have found is not latent, and is very likely to be an example of want of diligence into the bargain.

blocks.h: 5. Where the onus of proof lies, and why it matters

blocks.p: The stem asks specifically about the onus of proof being on the insurer, so the allocation of the burden has to be stated as a rule and not merely asserted for this clause:

ul: The assured proves that the loss occurred and that it was proximately caused by a peril insured against. That is his case, and until he makes it there is nothing to answer.
The insurer proves any exception, exclusion or proviso on which it seeks to rely. He who relies on a limitation must establish it.

blocks.p: The due-diligence provision is a proviso limiting liability, not a condition precedent to cover. It follows directly that the onus of proving want of due diligence lies on the underwriters. The assured does not have to prove he was diligent; the insurer has to prove he was not - which is a materially harder thing to do, and is why the clause is as valuable to owners as it is.

So the direct answer to the printed question is: boilers, shafts, latent defect, negligence of master, officers, crew and pilots, negligence of repairers and charterers, and barratry. Those are the perils that are covered but where the insurer bears the burden of proving want of due diligence in order to defeat the claim.

In practice these claims are fought on documents, and that is the point at which this ceases to be a legal question and becomes an engineering one. What decides them is the planned maintenance records, the defect reports and what was done about them, the superintendent's reports and correspondence, any condition of class, and the safety management system records. A defect reported by the ship, acknowledged ashore and not attended to is the most damaging document that can appear in a machinery casualty file, because it is precisely the want of diligence by shore management that the proviso is aimed at.

blocks.h: 6. The Indian frame, and what it means on board

ul: The governing statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. It is modelled on the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906, and the English authorities are persuasive - but the operative statute in India is the 1963 Act, and saying "the Marine Insurance Act 1906" in an Indian examination is a straightforward error.

Section 19 makes marine insurance a contract of utmost good faith. Section 20 requires disclosure of every material circumstance known to the assured before the contract is concluded. Section 66 deals with general average loss.

The perils are in the policy, not in the statute. The Act supplies the framework and the definitions; the perils clause and the Inchmaree clause are market wording. Indian hull policies are ordinarily written on London market forms, which is why the substance is common across the market even though no single form is quoted here.
The shipping statute in force is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, administered by DG Shipping.
Your own negligence as an engineer is insured. Shore management's failure to act is what puts the claim at risk. That asymmetry is the practical lesson of the whole question.

On a casualty: notify promptly, preserve the failed component, photograph before anything is disturbed, and do not dismantle beyond what is necessary to make the ship safe until the surveyor has attended. The evidence that establishes a latent defect is destroyed by a tidy engine room.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks and three distinct questions in one stem, which is why the structure matters more here than the content. Question one: what are perils of the sea. Question two: what does an insured do about a peril that is not an insured peril. Question three: which covered perils put the onus of proof on the insurer to show want of due diligence. Answer them in that order and the answer builds; answer them as one essay on marine insurance and two of the three go unanswered.

The single most common failure is to treat "perils of the sea" as meaning everything covered by a marine policy. It is the narrowest term in the question, and the marks are in showing that you know how narrow it is.

blocks.h: The two tests, and why they are the whole of limb one

blocks.p: Fortuity, and of the sea rather than merely at sea. Rust fails the first because it is inevitable. Wet-loaded cargo fails the second because the sea did not cause it. If you can state those two tests and give an example of each failing, limb one is essentially answered before you list a single peril.

blocks.h: The line that leads into the rest of the question

blocks.p: Machinery damage is not a peril of the sea. Write that sentence, because it is the hinge of the whole answer: it is the reason the Inchmaree clause exists, and the reason the third limb has anything to ask about. A broken shaft is covered - but by a different provision, and that provision comes with a proviso.

blocks.h: The Inchmaree six

ol: Bursting of boilers
Breakage of shafts
Latent defect in machinery or hull
Negligence of Master, Officers, Crew or Pilots
Negligence of repairers or charterers not assured under the policy
Barratry

blocks.p: Learn them as a list of six, because the stem's last sentence is asking for exactly this list. And remember the origin of the name: the Inchmaree was the case in which a donkey-engine casualty was held not to be a peril of the seas - the clause was written to fill the gap the decision exposed.

blocks.h: The proviso, and the omission inside it

blocks.p: The proviso is want of due diligence by the assured, owners, managers or superintendents. Notice who is not in that list: the Master, Officers and Crew. Their negligence is the insured peril itself, so it cannot also be the thing that defeats the claim. If you can explain why they are absent, you have shown that you understand the clause rather than memorised it.

blocks.h: Burden of proof - state it as a general rule first

blocks.p: The assured proves the loss was caused by an insured peril. The insurer proves any exception, exclusion or proviso it relies on. The due-diligence provision is a proviso, not a condition precedent - so the onus of proving want of due diligence is on the underwriters. Deriving the answer from the general rule scores better than simply asserting it, because it shows the reasoning that makes it true.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Treating "perils of the sea" as everything a marine policy covers. It is the narrowest term in the question.
Forgetting the ordinary action of the winds and waves exclusion, which is expressly in the statutory definition.
Answering the middle limb with theory instead of examples - the stem asks for them by name.
Omitting the P&I club entirely, and so leaving pollution, cargo, crew and wreck-removal liabilities with no home.
Listing the Inchmaree perils but not the proviso, or the proviso but not the perils.
Putting the Master and crew into the due-diligence list. Their negligence is the insured peril.
Saying latent defect cover pays for the defective part. It pays for the resulting damage unless additional perils cover is bought.
Putting the onus on the assured. It is on the insurer, because it is relying on a proviso.
Citing the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 as the governing statute in an Indian examination. It is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Is heavy weather a peril of the sea?" Extraordinary heavy weather, yes. The ordinary action of the winds and waves, expressly no.
"Your main engine crankshaft breaks at sea. Peril of the sea?" No - but very probably covered under the Inchmaree clause, subject to due diligence.
"Who proves want of due diligence?" The underwriters. It is a proviso limiting liability, and he who relies on a limitation must prove it.
"Is the Chief Engineer's negligence covered?" Yes - crew negligence is an insured peril, and the crew are deliberately absent from the diligence list.
"Latent defect - do you get a new part?" No, only the resulting damage - unless additional perils cover has been purchased.
"Which Act governs in India?" The Marine Insurance Act, 1963. The 1906 Act is the model, not the law.
"How do you cover pollution liability?" Not on the hull policy at all - through the P&I club.
"What kills a machinery claim faster than anything else?" A defect reported by the ship, acknowledged ashore and never attended to.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Give me an example of a loss at sea that is not a loss by a peril of the sea.
What is barratry, and give me an example of it.
Your turbocharger fails from a manufacturing flaw nobody could have found. What is covered, and what is not?
What documents would an underwriter's surveyor ask you for after a bearing failure?
Why is war risk not on the hull policy?
What would you do in the first hour after a machinery casualty, before anyone tells you to?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Narrow, wider, outside, and the proviso. NARROW (1): perils of the seas - fortuitous, and of the sea. WIDER (2): the rest of the perils clause - fire, theft, jettison, piracy, contact, earthquake and lightning, loading accidents. OUTSIDE (3): extend the policy, buy a separate one, go to the club, or change the terms. THE PROVISO (4 and 5): the Inchmaree six - boilers, shafts, latent defect, negligence of crew, negligence of repairers, barratry - covered unless the insurer proves want of diligence by the assured, owners, managers or superintendents. Then the Indian frame (6).

blocks.h: Uncertainty and jurisdiction notes

blocks.p: This is one of the most temporally stable questions on the paper, and deliberately so. The governing statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 and it did not move in the relevant period; the doctrine relied on - the fortuity test, the burden rule and the diligence allocation - is settled and long predates the sitting. The UK Insurance Act 2015 reformed the avoidance remedy in English law and appears nowhere here, because it is not Indian law. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 is three years after this sitting and is not cited.

The clause layer is deliberately undated, and that is a strength rather than an evasion. MIW holds no Institute Time Clauses, no International Hull Clauses and no policy wording. Several editions ran concurrently in the market and their numbering differs between them, so no clause number and no edition is asserted anywhere and the perils are enumerated by their substance and their grouping - which is common to all the forms in use. An answer that named a clause number would be more precise-looking and less accurate.

Equally, the statutory rule number carrying the definition of perils of the seas is not asserted, because the Act's text is not held: the rule is stated as law and its address is not. steps.title: What 'perils of the sea' actually means
points: The Rules for Construction of Policy in the Schedule to the Marine Insurance Act, 1963
Fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas; NOT the ordinary action of the winds and waves
Test one - fortuity: accidental, not inevitable, not the natural consequence of going to sea
Test two - of the sea, not merely at sea: the sea must be the cause
Covered: stranding, grounding, sinking, foundering, collision, striking a submerged object, extraordinary heavy weather, accidental entry of seawater, capsizing
Excluded: wear and tear, ordinary leakage and breakage, inherent vice, corrosion, vermin
And machinery damage not proximately caused by a maritime peril - the hinge of the whole question

steps.title: The maritime perils that are covered but are NOT perils of the sea
points: Perils of the seas is only the FIRST item in the perils clause
Fire and explosion - listed separately precisely because the sea did not cause it
Violent theft by persons from outside the vessel; jettison; piracy
Contact with land conveyance, dock or harbour equipment or installation
Earthquake, volcanic eruption or lightning
Accidents in loading, discharging or shifting cargo or fuel

steps.title: How an insured covers a peril that is not an insured peril - with examples
points: Extend the policy by an additional clause for extra premium - example: additional perils cover, buying back the defective part itself
Buy a separate policy - examples: war and strikes, loss of hire, increased value and hull interest, freight
Cover it mutually through a P&I club - examples: pollution, cargo claims, crew injury and repatriation, wreck removal, fixed and floating objects
Adjust the terms rather than the perils - higher sum insured, lower deductible, removal of a restrictive warranty
Limit one: an inevitable loss is not insurable - no fortuity, no risk to transfer
Limit two: a known existing defect is a repair bill, not a risk - and section 20 disclosure puts the whole policy at stake

steps.title: The perils whose cover is qualified by due diligence - the Inchmaree group
points: The Inchmaree clause, named from the case in which a donkey-engine casualty was held not to be a peril of the seas
Bursting of boilers; breakage of shafts; latent defect in machinery or hull
Negligence of Master, Officers, Crew or Pilots; negligence of repairers or charterers not assured under the policy; barratry
The proviso - provided the loss has not resulted from want of due diligence by the assured, owners, managers or superintendents
The Master, Officers and Crew are NOT in the diligence list - their negligence is the insured peril
Latent defect cover pays the resulting damage, not the renewal of the defective part
A defect a reasonable inspection would have found is not latent - and is probably want of diligence too

steps.title: Where the onus of proof lies, and why it matters
points: The assured proves the loss was proximately caused by a peril insured against
The insurer proves any exception, exclusion or proviso on which it relies
The due-diligence provision is a proviso limiting liability, not a condition precedent
Therefore THE ONUS OF PROVING WANT OF DUE DILIGENCE LIES ON THE UNDERWRITERS
The direct answer to the stem: boilers, shafts, latent defect, negligence, repairers, barratry
In practice fought on documents - planned maintenance, defect reports, superintendent's reports, conditions of class, SMS records

questions.memory_cue: Narrow, wider, outside, proviso, burden, frame. NARROW (1): fortuitous, and of the sea. WIDER (2): fire, theft, jettison, piracy, contact, earthquake, loading accidents. OUTSIDE (3): extend, separate policy, P&I club, change the terms. PROVISO (4): the Inchmaree six, and the crew are not in the diligence list. BURDEN (5): the insurer proves want of diligence. FRAME (6): the 1963 Act, and preserve the evidence.
questions.understand_first: Almost everything in this question follows from one idea: the law's phrase 'perils of the sea' is much narrower than an engineer's instinct suggests. It does not mean bad luck at sea. It means something accidental, caused by the sea itself - the ship grounds, she is holed, she is knocked about by weather beyond the ordinary. Rust is not a peril of the sea, because rust was always going to happen. Cargo that was loaded wet and spoils is not a peril of the sea, because the sea had nothing to do with it. And, most importantly for you, a broken shaft or a burst boiler is not a peril of the sea either - a fact established in a real case a very long time ago, and one that left shipowners with the uncomfortable discovery that the most expensive thing that could happen to their machinery was not covered at all. The market's answer was to write an extra clause naming those machinery casualties expressly, together with the negligence of the people operating the ship. That clause still carries the name of the ship in the case that exposed the gap. But it comes with a condition: the cover holds unless the loss came from a failure of diligence by the owner and his shore management. Notice who is left out of that condition - the Master, the officers and the crew. Their carelessness is the very thing being insured, so it cannot also be the thing that voids the cover. And because that condition is a limitation on the insurer's promise rather than a precondition of it, it is the insurer who has to prove it, not you who has to disprove it. Which is why the whole argument, in the end, is fought over your maintenance records.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Perils of the sea = fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas, per the Rules for Construction of Policy in the Schedule to the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 - NOT the ordinary action of the winds and waves. Two tests: fortuity, and of the sea rather than merely at sea. In: stranding, grounding, sinking, foundering, collision, striking a submerged object, extraordinary heavy weather, accidental seawater entry, capsizing. Out: wear and tear, ordinary leakage and breakage, inherent vice, corrosion, vermin - and machinery damage. The perils clause also names, separately: fire and explosion, violent theft by outsiders, jettison, piracy, contact with dock or harbour equipment, earthquake and lightning, accidents in loading and discharging. To cover an uninsured peril: extend the policy (additional perils cover buys back the defective part), buy a separate policy (war and strikes, loss of hire, freight), go to the P&I club (pollution, cargo, crew, wreck removal, fixed and floating objects), or change the terms (sum insured, deductible, warranties). The Inchmaree six: bursting of boilers, breakage of shafts, latent defect, negligence of Master/Officers/Crew/Pilots, negligence of repairers or charterers, barratry - all subject to want of due diligence by the assured, owners, managers or superintendents. The crew are deliberately NOT in that list, because their negligence is the insured peril. Latent defect pays the resulting damage, not the part. Burden: the assured proves the insured peril; the insurer proves the proviso - so the onus of proving want of due diligence is on the underwriters. Indian statute: 1963, not 1906.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the perils of the sea and due diligence question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What perils of the sea means - the two tests. 2 The wider maritime perils in the same clause. 3 How to cover an uninsured peril, with examples. 4 The Inchmaree group and its proviso. 5 Where the onus of proof lies. 6 The Indian frame and conduct after a casualty.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem contains three separate questions. Answering them in order builds the answer; running them together leaves two of the three unanswered.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define perils of the sea, and give the two tests.
retrieval_cards.answer: Fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas, expressly not including the ordinary action of the winds and waves - the Rules for Construction of Policy in the Schedule to the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. Test one, fortuity: accidental, not inevitable. Test two, of the sea and not merely at sea: the sea must be the cause and not just the place.
retrieval_cards.why: The narrowness of the term is the whole of the first limb, and both tests are needed to apply it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your crankshaft breaks at sea. Is that a peril of the sea?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Machinery damage not proximately caused by a maritime peril is not a peril of the sea - which is the very point established in the Inchmaree case. It is very probably covered nonetheless, under the Inchmaree clause as breakage of shafts or as latent defect, subject to the due-diligence proviso.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the hinge of the question: the gap in the narrow definition is exactly what the third limb is about.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does an owner cover a peril that is not an insured peril? Give examples.
retrieval_cards.answer: Extend the policy for extra premium - additional perils cover, which buys back the defective part itself. Buy a separate policy - war and strikes, loss of hire, increased value, freight. Cover it mutually through a P&I club - pollution, cargo claims, crew injury and repatriation, wreck removal, damage to fixed and floating objects. Or adjust the terms - sum insured, deductible, removal of a restrictive warranty.
retrieval_cards.why: The middle limb asks for examples by name, and the P&I club is the one most often omitted entirely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the Inchmaree perils.
retrieval_cards.answer: Bursting of boilers; breakage of shafts; latent defect in machinery or hull; negligence of Master, Officers, Crew or Pilots; negligence of repairers or charterers not assured under the policy; and barratry. All six are subject to the proviso that the loss did not result from want of due diligence by the assured, owners, managers or superintendents.
retrieval_cards.why: This list IS the direct answer to the final sentence of the printed stem.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why are the Master and crew absent from the due-diligence list?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because their negligence is the insured peril. The clause exists to cover crew and pilot negligence, so it would be incoherent to then defeat the claim on the ground that the crew were negligent. The diligence obligation is placed on the assured, owners, managers and superintendents - the shore management.
retrieval_cards.why: Explaining the omission proves the clause is understood rather than memorised, and it is a standard oral question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who bears the onus of proving want of due diligence, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: The underwriters. The general rule is that the assured proves the loss was proximately caused by an insured peril, and the insurer proves any exception, exclusion or proviso on which it relies. The due-diligence provision is a proviso limiting liability, not a condition precedent to cover - so the burden of establishing it falls on the party relying on it.
retrieval_cards.why: Deriving the answer from the general rule scores better than asserting it, and the stem asks about the burden specifically.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Latent defect wrecks your gearing. What does the policy pay for?
retrieval_cards.answer: The resulting damage to the gearing - not the renewal of the defective part itself. The part is bought back only if additional perils cover has been purchased as an extension. And a defect that a reasonable inspection would have found is not latent at all, and is likely to be evidence of want of diligence into the bargain.
retrieval_cards.why: The distinction between the resulting damage and the defective part is where the money is, and it is regularly got wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which statute governs marine insurance in India, and which sections should you name?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Marine Insurance Act, 1963. The UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 is the model on which it was drawn and is not the operative statute. Name section 19 (utmost good faith), section 20 (disclosure of every material circumstance) and section 66 (general average loss). The perils themselves are in the policy, which is market wording, not in the statute.
retrieval_cards.why: Citing the 1906 Act in an Indian examination is a straightforward error, and the statute/policy division is a real mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What should the Chief Engineer do in the first hours after a machinery casualty?
retrieval_cards.answer: Notify promptly through the Master and the Company. Preserve the failed component and photograph everything before it is disturbed. Do not dismantle beyond what is needed to make the ship safe until the surveyor has attended. Gather the planned maintenance records, defect reports and correspondence. The claim will be decided on documents and on the failed part, and a tidy engine room destroys both.
retrieval_cards.why: The whole due-diligence argument is fought on the maintenance record, so preserving it is an engineering duty with a commercial consequence.

blocks.h: 1. Why NOx forms at all, and the three levers every measure pulls

blocks.p: Nothing in this question can be organised sensibly until one fact is stated: the nitrogen in marine diesel exhaust comes overwhelmingly from the air, not from the fuel. At the temperatures reached in the flame, atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen combine. The rate at which they do so rises very steeply with peak temperature, and depends besides on how much oxygen is available and on how long the gas stays hot.
So there are exactly three levers, and every measure described in the rest of this answer pulls at least one of them:

rows: Peak temperature
By far the strongest influence - formation rises very steeply with it
Introduce something into the charge that absorbs heat or raises its specific heat; spread the burn out in time
Oxygen availability
Nitrogen cannot oxidise without free oxygen at the flame front
Displace part of the oxygen in the charge with an inert gas
Residence time
The reaction needs time at temperature; a short, sharp peak produces less than a long plateau
Change injection timing, rate and duration so the peak is shorter

blocks.p: And one trade-off governs the whole subject. The conditions that suppress NOx - a lower, later, cooler burn - are broadly the conditions that reduce thermal efficiency. NOx and fuel consumption pull against each other, and every primary measure described below is bought partly with fuel. That trade-off is what makes the primary-versus-secondary comparison the limb asks for a real engineering decision rather than a preference.

blocks.h: 2. A) Primary measures - preventing NOx from forming

blocks.p: A primary measure acts inside the engine, on the combustion process, so that less NOx is ever created. The exhaust leaving the cylinder is already cleaner. They divide into three families:
(i) Measures acting on the combustion event itself.

ul: Retarded injection timing. Injecting later moves the burn further down the expansion stroke, so it takes place in a larger volume at lower peak pressure and temperature. It is the simplest measure of all, it needs no new plant, and it is the classic illustration of the trade-off: it costs fuel directly.

Rate shaping and injection pressure. Higher injection pressure with a shaped or multi-event delivery gives better atomisation and shortens the diffusion burn, reducing the time spent at peak temperature. Common-rail injection makes timing and rate independent of engine speed and load, which is what allows an engine to be optimised at part load rather than only at full.

Miller timing with high-pressure charging. Closing the inlet early gives an expansion inside the cylinder before compression begins, lowering the charge temperature at the start of compression and therefore the peak. It requires a higher charge-air pressure to keep the mass of air up, so it is bought with turbocharger capability rather than with fuel.
Combustion chamber, nozzle and swirl geometry, and higher compression ratio with adjusted timing - all design measures rather than operating measures, fixed at the drawing board.

blocks.p: (ii) Measures adding water to the process. Water is the most effective single tool available in the cylinder, because it absorbs a very large quantity of heat as it evaporates and because water vapour has a higher specific heat than air:

ul: Fuel-water emulsion - water emulsified into the fuel before injection, so it enters exactly where the flame is.
Direct water injection - water injected into the cylinder through its own nozzle, separately timed from the fuel.
Scavenge air moisturizing - water evaporated into the scavenge air, so the whole charge carries it in. This is limb B and is treated at section 6.

blocks.p: (iii) Measures acting on the composition of the charge. Principally exhaust gas recirculation, which displaces oxygen and raises the specific heat of the charge at the same time - two levers with one system. It is limb B and is treated at section 7. Gas operation in a dual-fuel engine belongs in this family too, since a lean premixed gas burn is inherently a lower-temperature one.

blocks.h: 3. A) Secondary measures - removing NOx after it has formed

blocks.p: A secondary measure lets the engine burn as it likes and treats the exhaust afterwards. The combustion is untouched, so the fuel penalty of the primary measures is avoided - but a plant now sits in the exhaust system and has to be paid for, accommodated, and kept running.

Selective catalytic reduction is the only mature secondary measure for NOx, and in practice the limb's second half is about it. A reducing agent - ammonia, normally carried and dosed as an aqueous urea solution - is injected into the exhaust stream upstream of a catalyst. Over the catalyst the nitrogen oxides and the reagent react to nitrogen and water vapour, both harmless. The essential characteristics are these:

ul: It is temperature-sensitive. The reaction requires the exhaust to be within a working temperature band. Too cold and conversion collapses; too hot and the catalyst degrades. On a two-stroke engine that constraint largely dictates where in the exhaust system the reactor is placed - before the turbocharger, where the gas is hot, or after it, where it is not - and each position brings its own difficulties of pressure, sizing and transient behaviour.

It is sulphur-sensitive. Sulphur in the fuel leads to salts forming on the catalyst at low temperature, which blind it. Low-sulphur fuel and a maintained temperature are therefore part of the operating condition, not optional refinements.

Dosing must be right. Too little reagent and the conversion is incomplete; too much and unreacted ammonia passes out of the funnel - ammonia slip - which is both an emission in itself and a smell nobody can ignore.
It brings a consumable and a tank. Reagent has to be bunkered, stored, heated in some climates and dosed, and the ship has a new supply chain to manage.
It occupies space and creates back pressure, both of which are severe constraints in a retrofit and are why the reactor is often the single largest item in a Tier III installation.

blocks.p: Exhaust gas scrubbing is not a NOx measure and must not be offered as one - a scrubber addresses sulphur oxides and particulate matter and has essentially no effect on nitrogen oxides. Non-thermal plasma and other electro-chemical routes exist in development but are not the answer to a question about ships in service.

blocks.h: 4. A) Primary against secondary - the comparison the limb asks for

blocks.p: The stem says vis-a-vis, so the marks are in the comparison and not in two descriptions placed side by side. Six axes carry it:

rows: Where it acts
Inside the cylinder, on the combustion process. Less NOx is created
In the exhaust system, after the cylinder. NOx is destroyed once created
Effect on the engine
The combustion is deliberately altered, so fuel consumption generally rises - the NOx-efficiency trade-off
Combustion is untouched, so no direct fuel penalty from the process itself
Plant required
Little or none for timing measures; a water or gas system for the others
A substantial installation - reactor, dosing plant, reagent tanks - with weight, space and back pressure
Consumables
Water, treated, for the water-based measures. No chemical reagent
A chemical reagent that must be bunkered, stored and dosed, with its own supply chain
Reduction achievable
Modest to substantial. Timing measures alone are modest; water-based measures and EGR reach much further
The largest single reduction available, which is why it is the standard Tier III route
Failure mode
Degrades gradually and shows up as consumption or as combustion condition
Can fail as a system - a blinded catalyst or a dosing failure removes the whole benefit at once

blocks.p: Three points are worth stating explicitly because they are what the comparison is for.

ol: Primary measures are cumulative and are used together. No single one is enough; an engine meeting a strict limit is using several at once, and they were designed in rather than added on.

The dividing line is not where the equipment sits but where the NOx goes. EGR is fitted outside the cylinder and looks like after-treatment, but it is a primary measure, because it prevents formation rather than removing what has formed. That is precisely the discrimination this limb is testing, and it is the commonest error in the question.

They are complements rather than rivals. A modern installation uses primary measures to reach the ordinary limit economically, and adds a secondary measure - or a heavy primary one such as EGR - only to reach the strict limit, and often only in the areas where the strict limit applies.

blocks.h: 5. A) The regulatory frame that decides which you need

blocks.p: The stem opens on exhaust emission control being a major global issue under serious consideration by world shipping, so the answer should place the engineering in its regulatory frame - briefly, and without pretending to quote.

NOx from marine diesel engines is controlled by MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13. At this sitting the applicable text is the Revised Annex VI introduced by resolution MEPC.328(76), which entered into force on 1 November 2022. The structure is a tiered one:

ul: There are three tiers of progressively stricter limits, and the limit in each tier is expressed as a function of the engine's rated speed - a slow-running engine being permitted more than a fast-running one, because of how the limits were framed.

Which tier applies is fixed by the ship's construction date, and for the strictest tier also by where she is operating: it bites when the ship is inside a designated NOx emission control area, and the less strict tier applies outside it.
Because the strict tier can be geographic, an engine may run in two modes, and the changeover - with date, time and position - has to be recorded.
The regulation applies above a stated engine output threshold and excludes certain emergency and survival-craft engines.

Compliance is established at certification under the revised NOx Technical Code 2008, and is demonstrated in service through the engine's NOx Technical File and its record book of engine parameters - which is why an unrecorded modification to injection timing or to a nozzle is a compliance matter and not merely an engineering one.

blocks.p: No limit value is quoted here, and that is deliberate. The limits are set out in the instrument as functions of rated speed; MIW holds Annex VI in a form that may be cited but not quoted from, so the tiers are given by what fixes which one applies and by their relative severity rather than by their numbers. What the candidate must carry away is the practical consequence: the strictest tier is a step change rather than an increment, and it is not reachable by injection timing and combustion design alone. It requires either a heavy primary measure such as exhaust gas recirculation, or a secondary measure - which is exactly why limb B asks about the two systems it does.

blocks.h: 6. B) Scavenge Air Moisturizing

blocks.p: Principle. Water is introduced into the scavenge air after the charge air cooler and evaporated into it, so that the air delivered to the cylinder is heavily laden with water vapour. It acts on the temperature lever in two ways at once: the water absorbs a large quantity of latent heat as it evaporates, and the vapour it forms has a higher specific heat than air, so the same heat release produces a lower temperature rise. The peak combustion temperature falls, and with it the rate of NOx formation.
Arrangement. The essentials are the same whatever the commercial implementation:

ul: A humidification section in the scavenge air path, downstream of the cooler, in which water is atomised into the air stream and evaporated - often in more than one stage, and often with the air re-heated between stages so that it can absorb more.

A water supply and treatment plant. Seawater may be used for the bulk duty in some arrangements, but the water that reaches the cylinder must be fresh and clean: salt carried into the cylinder is an unmitigated disaster for the liner, rings and exhaust valve.
A water mist catcher after the humidification section, so that what enters the cylinder is vapour and not droplets. This is the safety-critical item in the system.
A circulating, collecting and drain arrangement for the water that does not evaporate, and control of the humidification against engine load.

blocks.p: What it costs, and what has to be watched.

ul: Corrosion. A wet charge in the presence of combustion acids is corrosive. The scavenge space, the receiver, the liner and the exhaust side all see more moisture than they were designed around, and the cylinder oil is asked to do more.

Cylinder lubrication. Water washing the liner disturbs the oil film. Feed rate, oil selection and residual base number need watching, and scrape-down analysis is the way it is watched - which is the direct link to the oil analysis question on this paper.
Fresh water demand, and the generating or bunkering capacity to meet it.
A small efficiency penalty, since the charge is being deliberately cooled and part of the heat release is going into water rather than into work.
Control complexity - the humidification must follow load changes, and a system that lags on a rapid manoeuvre either over-wets or does nothing.

blocks.p: Where it sits. Scavenge air moisturizing is a primary measure, and a substantial one - considerably more effective than timing measures alone. But on its own it does not usually reach the strictest tier, and it is used as part of a package rather than as a complete answer to it.

blocks.h: 7. B) Exhaust Gas Recirculation

blocks.p: Principle. A proportion of the exhaust gas is cleaned, cooled and returned to the scavenge air. The charge entering the cylinder therefore contains recirculated products of combustion in place of part of the fresh air, and that does two things simultaneously - which is what makes EGR unusually powerful:

ol: It reduces the oxygen concentration of the charge. Less free oxygen at the flame front means less nitrogen oxidised. That is the oxygen lever.

It raises the specific heat of the charge, because carbon dioxide and water vapour both absorb more heat per degree than air does. The same heat release therefore produces a lower peak temperature. That is the temperature lever.

blocks.p: Arrangement on a two-stroke main engine. This is where EGR becomes a system rather than a pipe, and the reason is that marine exhaust is dirty:

ul: A scrubber in the recirculation loop, washing sulphur oxides, soot and particulate out of the gas before it goes anywhere near the scavenge air. Without it the recirculated gas would carry acid and abrasive straight back into the cylinder.
A cooler, since hot recirculated gas would defeat the purpose.
A water mist catcher, so that scrubbing water does not follow the gas into the engine.
An EGR blower, because in a uniflow two-stroke the exhaust is at a lower pressure than the scavenge air and the gas will not flow the right way on its own.
Shut-off and change-over valves, so that the system can be brought in and out as the ship enters and leaves the area where the strict limit applies.

Turbocharger arrangements to suit, since diverting exhaust away from the turbine upsets the air balance - typically by cutting out a turbocharger, by variable geometry, or by running auxiliary blowers.
A bleed-off water treatment plant. The scrubbing water becomes acidic and laden with soot and metals; it must be treated and monitored before any discharge, and the residue lands in the sludge tank.

blocks.p: What it costs, and what has to be watched.

ul: Fouling of the cooler and the loop, which is continuous and is the main maintenance burden.
Acid corrosion throughout the wet parts of the loop, and an increased acid load in the cylinder if the scrubbing is not doing its job.
Cylinder condition. Recirculated soot reaching the cylinder increases wear and loads the oil - again, scrape-down analysis is how it is watched.
Complexity and reliability. There is a great deal of plant, much of it wet and acidic, and it must work when the ship enters the area, not merely when it was last tested.
Some efficiency penalty, and a real one in blower power.
Waste streams - bleed-off water and sludge - and the monitoring and record-keeping that go with them.

blocks.p: Where it sits, and the point most often got wrong. EGR is a PRIMARY measure. All its equipment is outside the cylinder, so it looks like after-treatment - but it acts by preventing formation, not by removing what has formed, and that is what classifies it. It is capable of reaching the strictest tier on its own, which is why it stands alongside selective catalytic reduction as one of the two practical routes to it.

blocks.h: 8. B) SAM against EGR - what each costs to fit and to run

rows: Lever pulled
Temperature only - latent heat and higher specific heat
Temperature AND oxygen - which is why it reaches further
What is added to the charge
Water vapour
Cleaned, cooled exhaust gas
Plant complexity
Moderate - humidifier, water treatment, mist catcher, controls
High - scrubber, cooler, mist catcher, blower, valves, turbocharger arrangements, bleed-off water plant
Consumable
Fresh water
No reagent, but blower power, treatment chemicals and sludge handling
Reach
Substantial, but normally part of a package rather than a complete answer to the strictest tier
Capable of the strictest tier on its own
Principal risk
Water carry-over into the cylinder, and disturbance of the cylinder oil film
Fouling and acid corrosion in the loop, and soot returned to the cylinder
Waste stream
Drain water only
Acidic bleed-off water and sludge, with monitoring and records

blocks.p: What they have in common is the more useful observation. Both work by making the combustion cooler; both put water and acid where the designer of a dry engine did not intend them; and both therefore transfer a burden onto cylinder lubrication and monitoring. Whichever is fitted, the engineer's routine work is the same - keep the water where it belongs, keep the mist catcher in order, watch the cylinder condition, and read the scrape-down analysis. The system reduces the emission; the watchkeeping is what stops it costing a liner.

And the closing point, which answers the stem's opening sentence: neither of these is an optional refinement. They exist because the tiered limits under Annex VI cannot be met by combustion tuning alone, and because the strictest tier applies precisely where ships are closest to the people affected by what comes out of the funnel.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Limb A prints (8) and limb B prints no marks at all. Read that as eight and eight and treat them as equal; it is what the rubric requires, and the printed asymmetry is a printing feature of this paper rather than a marking instruction. Limb A says vis-a-vis, which means compare - two descriptions placed side by side is not a comparison, and the marks are in the axes along which they differ. Limb B names two technologies and expects each to be treated properly: principle, arrangement, and consequences.

Open with the formation mechanism, because it makes everything afterwards derivable rather than memorised. If the three levers are written down first, every measure in the answer can be explained by which lever it pulls.

blocks.h: The three levers

blocks.p: TEMPERATURE, OXYGEN, TIME. Nitrogen and oxygen from the air combine at flame temperature; the rate rises very steeply with peak temperature and depends on available oxygen and on residence time. Every primary measure pulls one of those three. Write the three words at the top of the answer and refer back to them.

blocks.h: The trade-off that governs the whole subject

blocks.p: NOx and fuel consumption pull against each other. The conditions that suppress NOx - lower, later, cooler burning - are broadly the conditions that reduce thermal efficiency. That single sentence explains why anyone bothers with after-treatment at all, and it is the reason the comparison in limb A is a real engineering decision.

blocks.h: The definition that decides limb A

blocks.p: PRIMARY = less NOx is created. SECONDARY = NOx created is then destroyed. Not 'inside the engine' against 'outside the engine' - that formulation gets EGR wrong, and getting EGR wrong is the single commonest error in the question. EGR is a PRIMARY measure even though every piece of its equipment is outside the cylinder, because it prevents formation.

blocks.h: Primary measures - three families

ul: Combustion event - retarded timing (the classic, and it costs fuel); injection pressure and rate shaping; common rail; Miller timing with high-pressure charging; chamber, nozzle and swirl design.
Adding water - fuel-water emulsion, direct water injection, scavenge air moisturizing. Water is the most effective in-cylinder tool because of latent heat plus higher specific heat.
Changing the charge - EGR, and lean premixed gas operation in a dual-fuel engine.

blocks.h: Secondary - essentially one technology

blocks.p: Selective catalytic reduction. Reagent (urea solution, giving ammonia) injected upstream of a catalyst; NOx and reagent react to nitrogen and water. Remember four things: it needs a temperature window (which decides whether the reactor goes before or after the turbocharger); it is sulphur-sensitive, because salts blind the catalyst; dosing must be right or you get ammonia slip; and it brings a reagent, a tank, space and back pressure. And say plainly that a scrubber is not a NOx measure - it is for sulphur oxides and particulates.

blocks.h: The comparison in six axes

blocks.p: Where it acts; effect on the engine; plant required; consumables; reduction achievable; failure mode. Build the answer to limb A around those six and the comparison writes itself. Then add the three closing points: primary measures are cumulative; the dividing line is where the NOx goes, not where the equipment sits; and the two are complements, primary for the ordinary limit and a heavy primary or a secondary measure for the strict one.

blocks.h: The regulatory frame in five lines

ul: NOx is controlled by MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13; at this sitting the text is the Revised Annex VI, in force 1 November 2022.
Three tiers, each limit a function of the engine's rated speed.
Construction date fixes the tier; the strictest tier also depends on where you are - inside a designated NOx emission control area.
Because it is geographic, the engine runs in two modes and the changeover must be recorded with date, time and position.
Certification is under the revised NOx Technical Code 2008, and compliance in service rests on the NOx Technical File and the record book of engine parameters.

blocks.p: Do not quote limit values. They are functions of rated speed and are set out in the instrument. What earns the mark is the practical consequence: the strictest tier is a step change, not an increment, and combustion tuning alone will not reach it - which is exactly why limb B asks about EGR and why SCR exists.

blocks.h: SAM and EGR - the shortest correct account of each

blocks.p: SAM: water evaporated into the scavenge air after the charge air cooler; latent heat plus higher specific heat lower the peak temperature. Needs a humidification section, clean fresh water, and above all a water mist catcher - vapour into the cylinder, never droplets. Watch corrosion and cylinder lubrication.

EGR: exhaust cleaned, cooled and returned to the scavenge air; less oxygen AND higher specific heat - two levers at once, which is why it reaches Tier III alone. Needs a scrubber, cooler, mist catcher, blower, shut-off valves, turbocharger arrangements and bleed-off water treatment. Watch fouling, acid corrosion and soot in the cylinder.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Calling EGR a secondary measure. It is primary - it prevents formation.
Defining the primary/secondary split as inside against outside the engine, which produces exactly that error.
Saying the nitrogen comes from the fuel. Overwhelmingly it comes from the air.
Offering an exhaust gas scrubber as a NOx measure. It addresses sulphur oxides and particulates.
Describing the two technologies but never comparing primary with secondary, when the stem says vis-a-vis.
Omitting the NOx-fuel consumption trade-off, which is the reason the whole choice exists.
Forgetting the water mist catcher on SAM, or the scrubber on the EGR loop - the two items that make each system survivable.
Quoting limit values, percentage reductions or recirculation rates as general figures.
Forgetting that the strict tier is geographic, so the engine has two modes and the changeover is recorded.
Ignoring what these systems do to cylinder lubrication, which is the part that lands on the Chief Engineer.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Is EGR primary or secondary?" Primary. The plant is outside the cylinder but it prevents formation.
"Where does the nitrogen come from?" The air.
"Why does retarding the timing cost fuel?" Because the burn happens later in the expansion, at lower pressure and temperature - which is the same reason it lowers NOx.
"Will a scrubber reduce your NOx?" No - it addresses SOx and particulates.
"What is ammonia slip and why does it matter?" Unreacted reagent passing out of the funnel, from overdosing or from poor conversion. It is an emission in itself.
"Why does SCR care about fuel sulphur?" Salts form on the catalyst at low temperature and blind it.
"What is the most important single component in a SAM system?" The water mist catcher - vapour into the cylinder, never droplets.
"Why does EGR need a blower?" In a uniflow two-stroke the exhaust is at lower pressure than the scavenge air; the gas will not flow the right way unaided.
"What do you do with the EGR bleed-off water?" Treat and monitor it before any discharge - it is acidic and carries soot and metals.
"How do you know EGR is hurting your liners?" Cylinder condition and scrape-down analysis - iron and residual base number.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which tier is your main engine certified to, and how do you know?
Show me your NOx Technical File and tell me what is in it.
You change an injector nozzle to a different specification. What is the compliance issue?
How does your engine know it has entered an emission control area, and what is recorded?
If your EGR system failed on passage into the area, what would you do?
What happens to your cylinder oil feed rate when the moisturizing system is in service?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Three levers, two families, two systems. LEVERS (1): temperature, oxygen, time - and NOx trades against fuel. FAMILIES: PRIMARY = less created - timing, Miller, injection, water, EGR (2); SECONDARY = destroyed after - essentially SCR alone (3). Compare on where, engine effect, plant, consumable, reach, failure (4), then the tier frame (5). SYSTEMS: SAM = water vapour, temperature lever, mist catcher (6); EGR = cleaned exhaust, temperature AND oxygen, scrubber and blower (7); and both put water and acid where the engine did not want them (8).
