blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: The entry-into-force date carries this whole regulatory frame, and it must come from the resolution rather than from a summary. Resolution MEPC.328(76) records deemed acceptance on 1 May 2022 at operative paragraph 2 and entry into force on 1 NOVEMBER 2022 at operative paragraph 3. Secondary summaries of this amendment circulate with the year wrong, giving 1 November 2023. Taken at face value that would place the Revised Annex VI eight months after this examination and make the whole frame inapplicable to it - which is the quickest way to recognise the error. Go to the operative paragraphs.

No provision of MARPOL Annex VI is quoted anywhere in this answer, and no NOx limit value is given. MIW holds Annex VI in a form that may be cited but not quoted from, so regulation 13 is named and its content described in substance. The limits are functions of the engine's rated speed and are set out in the instrument; the tiers are therefore given by what fixes which one applies and by their relative severity. That is a limitation, and it is stated rather than disguised - but it costs the answer very little, because the examinable content is the structure and not the numbers.

The regulatory text is the one applicable at this sitting and not a later consolidation. Regulation 13 as consolidated to 1 May 2024 incorporates a 2024 amendment to the major-conversion provision. That amendment is after this examination and is excluded entirely; do not 'update' this answer to the later consolidation, and be careful with any printed copy of Annex VI dated after the sitting you are answering for.

No percentage reduction, water ratio, recirculation rate, catalyst temperature window or reagent consumption figure is asserted anywhere, because every one is engine, fuel, load and installation specific. No engine builder, licensor, catalyst supplier, system trade name or proprietary arrangement is named - both of the technologies in limb B exist in more than one commercial implementation, and the answer describes the principle rather than any one product. The treatment and discharge requirements for EGR bleed-off water are stated in substance without citing the governing guidelines, which MIW does not hold in readable form. The revised NOx Technical Code 2008 is likewise cited by identity only.

steps.title: Why NOx forms at all, and the three levers every measure pulls
points: The nitrogen comes overwhelmingly from the AIR, not from the fuel
Nitrogen and oxygen combine at flame temperature; the rate rises very steeply with peak temperature
Lever one - peak temperature: add something that absorbs heat or raises the charge's specific heat
Lever two - oxygen availability: displace part of the oxygen with inert gas
Lever three - residence time: shorten the time spent at peak through timing and rate
The governing trade-off: NOx and fuel consumption pull against each other

steps.title: A) Primary measures - preventing NOx from forming
points: Definition: acts inside the cylinder so that less NOx is ever created
Combustion event - retarded injection timing (simplest, and costs fuel directly)
Injection pressure and rate shaping; common rail decoupling timing from speed and load
Miller timing with high-pressure charging - lower charge temperature at start of compression
Chamber, nozzle and swirl geometry, and compression ratio - design measures
Adding water - fuel-water emulsion, direct water injection, scavenge air moisturizing
Changing the charge - exhaust gas recirculation, and lean premixed gas operation

steps.title: A) Secondary measures - removing NOx after it has formed
points: Definition: the combustion is untouched and the exhaust is treated
Selective catalytic reduction is the only mature secondary measure
Reagent injected upstream of a catalyst; NOx and reagent react to nitrogen and water
Temperature-sensitive - which decides whether the reactor sits before or after the turbocharger
Sulphur-sensitive - salts form at low temperature and blind the catalyst
Dosing must be right, or ammonia slip; and a reagent, tank and supply chain are added
Space and back pressure - severe constraints in a retrofit
An exhaust gas scrubber is NOT a NOx measure - it addresses SOx and particulates

steps.title: A) Primary against secondary - the comparison the limb asks for
points: Compare on where it acts, engine effect, plant, consumables, reach, failure mode
Primary: no plant or modest plant, but a fuel penalty; secondary: no fuel penalty, but a large installation and a reagent
Primary degrades gradually; secondary can fail as a system and lose the whole benefit at once
Primary measures are cumulative and are used together, designed in rather than added on
The dividing line is where the NOx goes, not where the equipment sits
Which is why EGR is PRIMARY - the commonest error in the question
They are complements: primary for the ordinary limit, a heavy primary or a secondary measure for the strict one

steps.title: A) The regulatory frame that decides which you need
points: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13; at this sitting the Revised Annex VI, in force 1 November 2022
Three tiers, each limit a function of the engine's rated speed
Construction date fixes the tier; the strictest tier also depends on where the ship is operating
Two operating modes, and the changeover recorded with date, time and position
An output threshold applies, and certain emergency and survival-craft engines are excluded
Certification under the revised NOx Technical Code 2008; compliance in service through the NOx Technical File
No limit value is quoted - and the point that matters is that the strictest tier is a step change unreachable by combustion tuning alone

steps.title: B) Scavenge Air Moisturizing
points: Water evaporated into the scavenge air after the charge air cooler
Latent heat absorbed on evaporation, and water vapour's higher specific heat - both lower the peak temperature
A humidification section, often multi-stage with re-heat between stages
Water supply and treatment - what reaches the cylinder must be fresh and clean; salt would be ruinous
A water mist catcher - vapour into the cylinder, never droplets. The safety-critical item
Costs: corrosion, disturbed cylinder lubrication, fresh water demand, a small efficiency penalty, control complexity
A primary measure, substantial, but normally part of a package rather than a complete Tier III answer

steps.title: B) Exhaust Gas Recirculation
points: Part of the exhaust cleaned, cooled and returned to the scavenge air
Reduces oxygen concentration - the oxygen lever
Raises the charge's specific heat via CO2 and water vapour - the temperature lever. Two levers at once
Arrangement: scrubber, cooler, water mist catcher, EGR blower, shut-off and change-over valves
Turbocharger arrangements to suit - cut-out, variable geometry or auxiliary blowers
Bleed-off water treatment - acidic, soot and metal laden, monitored before any discharge
Costs: fouling, acid corrosion, soot in the cylinder, complexity, blower power, waste streams
A PRIMARY measure, capable of the strictest tier on its own

steps.title: B) SAM against EGR - what each costs to fit and to run
points: SAM pulls temperature only; EGR pulls temperature AND oxygen, which is why it reaches further
SAM adds water vapour; EGR adds cleaned, cooled exhaust
SAM is moderate plant; EGR is high plant with a scrubber, blower and water treatment
SAM consumes fresh water; EGR consumes blower power and produces sludge and bleed-off water
SAM's principal risk is water carry-over; EGR's is fouling and acid corrosion
Both put water and acid where the engine's designer did not intend them
So both transfer a burden onto cylinder lubrication and monitoring - scrape-down analysis is how it is watched

questions.memory_cue: Three levers, two families, two systems. LEVERS (1): temperature, oxygen, time, and NOx trades against fuel. FAMILIES: PRIMARY = less created - timing, Miller, water, EGR (2); SECONDARY = destroyed after - essentially SCR alone (3); compare on where, engine, plant, consumable, reach, failure (4); then the tier frame (5). SYSTEMS: SAM = water vapour, temperature lever, mist catcher (6); EGR = cleaned exhaust, two levers, scrubber and blower (7); both leave water and acid in the cylinder (8).
questions.understand_first: The first thing to get straight is where the nitrogen comes from, because it explains everything else. It is not in the fuel in any quantity that matters - it comes out of the air the engine breathes, which is four-fifths nitrogen and normally quite happy to stay that way. What changes that is heat. Make the flame hot enough and the nitrogen and oxygen in the charge start combining, and the hotter it gets the more dramatically that happens. So every method of controlling NOx is really a way of doing one of three things: making the flame cooler, giving it less oxygen to work with, or giving it less time at its hottest. And here is the cruel part, which is the reason this is an engineering problem rather than a solved one: a hot, fast, oxygen-rich burn is exactly what a thermally efficient diesel engine wants. Everything you do to reduce NOx costs you fuel, one way or another. That is why the industry ended up with two philosophies. Either you interfere with the combustion and accept the penalty - which people call a primary measure - or you let the engine burn as it pleases and clean up the exhaust afterwards, which is a secondary measure. And the classification is about what happens to the NOx, not about where the machinery is bolted. Exhaust gas recirculation has a scrubber, a cooler and a blower all sitting outside the engine, and it is still a primary measure - because what it actually does is send some used exhaust back round into the charge, which both cools the burn and starves it of oxygen, so the NOx is never made in the first place. Scavenge air moisturizing does the same job more simply, by loading the incoming air with water vapour: the water soaks up heat as it evaporates, the burn runs cooler, and less NOx forms. Both leave you with the same practical problem down in the engine room - water and acid in places the engine was not designed to have them, which is why the cylinder oil and the scrape-down samples become the thing you watch.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Formation. The nitrogen comes from the AIR. Rate rises very steeply with peak temperature, and depends on oxygen and residence time - the three levers. NOx trades against fuel consumption: everything that cools the burn costs efficiency. PRIMARY = less NOx created (in-cylinder): retarded injection timing; injection pressure and rate shaping; common rail; Miller timing with high-pressure charging; chamber and nozzle design; water - fuel-water emulsion, direct water injection, scavenge air moisturizing; and EGR. SECONDARY = NOx destroyed after forming: essentially SCR alone - reagent injected upstream of a catalyst, reacting to nitrogen and water; temperature-sensitive (deciding pre- or post-turbocharger placement), sulphur-sensitive (salts blind the catalyst), dosing-sensitive (ammonia slip), and it brings a reagent, a tank, space and back pressure. A scrubber is NOT a NOx measure. Compare on where it acts, engine effect, plant, consumables, reach, failure mode. EGR IS PRIMARY despite all its plant being outside the cylinder - classify by where the NOx goes. Frame: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13, Revised Annex VI in force 1 November 2022; three tiers, each a function of rated speed; construction date fixes the tier and the strictest tier is geographic, so two modes and a recorded changeover; certification under the revised NOx Technical Code 2008 with the NOx Technical File. SAM: water evaporated into scavenge air after the cooler - latent heat plus higher specific heat; needs humidification, clean fresh water and a water mist catcher; watch corrosion and cylinder lubrication. EGR: exhaust cleaned, cooled and returned - less oxygen AND higher specific heat; needs scrubber, cooler, mist catcher, blower, valves, turbocharger arrangements and bleed-off water treatment; watch fouling, acid and soot. Both leave water and acid in the cylinder.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13 controls nitrogen oxides from marine diesel engines. At this sitting the applicable text is the Revised Annex VI introduced by resolution MEPC.328(76), which entered into force on 1 November 2022 - established from the resolution's own operative paragraph 3, because secondary summaries of this amendment circulate with the date one year late. The regulation sets three tiers of progressively stricter limits, each expressed as a function of the engine's rated speed; which tier applies is fixed by the ship's construction date, and the strictest tier depends besides on operation within a designated NOx emission control area, so the engine runs in two modes and the changeover is recorded with date, time and position. Certification is under the revised NOx Technical Code 2008 and compliance in service rests on the NOx Technical File. No provision is quoted and no limit value is asserted.
quick_revision.major_trap: Calling exhaust gas recirculation a secondary measure. All of its plant sits outside the cylinder, which makes it look like after-treatment - but it works by preventing formation, so it is primary. Classify by where the NOx goes, not by where the equipment is bolted. Second trap: offering an exhaust gas scrubber as a NOx measure - it addresses sulphur oxides and particulates and does essentially nothing for NOx. Third: saying the nitrogen comes from the fuel; it comes overwhelmingly from the air. Fourth: describing primary and secondary measures separately and never comparing them, when the stem prints vis-a-vis. Fifth: omitting the NOx-fuel consumption trade-off, which is the whole reason the choice exists. Sixth: forgetting the water mist catcher on a SAM system or the scrubber on an EGR loop - the two components that make each system survivable. Seventh: quoting limit values or percentage reductions as though they were general figures.

retrieval_cards.answer: Limb A: 1 formation and the three levers. 2 primary measures in three families. 3 secondary measures - essentially SCR. 4 the comparison on six axes, placing EGR on the primary side. 5 the tier frame that decides what you need. Limb B: 6 scavenge air moisturizing. 7 exhaust gas recirculation. 8 the two compared, and what they cost to run.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does NOx form, and what are the three levers for controlling it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The nitrogen comes overwhelmingly from the air, not the fuel. At flame temperature nitrogen and oxygen combine, and the rate rises very steeply with peak temperature and depends besides on oxygen availability and on residence time at temperature. Those three are the only levers there are, and every control measure pulls at least one of them.
retrieval_cards.why: Stating the mechanism first makes every measure in the answer derivable instead of memorised.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish primary from secondary NOx reduction.
retrieval_cards.answer: Primary acts on the combustion so that less NOx is ever created - the exhaust leaving the cylinder is already cleaner. Secondary leaves the combustion alone and destroys the NOx after it has formed, in the exhaust system. The dividing line is where the NOx goes, not where the equipment sits - which is why EGR, whose plant is entirely outside the cylinder, is a primary measure.
retrieval_cards.why: The classification rule is the whole of limb A, and the wrong formulation of it produces the question's commonest error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is exhaust gas recirculation a primary or a secondary measure?
retrieval_cards.answer: Primary. Every part of an EGR installation - scrubber, cooler, mist catcher, blower - sits outside the cylinder, which makes it look like after-treatment. But it works by returning cleaned exhaust to the charge, which reduces oxygen concentration and raises the charge's specific heat, so the NOx is never formed. Prevention, not removal.
retrieval_cards.why: The single commonest error in the question, and the discrimination the limb is built to test.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain scavenge air moisturizing.
retrieval_cards.answer: Water is evaporated into the scavenge air after the charge air cooler, so the charge carries a large mass of water vapour into the cylinder. The water absorbs latent heat as it evaporates and the vapour has a higher specific heat than air, so the peak combustion temperature falls and less NOx forms. It needs a humidification section, clean fresh water, and a water mist catcher - vapour must enter the cylinder, never droplets.
retrieval_cards.why: It pulls only the temperature lever, and the mist catcher is the component that makes it survivable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain exhaust gas recirculation, and why it needs so much plant.
retrieval_cards.answer: Part of the exhaust is cleaned, cooled and returned to the scavenge air, which reduces oxygen and raises specific heat - two levers at once, which is why it can reach the strictest tier alone. The plant is large because marine exhaust is dirty: a scrubber to remove sulphur oxides and soot, a cooler, a water mist catcher, an EGR blower (the exhaust is at lower pressure than the scavenge air), shut-off valves, turbocharger arrangements, and bleed-off water treatment.
retrieval_cards.why: The arrangement follows from the mechanism, and the blower and the scrubber are the two items candidates omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does selective catalytic reduction work, and what are its four sensitivities?
retrieval_cards.answer: A reducing agent - normally an aqueous urea solution giving ammonia - is injected into the exhaust upstream of a catalyst, over which the nitrogen oxides and the reagent react to nitrogen and water. It is sensitive to temperature (which decides whether the reactor sits before or after the turbocharger), to fuel sulphur (salts form at low temperature and blind the catalyst), to dosing (too much gives ammonia slip), and to space and back pressure.
retrieval_cards.why: SCR is effectively the whole of the secondary side, so its characteristics carry half of limb A's second part.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Will an exhaust gas scrubber reduce your NOx?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. A scrubber addresses sulphur oxides and particulate matter and has essentially no effect on nitrogen oxides. The confusion arises because an EGR loop also contains a scrubber - but there the scrubber is cleaning gas that is about to go back into the engine, not cleaning the exhaust on its way out.
retrieval_cards.why: A frequent and expensive confusion, and the EGR loop's own scrubber is what causes it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is NOx regulated, and what fixes which tier applies?
retrieval_cards.answer: By MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13 - at this sitting, the Revised Annex VI introduced by resolution MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022. There are three tiers, each limit a function of the engine's rated speed. The ship's construction date fixes the tier, and the strictest tier applies besides only within a designated NOx emission control area - so the engine runs in two modes and the changeover is recorded with date, time and position.
retrieval_cards.why: The tier structure is the frame; the values are not quotable and are not what is being examined.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What do SAM and EGR have in common that lands on the Chief Engineer?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both work by making the combustion cooler, and both put water and acid where the designer of a dry engine did not intend them. Both therefore transfer a burden onto cylinder lubrication: the oil film is disturbed, the acid load rises, and feed rate and residual base number need watching. Scrape-down analysis is how it is watched, whichever system is fitted.
retrieval_cards.why: It joins this question to the oil analysis question on the same paper and is the practical consequence an examiner will press on.

blocks.h: 1. What the question is asking - the power chain, and where effective power sits

blocks.p: Limb A asks for the stages by which the power produced in the cylinder becomes the power that actually moves the ship. The answer is a chain of named powers, each smaller than the one before it, with a named efficiency across every step. Setting the chain out first and then walking down it is what turns this into a structured answer rather than a list of definitions.

rows: Indicated power
The power developed in the cylinders, from the work done on the pistons
From the indicator diagram - in the engine itself
Brake power
The power delivered at the engine coupling, after the engine's own friction
At the output flange - historically on a brake, which is where the name comes from
Shaft power
The power transmitted along the shafting
By torsionmeter, on the line shaft
Delivered power
The power actually reaching the propeller, after the stern tube
Not directly measurable in service - inferred from shaft power
Thrust power
The power in the thrust the propeller produces
Thrust multiplied by speed of advance
Effective power
The power needed to move the hull at that speed
Total resistance multiplied by ship speed - the towrope power

blocks.p: Effective power is the destination, and its definition is the key to the whole limb. It is the power that would be required to tow the hull through the water at that speed - resistance multiplied by speed - which is why it is also called towrope power. It is the useful output of the entire installation, and everything between the cylinder and it is loss.

Note the direction of travel, because it is where candidates get confused. The naval architect works upwards: he predicts the resistance of the hull, obtains the effective power required, and divides by the efficiencies to find what the engine must produce. The engineer measures downwards: he reads what the engine is producing and asks how much of it is reaching the water. They are the same chain read in opposite directions.

blocks.h: 2. A) Indicated power to brake power - the engine's own losses

blocks.p: Indicated power is derived from the indicator diagram - the pressure-volume trace taken from the cylinder. The area of that diagram gives the work done on the piston in one cycle; multiplied by the number of cycles in unit time and by the piston area and stroke, it gives the power developed inside the cylinder. It is the true gross output of the combustion process and it is the only power in the chain that is measured in the engine rather than outside it.
Between the piston and the coupling flange, the engine consumes part of its own output:

ul: Friction at the piston rings and skirt, at the crosshead, crankpin and main bearings, and in the running gear generally - by a wide margin the largest of these losses.
Driven auxiliaries hung on the engine - camshaft drive, lubricating and cooling pumps, governor drive, and the scavenge or supercharging arrangement where it is engine-driven.
Pumping and windage losses within the engine itself.

blocks.p: What is left at the coupling is brake power, and the ratio between them is the mechanical efficiency of the engine. Two practical points belong here. First, mechanical efficiency is not constant - the friction loss is relatively steady while the output varies, so the engine is mechanically least efficient at low load, which is one reason slow steaming is not free. Second, the difference between indicated and brake power is exactly the quantity a friction power or motoring test measures, and it is the figure that changes when the running gear deteriorates.

blocks.h: 3. A) Brake power to shaft power to delivered power - the transmission

blocks.p: From the coupling the power passes down the shafting, and each element in it takes a share:

ul: Thrust block - which transfers the propeller's thrust into the hull and, in doing so, absorbs power in its bearing surfaces.
Intermediate and line shaft bearings - a small loss each, but there may be many of them in a long shaft line.
Stern tube bearing and seals - the last and often the largest single element of the transmission loss, and the one most affected by alignment and by wear.
Reduction gearing, where fitted - a medium-speed or geared installation adds a gearbox loss that a direct-coupled slow-speed engine does not have.
The electrical chain, in a diesel-electric installation - generator, switchboard and converter, propulsion motor - which replaces the gearbox with a longer chain of its own.

blocks.p: Shaft power is the power measured on the line shafting, normally by a torsionmeter reading the angle of twist over a known length: torque multiplied by angular velocity. It is the most useful measurement in the whole chain, because it is the last point at which power can be measured directly and it is measured in service, continuously, on a modern ship.

Delivered power is what remains at the propeller after the stern tube. It cannot be measured directly - there is nothing to instrument aft of the stern tube - so it is inferred from shaft power and the estimated stern tube loss. The ratio of delivered to brake power is the transmission or shaft efficiency, and its most important practical property is that it is sensitive to alignment: a shaft line out of alignment loses power continuously and heats bearings while it does so.

blocks.h: 4. A) Delivered power to thrust power to effective power - the propeller and the hull

blocks.p: This is where the largest losses occur, and it is the part of the chain candidates most often skip. Three separate effects sit between the delivered power and the effective power, and each has its own named efficiency.

First, the propeller in open water. A propeller turning in undisturbed water converts delivered power into thrust power - thrust multiplied by the speed of advance, which is the speed of the water into the propeller and not the speed of the ship. The ratio is the open-water efficiency, and the losses are real and unavoidable: the water is accelerated astern and carries kinetic energy away with it, there is rotational energy in the slipstream, and there is blade friction. This is normally the single biggest loss in the entire chain.

Second, the propeller behind the hull is not the propeller in open water. It works in the wake, in a flow that is neither uniform nor at ship speed, so its efficiency there differs from its open-water efficiency. The ratio between the two is the relative rotative efficiency.
Third, the hull and the propeller interact, in two opposite directions. This is the interesting part of the limb and it is worth stating carefully:

rows: Wake, expressed as the wake fraction
The hull drags a layer of water along with it, so the water entering the propeller is slower than the ship. The speed of advance is therefore less than the ship speed
Helps. The propeller does its work in slower water and needs less power for the same thrust
Thrust deduction, expressed as the thrust deduction fraction
The working propeller lowers the pressure ahead of itself and therefore increases the hull's resistance. The thrust required is greater than the towed resistance would suggest
Hurts. Some of the thrust produced is spent overcoming resistance the propeller itself created

blocks.p: The two combine into the hull efficiency, which - uniquely in this chain - can exceed unity, because the wake gain often outweighs the thrust deduction penalty. That is not a paradox and it is not an error: hull efficiency is not a thermodynamic efficiency but a ratio between two ways of accounting for the same work, and a candidate who states it and explains why has demonstrated that he understands the chain rather than memorised it.

What emerges at the end is the effective power - resistance multiplied by ship speed, the power that would tow the bare hull at that speed against the sum of frictional, residuary and appendage resistance, plus whatever the wind and the sea are adding on the day.

blocks.h: 5. A) The efficiencies pulled together - the propulsive coefficient

blocks.p: The stem asks for stages, so the answer should close the limb by putting them back together. Two combined figures are used in practice, and the distinction between them is a reliable mark:

ul: The quasi-propulsive coefficient - effective power divided by delivered power. It combines the open-water efficiency, the relative rotative efficiency and the hull efficiency, and it is therefore a statement about the hull and propeller together. It says nothing about the machinery.

The propulsive coefficient - effective power divided by shaft or brake power. It is the quasi-propulsive coefficient multiplied by the transmission efficiency, and it is therefore a statement about the whole installation.

blocks.p: No typical value is offered for any efficiency in this chain, and that is deliberate. Every one of them is specific to the hull form, the propeller, the machinery arrangement and the loading condition, and a figure carried from one ship to another is misleading rather than merely imprecise. What matters in the examination is that the chain, the names and the direction of each effect are right.

And the practical use of the whole limb is this: the chain is how a fouled hull, a damaged propeller and a worn engine are told apart. If shaft power is up for the same speed, the loss is aft of the shaft - hull or propeller. If fuel consumption is up for the same shaft power, the loss is in the engine. Without the chain the two look identical from the bridge.

blocks.h: 6. B) What sea trials are for, and the conditions that make them valid

blocks.p: Sea trials exist to verify by measurement what has until then only been predicted. The naval architect's model tests and calculations, the engine builder's shop trials and the manoeuvring predictions are all forecasts; the trial is the first and only occasion on which the complete ship, in her own water, is made to demonstrate them. They serve four distinct purposes at once:

ul: Contractual - the speed, power and consumption guarantees in the building contract are proved or not proved here, and money turns on the result.
Statutory and classification - flag State, class and the attending surveyors require certain demonstrations before the ship enters service.
Operational - the results become the manoeuvring information the ship carries for the rest of her life, which is the part that matters to those who will sail her.
Baseline - the trial figures are the datum against which every later performance measurement, and every argument about hull fouling, is judged.

blocks.p: The conditions are as important as the manoeuvres, because a trial run in the wrong conditions produces numbers that cannot be compared with anything. The standard requirements are:

ul: Deep, unrestricted water. Shallow water increases resistance and changes both squat and turning behaviour, and confined water changes them again.
Low sea state and wind, with the limits agreed beforehand, and the state recorded.
The specified loading condition and trim, which is normally ballast for a newbuilding and must be recorded either way, since displacement changes everything measured.
A steady approach - the ship settled on a constant heading at constant revolutions before the manoeuvre begins, or the result belongs to the approach rather than to the ship.
Runs on reciprocal headings, so that current and tidal stream cancel in the mean. A speed trial run one way only measures the current as much as the ship.
A clean hull and propeller, and a calibrated instrument set - shaft torsionmeter, fuel meters, position and speed reference.

blocks.h: 7. B) The navigation trials, and what each establishes

rows: Progressive speed trial
Measured runs at several power settings, each on reciprocal headings, with speed, shaft power and revolutions recorded
The power-speed and power-revolution curves, the contract speed at the contract power, and the datum for the ship's whole service life. This is the trial that closes the power chain of limb A
Endurance and fuel consumption trial
A sustained run at a specified power for an agreed period
Specific fuel consumption against the guarantee, and the stability of the plant under continuous load
Turning circle
From a steady approach at a defined speed, rudder put hard over and held through at least 360 degrees. Run to both port and starboard
Advance, transfer, tactical diameter, drift angle and speed loss in the turn - the ship's turning ability, and the numbers a master needs to know before he needs them
Zig-zag manoeuvre

Rudder put over a set angle; when the heading has changed by a set amount the rudder is reversed to the same angle on the other side, and so on. Run in the two standard combinations - equal rudder and heading angles, at a smaller and at a larger value
Yaw-checking and course-changing ability, read from the overshoot angles - how far the head continues to swing after the rudder is reversed. The single most informative manoeuvring trial there is
Spiral and reverse spiral
Steady rates of turn are recorded against a series of rudder angles, from hard over to hard over and back
Whether the ship is dynamically stable in course, and if not, the width of the loop - which tells the master how much rudder she needs simply to go straight
Pull-out test
The ship is brought to a steady turn, the rudder returned to midships, and the rate of turn recorded as it decays
A quicker check on course stability. On a stable ship the rate of turn decays to zero; on an unstable ship it settles at a residual rate
Crash stop, or stopping test
From full ahead at a steady heading, the engine is ordered full astern and held until the ship is dead in the water
Head reach, track reach, lateral deviation and time to stop. Also a severe test of the engine's astern capability and of the shafting
Astern trial
Running astern at specified powers, and the ahead-astern-ahead sequence
Astern power, the number of consecutive starts available, and steering behaviour going astern
Minimum revolutions and steerage trial
The lowest stable engine speed is established, and the lowest ship speed at which the ship still answers her helm
The minimum manoeuvring speed - which decides what is possible in a channel or alongside
Steering gear trial
The rudder is run hard over to hard over at service speed and at the deepest draught, on the main and then on the auxiliary power unit, with changeover and emergency steering demonstrated
That the steering gear meets its required rate of movement and that control from the alternative position works
Anchoring trial
Anchor let go and recovered from a specified depth, on both sides
Windlass hoisting capability and brake holding power - the trial most often treated as a formality and most missed when it was not run properly

blocks.p: Several other demonstrations are run in the same period and are worth naming even though they are not navigation trials in the strict sense: the inclining experiment to establish the lightship weight and centre of gravity; machinery trials including blackout and dead-ship recovery, alarm and safety-device demonstrations, and remote-control and bridge-control response; and vibration and noise measurement through the speed range to identify critical revolutions and any barred speed range.

blocks.h: 8. B) What the results become

blocks.p: A trial that produces a report and nothing else has been half wasted. The results are turned into the documents the ship then carries and uses, which is the point at which the whole exercise becomes operational rather than contractual:

ul: The manoeuvring booklet, holding the full trial results - turning circles, stopping distances, zig-zag data, and the behaviour in shallow water and in the ballast and loaded conditions.
The wheelhouse poster, being the essential figures displayed permanently where they will actually be read.
The pilot card, completed by the master and handed to the pilot on boarding - the single most useful piece of paper in the exchange.

The speed-power curve and the trial datum, against which every subsequent performance report is measured, and which is what makes an argument about hull fouling or a charterparty speed claim capable of being settled.

blocks.p: IMO's standards for ship manoeuvrability set the criteria against which turning, yaw-checking, course-keeping and stopping ability are judged, and the requirement that manoeuvring information be provided on board is what turns the trial results into the poster, the booklet and the card. Both are cited here by identity: no criterion value is quoted, because neither instrument was read at source for this answer.

And the sentence worth closing on, because it joins the two limbs the stem has deliberately put together: limb A is the theory of where the power goes, and the speed trial in limb B is the measurement that proves it. The trial produces the delivered power actually needed for a given speed; the chain explains why that number is what it is; and for the rest of the ship's life the difference between the two is the ship's condition.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Two limbs with no printed marks, so treat them as eight and eight. Limb A is a chain - name every stage, name the efficiency across every step, and finish by putting them back together. Limb B is a list with objectives, and the stem says so: it asks for the trials and the typical objectives of each test. A trial named without its objective earns half of what it could.

The single best way to open limb A is to write the chain down as a line before explaining any part of it: indicated, brake, shaft, delivered, thrust, effective. Six words, and the examiner can already see that you know the answer.

blocks.h: The chain in one line

blocks.p: INDICATED (in the cylinder, from the indicator diagram) → mechanical efficiency → BRAKE (at the coupling) → transmission and shaft efficiency → SHAFT (torsionmeter) → DELIVERED (at the propeller) → open-water and relative rotative efficiency → THRUST (thrust × speed of advance) → hull efficiency → EFFECTIVE (resistance × ship speed = towrope power).

blocks.h: Definitions that must be exact

ul: Effective power = total resistance × ship speed. The power to tow the hull at that speed. Also called towrope power.
Thrust power = thrust × speed of ADVANCE - the speed of the water into the propeller, not the ship's speed. Getting this wrong unravels the rest of the limb.
Shaft power is measured by torsionmeter - torque × angular velocity - and is the last power in the chain that can be measured directly.
Delivered power cannot be measured at all; it is inferred from shaft power less the stern tube loss.

blocks.h: The two hull-propeller interaction effects - and which way each acts

blocks.p: Wake HELPS. The hull drags water along with it, so the propeller works in slower water than the ship is moving through - the speed of advance is less than the ship speed. Thrust deduction HURTS. The working propeller lowers the pressure ahead of itself and increases the hull's resistance, so more thrust is needed than the towed resistance suggests. Together they give hull efficiency, and stating that hull efficiency can exceed unity - because the wake gain usually outweighs the thrust deduction penalty - is the mark that separates a good answer from an adequate one.

blocks.h: QPC against propulsive coefficient

blocks.p: Quasi-propulsive coefficient = effective ÷ DELIVERED power - hull and propeller only, and it says nothing about the machinery. Propulsive coefficient = effective ÷ SHAFT or BRAKE power - the whole installation, being the QPC multiplied by the transmission efficiency. Knowing which denominator belongs to which is a small, reliable mark.

blocks.h: Do not quote efficiency values

blocks.p: No typical value is given anywhere in this answer for any efficiency, and none should be. Each is hull-form, propeller, machinery and loading specific, and a figure carried from one ship to another is misleading rather than approximate. Naming the chain, the efficiencies and the direction of each effect is what is being examined.

blocks.h: The trials that carry the most marks

ul: Progressive speed trial - the power-speed curve, the contract speed, and the datum for the ship's life. Run on reciprocal headings or you are measuring the tide.
Turning circle - advance, transfer, tactical diameter, drift angle and speed loss. Both sides.
Zig-zag - the overshoot angles, giving yaw-checking and course-changing ability. The most informative single manoeuvre.
Spiral, reverse spiral and pull-out - course stability, and the width of the loop if she is unstable.
Crash stop - head reach, track reach and time to dead in the water.
Steering gear trial - hard over to hard over, main and auxiliary units, changeover and emergency steering.

blocks.h: Conditions - the marks nobody writes

blocks.p: Deep unrestricted water, low sea and wind, the specified loading condition, a steady approach, reciprocal headings, clean hull and calibrated instruments. Two or three lines on conditions will earn more than a tenth trial, because they show that you understand what a measurement is for. And the sharpest single point: shallow water changes both resistance and turning behaviour, so a trial run in shallow water measures a different ship.

blocks.h: Close both limbs together

blocks.p: The stem sets the two limbs side by side, and the connection is real: the speed trial is the measurement that closes the power chain. The chain predicts the delivered power needed for a speed; the trial measures what was actually needed; and for the rest of the ship's life the gap between them is the ship's condition. Say that in one sentence at the end and the answer reads as one argument rather than two.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Muddling the order of the chain, or omitting delivered power between shaft and thrust power.
Defining thrust power with the ship's speed instead of the speed of advance.
Leaving out the hull-propeller interaction entirely - the wake and thrust deduction pair is where the thinking is.
Saying an efficiency greater than one is impossible. Hull efficiency commonly exceeds unity, and the reason is explainable.
Confusing the quasi-propulsive coefficient with the propulsive coefficient.
Quoting typical efficiency values as though they were general.
Listing trials without their objectives, when the stem asks for the objective of each test.
Forgetting the conditions - deep water, low sea state, loading condition, reciprocal headings.
Omitting the steering gear and anchoring trials, which are easy marks.
Stopping at the trial report and never mentioning the manoeuvring booklet, wheelhouse poster and pilot card.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "What is effective power?" Resistance × ship speed - the power to tow the hull at that speed. Not anything the engine produces.
"Speed of advance or ship speed in thrust power?" Speed of advance, which is lower because of the wake.
"Can an efficiency exceed one?" Hull efficiency can, because the wake gain usually outweighs the thrust deduction penalty. It is a ratio of two accountings, not a thermodynamic efficiency.
"Where do you measure power on your ship?" Shaft power, by torsionmeter. Delivered power cannot be measured.
"Your speed is down. Engine or hull?" Compare shaft power against speed, and fuel against shaft power. The first isolates the hull and propeller, the second the engine.
"Why run a speed trial both ways?" To cancel current and tidal stream in the mean.
"Why must trials be in deep water?" Shallow water increases resistance and alters turning and squat - it is a different ship.
"What does a zig-zag tell you that a turning circle does not?" Yaw-checking ability - how quickly she stops swinging when you reverse the rudder, read from the overshoot angles.
"What is on the pilot card, and who fills it in?" The essential manoeuvring data, completed by the master and given to the pilot on boarding.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Show me your torsionmeter reading and tell me what you do with it.
What is your ship's tactical diameter loaded, and where would you find it?
How would you demonstrate the steering gear before departure?
How long does your ship take to stop from full ahead, and how far does she go?
What is a barred speed range and why does your ship have one?
How do you know your hull is fouled rather than your engine being down on power?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb A - six powers, five efficiencies. I-B-S-D-T-E: Indicated (1, 2), Brake (2), Shaft and Delivered (3), Thrust (4), Effective (4) - then pull them together as QPC and propulsive coefficient (5). Remember the two interaction effects by direction: wake helps, thrust deduction hurts. Limb B - conditions, then trials, then documents. CONDITIONS (6): deep water, calm, correct loading, reciprocal headings. TRIALS (7): speed, turning, zig-zag, spiral and pull-out, crash stop, astern, steering gear, anchor. DOCUMENTS (8): booklet, poster, pilot card, and the trial datum.

The trial manoeuvres, their method and their objectives
Established shipbuilding and trials practice. The precise programme is contractual - contract, owner's specification and flag State requirements
The criteria for turning, yaw-checking, course-keeping and stopping

blocks.h: Uncertainty and evidence notes

blocks.p: This is the only wholly fresh question on the paper. No solved question anywhere in the MIW set treats either limb, so this answer was written from first principles with no earlier answer to build on and no existing verification record to lean on. The compensating obligation is that every statement carries its own grade, and it does: the power chain and its efficiencies are engineering reference, the trials are established shipbuilding practice, and the connection drawn between the two limbs is engineering judgement and is identified as such.

No numerical value or typical range is asserted for any efficiency - not for mechanical, transmission, shaft, open-water, relative rotative or hull efficiency, and not for the quasi-propulsive or propulsive coefficient. Each is hull-form, propeller, machinery and installation specific, and a range carried between ships would be misleading rather than merely imprecise.

No sea trial acceptance criterion is quoted as a number. The three IMO instruments touched - the standards for ship manoeuvrability, the requirement to provide manoeuvring information on board, and the steering gear trial - are cited by identity only. None was read at source in this session; no provision is quoted, no regulation number is asserted beyond the identity of the instrument, and the application thresholds by ship length, type and date of build are not stated. The existence of overshoot, advance, tactical diameter and stopping criteria is stated; their values are not.

No shipyard, model basin, designer, engine builder, classification society rule or software is named anywhere. And the trial programme described is the standard one rather than a closed statutory list: which trials are run, in what order and to what tolerance is fixed by the building contract, the owner's specification and the flag State's requirements. The stem does not say which machinery arrangement is intended, so the chain is given for a direct-coupled installation and the additional stages of a geared or diesel-electric plant are identified where they arise rather than assumed away.

This question carries no temporal exposure at all. Naval architecture does not date, the trial set has been stable for decades, and the three instruments touched were all long operative at this sitting. Nothing here turns on the 2023 boundaries that govern the rest of the paper.

steps.title: What the question is asking - the power chain, and where effective power sits
points: A chain of named powers, each smaller than the last, with a named efficiency across every step
Indicated - in the cylinder, from the indicator diagram
Brake - at the coupling; Shaft - on the line shafting, by torsionmeter
Delivered - at the propeller; Thrust - thrust × speed of advance
Effective - resistance × ship speed, the towrope power
The naval architect reads the chain upwards; the engineer measures downwards

steps.title: A) Indicated power to brake power - the engine's own losses
points: Indicated power from the indicator diagram - work on the piston per cycle
The only power in the chain measured inside the engine
Losses: friction at rings, crosshead, crankpin and main bearings - much the largest
Engine-driven auxiliaries - camshaft, pumps, governor, scavenge arrangement
Pumping and windage within the engine
The ratio is mechanical efficiency
It is not constant - friction is steady while output varies, so the engine is worst at low load

steps.title: A) Brake power to shaft power to delivered power - the transmission
points: Thrust block, intermediate and line shaft bearings, and the stern tube - usually the largest single element
Reduction gearing where fitted; the electrical chain in a diesel-electric plant
Shaft power measured by torsionmeter - torque × angular velocity
The last point in the chain where power can be measured directly
Delivered power is what reaches the propeller and cannot be measured - it is inferred
The ratio is transmission or shaft efficiency, and it is sensitive to alignment

steps.title: A) Delivered power to thrust power to effective power - the propeller and the hull
points: Open-water efficiency - accelerated water astern, rotational slipstream energy, blade friction. Normally the biggest loss in the chain
Thrust power = thrust × SPEED OF ADVANCE, not ship speed
Relative rotative efficiency - the propeller behind the hull is not the propeller in open water
Wake fraction: the hull drags water along, so the propeller works in slower water - it HELPS
Thrust deduction fraction: the working propeller raises the hull's resistance - it HURTS
Together they give hull efficiency, which can exceed unity, and the reason is explainable
Effective power = resistance × ship speed - the destination

steps.title: A) The efficiencies pulled together - the propulsive coefficient
points: Quasi-propulsive coefficient = effective ÷ delivered - hull and propeller only
Propulsive coefficient = effective ÷ shaft or brake - the whole installation
The second is the first multiplied by the transmission efficiency
No typical value is offered for any efficiency - all are installation specific
The diagnostic use: shaft power up for the same speed means hull or propeller
Fuel up for the same shaft power means the engine

steps.title: B) What sea trials are for, and the conditions that make them valid
points: To verify by measurement what has until then been predicted
Four purposes at once: contractual, statutory, operational and baseline
Deep, unrestricted water - shallow water changes resistance, squat and turning
Low sea state and wind, recorded; the specified loading condition and trim
A steady approach before the manoeuvre begins
Reciprocal headings, so current and tide cancel in the mean
Clean hull and propeller, and calibrated instruments

steps.title: B) The navigation trials, and what each establishes
points: Progressive speed trial - the power-speed curve, the contract speed, and the service datum
Endurance and consumption - specific fuel consumption against the guarantee
Turning circle - advance, transfer, tactical diameter, drift angle, speed loss. Both sides
Zig-zag - overshoot angles, giving yaw-checking and course-changing ability
Spiral, reverse spiral and pull-out - course stability and the width of the loop
Crash stop - head reach, track reach and time to dead in the water
Astern and minimum steerage trials - astern power, consecutive starts, minimum manoeuvring speed
Steering gear trial - hard over to hard over, main and auxiliary, changeover and emergency steering
Anchoring trial - windlass capability and brake holding power

steps.title: B) What the results become
points: The manoeuvring booklet - the full trial results, loaded and ballast, deep and shallow
The wheelhouse poster - the essential figures where they will be read
The pilot card - completed by the master and handed over on boarding
The speed-power curve and trial datum - what makes a fouling or speed-claim argument settleable
The manoeuvrability standards and the manoeuvring-information requirement, cited by identity only
The joining sentence: limb A is the theory, and the speed trial is the measurement that proves it

questions.memory_cue: Limb A - six powers, five efficiencies. Indicated to Brake is mechanical (2); Brake to Shaft to Delivered is transmission (3); Delivered to Thrust to Effective is the propeller and the hull, where wake helps and thrust deduction hurts (4); then combine as QPC and propulsive coefficient (5). Limb B - conditions, trials, documents. Deep water, calm, correct loading, reciprocal headings (6); speed, turning, zig-zag, spiral, crash stop, astern, steering gear, anchor (7); booklet, poster, pilot card and the datum (8).
questions.understand_first: Think about what actually has to happen for a ship to move. Fuel burns in a cylinder and pushes a piston down - that is all the power there will ever be, and every single thing that happens afterwards takes a share of it. The bearings take some. The stern tube takes some. Then the propeller, which is by far the biggest thief, because the only way it can push the ship forward is by throwing water backwards, and all the energy in that thrown water is gone for good. What finally arrives is a force pushing the hull through the sea against its resistance - and if you multiply that resistance by the ship's speed you get the effective power, which is simply the power somebody would need to tow her along at that speed with a rope. So the first limb is just the accounting: name each stage, and name what is lost between them. There is one lovely complication worth understanding rather than memorising. The hull drags a layer of water along with itself, so the propeller is not working in still water - it is working in water already moving in the same direction, which makes its job easier. But the propeller, by sucking water past the hull, also increases the hull's drag, which makes its job harder. Those two effects both exist, they pull opposite ways, and the helpful one usually wins - which is why the 'hull efficiency' can come out greater than one and no law of physics has been broken. The second limb is what happens on the day the ship first goes to sea. Everything up to then has been a calculation. The trials are where the ship is made to prove it: how fast she really goes for a given power, how tightly she turns, how quickly she stops swinging when you reverse the wheel, and how far she runs before she stops. And the reason it matters to you rather than only to the shipyard is that those numbers become the poster on the bridge wall for the next twenty-five years.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Limb A - the chain. INDICATED (in the cylinder, from the indicator diagram) → mechanical efficiency, losing friction at rings, crosshead, crankpin and mains plus engine-driven auxiliaries → BRAKE (at the coupling) → transmission and shaft efficiency, losing the thrust block, line bearings, stern tube and any gearing → SHAFT (measured by torsionmeter, torque × angular velocity - the last directly measurable power) → DELIVERED (at the propeller; cannot be measured, only inferred) → open-water efficiency and relative rotative efficiency → THRUST POWER = thrust × SPEED OF ADVANCE (not ship speed) → hull efficiency, from the wake fraction (helps - the propeller works in slower water) and the thrust deduction fraction (hurts - the propeller raises hull resistance), which can exceed unity → EFFECTIVE POWER = total resistance × ship speed = towrope power. Combine as QPC = effective ÷ delivered (hull and propeller) and propulsive coefficient = effective ÷ shaft (whole installation). No typical values - all installation specific. Limb B - trials. Conditions first: deep unrestricted water, low sea and wind, specified loading, steady approach, reciprocal headings, clean hull, calibrated instruments. Then: progressive speed trial (power-speed curve, contract speed, service datum); endurance and consumption; turning circle (advance, transfer, tactical diameter, drift angle, both sides); zig-zag (overshoot angles - yaw-checking and course-changing ability); spiral, reverse spiral, pull-out (course stability); crash stop (head reach, track reach, time); astern and minimum steerage; steering gear hard over to hard over, main and auxiliary; anchoring. Results become the manoeuvring booklet, wheelhouse poster and pilot card.
critical_numbers: SIX powers in the chain: indicated, brake, shaft, delivered, thrust, effective
Effective power = total resistance × SHIP speed. Thrust power = thrust × SPEED OF ADVANCE
Quasi-propulsive coefficient divides by DELIVERED power; propulsive coefficient divides by SHAFT or BRAKE power
NO efficiency value or typical range is quoted anywhere - every one is hull-form, propeller and installation specific
NO sea trial acceptance criterion is quoted as a number - the manoeuvrability standards are cited by identity only
quick_revision.critical_regulation: None on limb A - no statutory instrument prescribes the power chain, and saying so is correct rather than evasive. On limb B, three instruments are engaged and all three are cited by identity only, with no criterion value and no provision quoted: the IMO standards for ship manoeuvrability, which set the criteria against which turning, yaw-checking, course-keeping and stopping ability are judged; the requirement that manoeuvring information be provided on board, which is what turns the trial results into the manoeuvring booklet, the wheelhouse poster and the pilot card; and the steering gear trial required before the ship enters service, in main and auxiliary modes.
quick_revision.major_trap: Defining thrust power on the ship's speed instead of the speed of advance. The speed of advance is lower because of the wake, and getting this wrong unravels the whole hull-propeller section. Second trap: skipping the hull-propeller interaction and going straight from the shaft to the ship - the wake and thrust deduction pair is where the thinking in limb A is, and stating that hull efficiency can exceed unity with the reason is what distinguishes a strong answer. Third: omitting delivered power from the chain, or confusing the quasi-propulsive coefficient with the propulsive coefficient. Fourth, and specific to limb B: listing trials without their objectives, when the stem asks for 'the typical objectives of each test' in terms - that is half the limb. Fifth: forgetting the trial conditions, above all deep unrestricted water and runs on reciprocal headings, without which the measurements mean nothing. Sixth: quoting typical efficiency values or trial criteria as numbers when both are installation and instrument specific.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the six powers in the chain, in order, and where each is measured.
retrieval_cards.answer: Indicated - in the cylinder, from the indicator diagram. Brake - at the engine coupling. Shaft - on the line shafting, by torsionmeter. Delivered - at the propeller, after the stern tube; not measurable, only inferred. Thrust - thrust multiplied by speed of advance. Effective - total resistance multiplied by ship speed, also called towrope power.
retrieval_cards.why: The chain in order is the spine of limb A, and delivered power is the stage most often omitted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define effective power and thrust power precisely.
retrieval_cards.answer: Effective power = total resistance × SHIP speed - the power that would be needed to tow the hull at that speed, which is why it is called towrope power. Thrust power = thrust × SPEED OF ADVANCE - the speed of the water entering the propeller, which is lower than the ship's speed because of the wake. Using ship speed for thrust power is the commonest error in the question.
retrieval_cards.why: These two definitions carry the limb; getting the speed of advance wrong unravels everything after it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain wake fraction and thrust deduction, and say which way each acts.
retrieval_cards.answer: Wake: the hull drags a layer of water along with it, so the water entering the propeller is slower than the ship - the propeller works in slower water and needs less power for the same thrust. It HELPS. Thrust deduction: the working propeller lowers the pressure ahead of itself and so increases the hull's resistance, meaning more thrust is required than the towed resistance suggests. It HURTS. Together they give hull efficiency.
retrieval_cards.why: The two opposite effects are where the thinking in limb A lives, and both must be given with their direction.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Can hull efficiency be greater than one?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, and commonly is. The wake gain usually outweighs the thrust deduction penalty. It is not a thermodynamic efficiency but a ratio between two ways of accounting for the same work - the towed resistance of the hull against the thrust the propeller must actually produce - so a value above unity breaks no physical law.
retrieval_cards.why: A standard oral trap, and explaining why proves the chain is understood rather than memorised.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the quasi-propulsive coefficient from the propulsive coefficient.
retrieval_cards.answer: Quasi-propulsive coefficient = effective power ÷ DELIVERED power. It combines open-water efficiency, relative rotative efficiency and hull efficiency, so it describes the hull and propeller and says nothing about the machinery. Propulsive coefficient = effective power ÷ SHAFT or BRAKE power - the QPC multiplied by the transmission efficiency, describing the whole installation.
retrieval_cards.why: A small, reliable mark that turns entirely on which power is the denominator.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What conditions must a sea trial be run in, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: Deep, unrestricted water - shallow water alters resistance, squat and turning behaviour. Low sea state and wind, recorded. The specified loading condition and trim, since displacement changes everything measured. A steady approach before the manoeuvre begins. Runs on reciprocal headings, so current and tidal stream cancel in the mean. And a clean hull and calibrated instruments.
retrieval_cards.why: Conditions are the marks nobody writes, and they show that you understand what a measurement is for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does a turning circle trial measure, and what does a zig-zag add?
retrieval_cards.answer: The turning circle gives advance, transfer, tactical diameter, drift angle and speed loss in the turn - the ship's turning ability - and is run to both sides. The zig-zag puts the rudder over, reverses it at a set heading change and repeats, giving the overshoot angles: how far the head keeps swinging after the rudder is reversed. That is yaw-checking and course-changing ability, which the turning circle cannot show.
retrieval_cards.why: The zig-zag is the most informative manoeuvring trial and the one candidates most often cannot explain.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which trials test course stability, and what do they show?
retrieval_cards.answer: The spiral and reverse spiral tests, in which steady rates of turn are recorded against a series of rudder angles from hard over to hard over and back; and the pull-out test, in which the ship is brought to a steady turn and the rudder returned amidships. On a stable ship the rate of turn decays to zero; on an unstable one it settles at a residual rate, and the spiral shows the width of the loop - how much rudder she needs simply to go straight.
retrieval_cards.why: Course stability is a distinct property from turning ability, and it is what makes a ship tiring or easy to steer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship is slower than usual. How do you tell a fouled hull from a tired engine?
retrieval_cards.answer: Use the chain. Compare shaft power against speed: if more shaft power is needed for the same speed, the loss is aft of the shaft - fouled hull, damaged propeller, or added resistance. Then compare fuel consumption against shaft power: if more fuel is needed for the same shaft power, the loss is in the engine. From the bridge the two look identical; only the chain separates them.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the practical payoff of limb A, and it is the answer a Chief Engineer is expected to give.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The criteria against which turning, yaw-checking, course-keeping and stopping ability are assessed on trials, and the requirement that manoeuvring information be provided on board.
reverify_before_publication.why: The IMO standards for ship manoeuvrability and the manoeuvring-information requirement are CITED BY IDENTITY ONLY. Neither was read at source in this session, NO CRITERION VALUE IS STATED anywhere, no provision is quoted, and no application threshold by ship length, type or date of build is asserted. Acquire and read both before publication, and do not add a criterion value until one has been read.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The steering gear trial required before a ship enters service, in main and auxiliary modes, including the hard-over to hard-over demonstration.
reverify_before_publication.why: Cited by identity only. The instrument was not read at source in this session and NO TIME LIMIT OR RATE OF MOVEMENT IS ASSERTED. The demonstration is described by what is done rather than by a quoted requirement.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The power chain, the efficiency definitions, and the standard set of navigation trials with their objectives.
reverify_before_publication.why: Carried as engineering reference and established shipbuilding practice, authored from first principles because NO DONOR EXISTS ANYWHERE IN THE CORPUS for either limb. NO EFFICIENCY VALUE OR TYPICAL RANGE IS ASSERTED, because every one is hull-form, propeller and installation specific, and none should be added. The trial programme is contractual as well as statutory and is described as the standard set rather than as a closed statutory list.
