blocks.h: 1. (a) Where the 80 per cent claim comes from, and what kind of statement it is

blocks.p: The examiner has printed a claim that circulates constantly in the industry, and the first thing a strong answer does is examine it rather than repeat it. It is not the finding of a study that four accidents in five are caused by defective people. It is an artefact of how investigations attribute causes.

The mechanism is simple, and worth setting out because everything in this limb follows from it. A ship is operated by people. Consequently a human action is present at the end of almost every causal chain - somebody opened something, closed something, ordered something, or failed to notice something. When an investigation reaches that action it has found something concrete, nameable and satisfying, and there is a strong tendency to stop there. Read carefully, the claim therefore says only this: in about eighty per cent of accidents, a human action can be identified somewhere in the chain. In a system operated by human beings that is close to a tautology.

So the figure is a stopping rule, not a finding - a description of where investigations tend to halt, dressed up as a description of why accidents happen. And reading it as a finding has two predictable and damaging consequences:

ul: It produces blame. If people cause accidents, the response is to identify the person and discipline him - which teaches everyone else not to report, and removes the information the organisation needs.

It produces more procedure. If the person failed to follow the rules, the answer must be more rules - and a procedure written to close a gap that was never the real cause adds workload without adding safety.

blocks.p: Neither response makes the next accident less likely, which is the practical test of whether an explanation is any good.

blocks.h: 2. (a) What 'a complex hierarchical socio-technical system' means for a ship

blocks.p: The phrase in the stem is doing real work, and the marks in this limb are in unpacking all three of its words against the ship you actually sail on.

rows: Socio-technical
Performance is produced by people and technology together, along with the procedures they work to and the environment they work in. Neither half can be assessed alone
A purifier does not run itself and an engineer cannot run it without it. What is delivered is the joint output of the machine, the man, the manual and the motion of the ship
Complex
Many parts, tightly coupled, interacting in ways that are not fully foreseeable. Small disturbances propagate; the behaviour of the whole is not the sum of the parts
A blackout is never one failure. It is a generator, a protection setting, a standby that did not start, and an alarm that had been accepted an hour earlier
Hierarchical
Arranged in layers, each of which sets the conditions for the layer below it
Regulator and flag State, then class, then the yard that built her, then the company, then the master, and at the bottom the watchkeeper with his hand on the valve

blocks.p: Two consequences follow from the hierarchy, and together they are the intellectual core of the limb.

First, decisions made in the upper layers create the conditions in which the lowest layer acts. The manning level, the watch pattern, the maintenance budget, the spare gear policy, the design of the alarm panel and the wording of the procedure are all settled by people who are not on board and who will not be present when the consequences arrive. The watchkeeper does not choose the conditions he works in; he only acts within them.

Second, those decisions leave latent conditions. A latent condition is a weakness built into the system that does no harm on its own and may lie dormant for years - two identical unlabelled valves side by side, a procedure that has never matched the plant, an alarm nobody can silence without acknowledging six others. It becomes an accident only when it combines with an active failure at the sharp end, on a particular night, with a particular person, under particular pressure.

That is why defences are described as layered, and why a casualty is properly described not as one failure but as the occasion on which the gaps in several defences happened to line up. Every one of those gaps was created by a decision, and most of the decisions were taken a long way from the ship.

blocks.h: 3. (a) What 'human error' therefore means here, and what follows

blocks.p: Putting sections 1 and 2 together answers the limb directly. In a complex hierarchical socio-technical system, the term 'human error' denotes the last human action in the chain - the point at which the investigation happened to stop asking why. It is a label applied at a boundary of enquiry, not a description of a cause.
From which four things follow, and they are the substance of the eight marks:

ol: Human error is a symptom, not a cause. It is where the investigation should begin, not where it should end. An investigation that concludes 'human error' has stated its stopping point and called it a finding.

The right question is not what he did wrong, but why it made sense to a competent person at the time. People do not come to work intending to make mistakes. If a reasonable, trained and conscientious person did that thing, then in his situation - with his information, his fatigue, his instrument, his time pressure - it seemed like the reasonable thing to do. Understanding why is the whole of the useful work.

Errors are not eliminated by instructing people not to make them. Posting a notice saying 'be careful' changes nothing, because nobody was intending to be careless. Exhortation is the least effective of all interventions and is very often the only one taken.

Errors are reduced by changing conditions. Interfaces and labelling, the design and the realism of procedures, manning and watch patterns, rest and fatigue management, tools, lighting, and above all a reporting culture in which people say what nearly happened without fear of what will happen to them for saying it.

blocks.p: This is not merely a theoretical position; it is the position international law takes. The Casualty Investigation Code, adopted by resolution MSC.255(84) on 16 May 2008, directs a marine safety investigation at the circumstances and the causes of a casualty so that safety may be enhanced - expressly separating that enquiry from the apportionment of blame or liability. The reason is exactly the one above: an investigation conducted to find fault stops at the last human act, and an investigation conducted to prevent recurrence has to go past it.

blocks.h: 4. (b) Human Element - the domain

blocks.p: Limb (b) turns on three terms that are used interchangeably in conversation and mean three quite different things. The cleanest way to hold them apart is to notice that each answers a different question.

Human Element is the domain - the subject area. It is the recognition that people are an integral part of the maritime system, and it is the broadest of the three terms. IMO frames it in the Human Element Vision, Principles and Goals at resolution A.947(23) as a complex, multi-dimensional issue affecting maritime safety, security and the marine environment.

Its scope is the point most often got wrong. The human element is not confined to seafarers. It spans ships' crews, shore-based management, regulators, recognized organizations, shipyards, designers and legislators - everyone whose decisions bear on how a ship is operated. Its regulatory expression is the ISM Code for organisation and management, STCW for competence and fitness for duty, and MLC 2006 for hours of rest and living and working conditions.
It answers the question: who and what is in scope?

blocks.h: 5. (b) Human Error - the outcome

blocks.p: Human Error is an event. It is a planned action failing to achieve its intended outcome, or a plan that was inadequate for the outcome intended. It is the narrowest of the three terms and it is retrospective - there is no such thing as an error before it happens.

rows: Skill-based slip or lapse
Right intention, failed execution - the action was automatic and went astray, or a step was simply forgotten
Opening the adjacent valve; omitting a step in a routine changeover
Design - labelling, separation, layout, checklists
Rule-based mistake
A good rule applied in the wrong situation, or a bad rule applied correctly
Following the normal starting procedure in an abnormal condition it was never written for
Procedures - and knowing which situation is which
Knowledge-based mistake
A novel situation reasoned through incorrectly, usually under time pressure and with incomplete information
Diagnosing an unfamiliar fault wrongly during a blackout
Training, decision support, and time

blocks.p: Violations are a separate category and are not errors at all. A violation is deliberate - the person knew the rule and departed from it. They are conventionally distinguished as routine (the shortcut everybody takes), situational (the rule could not be complied with in the circumstances) and exceptional (a departure in an emergency). The important insight is that a routine violation is a statement about the procedure, not about the person: when everybody does it, the procedure does not fit the work, and disciplining an individual will not change that.
It answers the question: what happened?

blocks.h: 6. (b) Human Factors - the discipline

blocks.p: Human Factors is the scientific discipline and its application. It is the study of the interaction between people, equipment, procedures, organisation and environment, and the use of that knowledge to design systems that fit the people who operate them - rather than selecting and training people to fit systems that do not.

It is the only one of the three that is proactive and prospective. Element is a field of concern and error is a past event; human factors is a method, and it can be applied to a plant that has not been built yet. Its working territory includes:

ul: Workload, fatigue and circadian rhythm - watch patterns, port workload, and the hours at which people are asked to make decisions.
Controls, displays and alarms - legibility, grouping, coding, and above all alarm management, because an alarm system that floods is an alarm system that is ignored.
Automation and mode awareness - the recurring problem that the operator does not know what the system is currently doing or why.
Anthropometry and workspace - reach, access, lighting, noise, vibration and motion.
Procedure design - writing instructions that can actually be followed by the person, in the place, in the conditions.
Communication and team behaviour - briefing, challenge and response, and the willingness of a junior to speak.

blocks.p: It answers the question: how do we study this, and what do we change?

blocks.h: 7. (b) The three distinguished through one incident

blocks.p: The stem asks for examples, and the most economical way to give them is to run one incident through all three terms. Take a constructed illustration - a fatigued engineer, at the end of a long port stay, opens the wrong valve and floods a space.

headers: What it names in this incident
rows: Human error
The act itself - opening that valve. A skill-based slip: the intention was correct and the execution went astray
A warning, a note in the record, a reminder to be careful. Changes nothing
Human factors
Why the act happened - two identical unlabelled valves side by side, poor lighting at that position, and a watch pattern that put him there at the end of eighteen hours
Redesign - label and separate the valves, light the space, and fix the watch pattern
Human element

The whole territory around it - the manning level that produced the eighteen hours, the training, the maintenance budget that left the labels off, and a reporting culture in which nobody had mentioned the valves before
Organisational change - manning, resources, and the safety management system under which all of it is decided

blocks.p: So the distinction, in one line each: the element is the field, the factors are the method, and the error is the event. Put the other way round - error is what you see, human factors is how you explain and prevent it, and the human element is the territory both of them sit in.

And the reason the distinction matters practically rather than merely semantically is in the third column of that table. Each term implies a different response, and only one of the three responses would stop it happening to the next engineer.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Eight and eight, both printed - and note that this paper splits the marks evenly where the same question elsewhere is set 6 and 10. Here limb (a) is worth exactly as much as limb (b), which means the analysis of the 80 per cent claim and of the socio-technical system is half the question, not a preamble to the definitions. Candidates who race through (a) to reach the three definitions throw away four marks.

Limb (a) is an argument: examine the claim, unpack the phrase, and state what follows. Limb (b) is a discrimination: three terms, three different questions answered, one worked example. Do not write limb (b)'s definitions inside limb (a).

blocks.h: The one sentence that carries limb (a)

blocks.p: The 80 per cent figure is a stopping rule, not a finding. It describes where investigations halt, not why accidents happen. A person is present at the end of almost every chain in a system operated by people, so finding one is close to a tautology. Write that, and the rest of the limb is the reasoning behind it.

blocks.h: Unpack all three words in the phrase

ul: Socio-technical - people and technology produce the outcome jointly; neither can be assessed alone.
Complex - many tightly coupled parts interacting unforeseeably. A blackout is never one failure.
Hierarchical - layers, from regulator and flag through class, yard and company to the watchkeeper - and each layer sets the conditions for the one below.

blocks.p: Then the two consequences: upper-layer decisions create the conditions the sharp end works in, and they leave latent conditions that do no harm until they meet an active failure on a particular night. That is what layered defences and lined-up gaps mean.

blocks.h: The four things that follow, and the one question to ask

blocks.p: Error is a symptom, not a cause. Errors are not removed by telling people not to make them. They are reduced by changing conditions. And the question that replaces 'what did he do wrong?' is: why did that action make sense to a competent person at the time? If you write nothing else in limb (a), write that question - it is the whole of modern casualty thinking in nine words, and it is why the Casualty Investigation Code, MSC.255(84), is directed at circumstances and causes rather than at blame.

blocks.h: The three terms, one question each

rows: Human Element
The domain - the broadest term. Framed by IMO at A.947(23); not confined to seafarers
Who and what is in scope?
Standing
Human Error
The outcome - an event, the narrowest term
What happened?
Retrospective
Human Factors
The discipline - study and design
How do we study it, and what do we change?
Prospective - the only proactive one

blocks.h: The error taxonomy, and the category that is not an error

ul: Skill-based slip or lapse - right intention, failed execution. Fixed by design.
Rule-based mistake - good rule in the wrong situation, or a bad rule applied properly. Fixed by procedures.
Knowledge-based mistake - a novel situation reasoned through wrongly. Fixed by training and time.
Violations are NOT errors - they are deliberate. Routine, situational or exceptional. And a routine violation is a statement about the procedure, not about the person.

blocks.h: Run one incident through all three

blocks.p: The tired engineer who opens the wrong valve. The error is the act - a skill-based slip. The factors are the identical unlabelled valves, the lighting and the watch pattern. The element is the manning, the training, the budget and the reporting culture behind all of it. And note what each implies: a warning, a redesign, or a change of manning - only two of which would prevent a recurrence. One example, three terms, and the discrimination is demonstrated rather than asserted.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Accepting the 80 per cent figure as a finding and then explaining why seafarers are careless. That is the trap the limb is built around.
Treating limb (a) as a preamble. On this paper it is worth eight marks, the same as limb (b).
Unpacking 'socio-technical' but ignoring 'complex' and 'hierarchical'. All three words carry marks.
Omitting latent conditions, without which the hierarchy argument has no conclusion.
Defining the human element as 'the seafarer'. It spans shore management, regulators, class, yards and legislators.
Treating human factors as a synonym for human error, when it is the discipline that studies and prevents it.
Calling a violation an error. It is deliberate, and the two need different responses.
Giving three definitions and no example, when the stem asks for examples expressly.
Quoting a statistic in reply. The figure in the stem is the thing being examined; offering another does not help.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Do you agree that 80 per cent of accidents are caused by human error?" Not as stated. A human action can be identified in about that proportion of chains, which is different - and nearly a tautology in a system run by people.
"Is human error a cause?" No - a symptom, and the point at which the investigation stopped asking why.
"How do you stop people making mistakes?" You do not. You change the conditions - labelling, layout, procedures, manning, rest, reporting.
"Give me a latent condition on your own ship." Two identical unlabelled valves; a procedure that does not match the plant; an alarm that floods.
"Is a violation an error?" No - it is deliberate. And a routine violation says the procedure does not fit the work.
"Is the human element about seafarers?" No - it includes shore management, regulators, class, shipyards and legislators.
"Which of the three is proactive?" Human factors, because it is a design discipline and applies before anything has gone wrong.

"Why does the Casualty Investigation Code separate the safety investigation from blame?" Because an enquiry conducted to find fault stops at the last human act, and one conducted to prevent recurrence has to go past it.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Tell me about a near miss you reported, and what happened to the report afterwards.
Would your junior engineer tell you if he had made a mistake nobody else had seen? What makes you sure?
How many alarms does your main engine control room show on a normal watch, and how many do you act on?
Show me two valves on this plant that could be confused, and tell me why they still can be.
How are your hours of rest recorded, and are the records true?
What did your company change after the last incident on this ship?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb (a): claim, phrase, consequence. The 80 per cent is a stopping rule (1); socio-technical, complex, hierarchical, giving latent conditions plus an active failure (2); therefore error is a symptom, and the question is why it made sense at the time (3). Limb (b): domain, event, discipline - then one incident. ELEMENT = who is in scope (4). ERROR = what happened (5). FACTORS = how we study and change it (6). Then the valve: act, conditions, organisation (7).

steps.title: (a) Where the 80 per cent claim comes from, and what kind of statement it is
points: It is not a study finding that four accidents in five are caused by defective people
It is an artefact of how investigations attribute causes
A person is present at the end of almost every chain, so the last human act is always available
Properly read: in about 80 per cent of accidents a human action can be identified in the chain
In a system operated by people that is close to a tautology
So it is a stopping rule, not a finding
Reading it as a finding produces blame and more procedure, and neither prevents the next accident

steps.title: (a) What 'a complex hierarchical socio-technical system' means for a ship
points: Socio-technical - performance is the joint output of people, technology, procedures and environment
Complex - many tightly coupled parts interacting unforeseeably; a blackout is never one failure
Hierarchical - regulator and flag, class, yard, company, master, watchkeeper
Upper-layer decisions create the conditions in which the lowest layer acts
Manning, watch pattern, budget, spare gear, alarm design and procedure wording are all set ashore
Those decisions leave latent conditions which do no harm alone
An accident is when a latent condition meets an active failure and the gaps in the defences line up

steps.title: (a) What 'human error' therefore means here, and what follows
points: It denotes the last human action in the chain, where the investigation happened to stop
A label applied at a boundary of enquiry, not a description of a cause
Therefore a symptom, not a cause
The right question: why did the action make sense to a competent person at the time?
Errors are not eliminated by instructing people not to make them
They are reduced by changing conditions - interfaces, procedures, manning, rest, reporting
Which is why the Casualty Investigation Code, MSC.255(84) of 16 May 2008 seeks circumstances and causes, not blame

steps.title: (b) Human Element - the domain
points: The subject area - people as an integral part of the maritime system. The broadest of the three
Framed by IMO in the Human Element Vision, Principles and Goals, resolution A.947(23)
A complex, multi-dimensional issue affecting safety, security and the environment
NOT confined to seafarers - it spans shore management, regulators, recognized organizations, shipyards, designers and legislators
Its regulatory expression is the ISM Code, STCW and MLC 2006
It answers: who and what is in scope?

steps.title: (b) Human Error - the outcome
points: An event - a planned action failing to achieve its outcome, or an inadequate plan
The narrowest of the three, and retrospective
Skill-based slips and lapses - right intention, failed execution; remedy is design
Rule-based mistakes - a good rule in the wrong situation, or a bad rule applied correctly
Knowledge-based mistakes - a novel situation reasoned through wrongly under pressure
Violations are deliberate and are NOT errors - routine, situational or exceptional
A routine violation is a statement about the procedure, not about the person
It answers: what happened?

steps.title: (b) Human Factors - the discipline
points: The scientific discipline and its application
The interaction between people, equipment, procedures, organisation and environment
And designing systems to fit the people who operate them
The only one of the three that is proactive and prospective
Workload, fatigue and circadian rhythm; controls, displays and alarm management
Automation and mode awareness; anthropometry and workspace
Procedure design; communication and team behaviour
It answers: how do we study this, and what do we change?

steps.title: (b) The three distinguished through one incident
points: One constructed incident - a fatigued engineer opens the wrong valve and floods a space
The error is the act - a skill-based slip
The factors are the conditions - identical unlabelled valves, the lighting, the watch pattern
The element is the territory - manning, training, budget, reporting culture
So: element is the field, factors the method, error the event
Error is what you see; factors is how you explain and prevent it; element is where both live
And each implies a different response - a warning, a redesign, or a change of manning

The 80 per cent is a stopping rule (1); socio-technical, complex, hierarchical giving latent conditions plus an active failure (2); so error is a symptom, and ask why it made sense at the time (3). questions.understand_first: Start with why the claim in the question is so appealing and so useless. Somebody looks at a pile of accident reports, notices that in nearly all of them a person did something at the end, and writes down that people cause accidents. But of course a person did something at the end - the ship is run by people, so there is always a human act available to point at. The figure is really telling you where investigations stop, not why accidents happen. And where an investigation stops matters enormously, because everything upstream of the stopping point escapes examination. Now think about what is upstream. The engineer who opened the wrong valve did not choose to have two identical valves side by side, did not decide the lighting, did not set the watch pattern that had him awake for eighteen hours, and did not write the procedure that assumed a plant he does not have. Those things were decided by people ashore, months or years earlier, and every one of them was harmless on the day it was decided. They sit in the ship as traps waiting for an occasion - and the occasion, when it comes, gets called human error. So the whole shift the question is testing for is this: stop asking what the man did wrong, and start asking why it made sense to him at the time. Because a sensible, trained, careful person did it, and if you cannot see why he did it you have not understood the accident yet. The second limb is then just tidiness about words. The element is the whole subject of people in shipping. An error is one event that has already happened. Human factors is the science you use to stop the next one. Field, event, method - and only the last of the three can be applied before anything has gone wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the human error and human element question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb (a): 1 where the 80 per cent claim comes from and what kind of statement it is. 2 socio-technical, complex and hierarchical unpacked, ending on latent conditions. 3 what human error therefore means, and the four consequences. Limb (b): 4 human element, the domain. 5 human error, the event. 6 human factors, the discipline. 7 one incident read three ways.
retrieval_cards.why: This paper prints 8 and 8, so limb (a) carries half the marks and needs three developed sections rather than a preamble.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Do you accept that 80 per cent of accidents are caused by human error?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not as stated. Properly read, the claim is that in about that proportion of accidents a human action can be identified in the chain - which, in a system operated by people, is close to a tautology. The figure describes where investigations stop, not why accidents happen. Read as a finding it produces blame and more procedure, and neither makes the next accident less likely.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the whole of limb (a) in one answer, and the trap the question is built around.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Unpack 'complex hierarchical socio-technical system' for a ship.
retrieval_cards.answer: Socio-technical: performance is the joint output of people, technology, procedures and environment - neither half can be assessed alone. Complex: many tightly coupled parts interacting in ways not fully foreseeable, so a blackout is never one failure. Hierarchical: layers from regulator and flag through class, yard and company to the watchkeeper - and each layer sets the conditions for the one below it.
retrieval_cards.why: All three words carry marks, and the hierarchy is what leads to latent conditions.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a latent condition, and how does it cause an accident?
retrieval_cards.answer: A weakness built into the system by an earlier decision - manning, budget, layout, procedure wording, alarm design - that does no harm on its own and may lie dormant for years. It becomes an accident only when it combines with an active failure at the sharp end on a particular occasion. Defences are layered, and a casualty is the occasion on which the gaps in several of them line up.
retrieval_cards.why: Without latent conditions, the hierarchy argument in limb (a) has no conclusion.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is human error a cause? And what question replaces 'what did he do wrong?'
retrieval_cards.answer: It is a symptom, not a cause - a label applied at the point where the investigation stopped asking why. The question that replaces it is: why did that action make sense to a competent person at the time? Nobody comes to work intending to make a mistake, so if a trained and conscientious person did it, it seemed reasonable in his situation - and understanding why is the whole of the useful work.
retrieval_cards.why: Nine words that contain the entire modern approach to casualty investigation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish human element, human error and human factors.
retrieval_cards.answer: Human element is the domain - the broadest term, framed by IMO at resolution A.947(23), and not confined to seafarers: it spans shore management, regulators, recognized organizations, shipyards and legislators. It answers who is in scope. Human error is the event - narrowest and retrospective. It answers what happened. Human factors is the discipline, the only proactive one. It answers how we study it and what we change.
retrieval_cards.why: Three terms, three different questions answered - which is the cleanest way to keep them apart under pressure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the error taxonomy, and say what is NOT an error.
retrieval_cards.answer: Skill-based slips and lapses - right intention, failed execution; fixed by design. Rule-based mistakes - a good rule in the wrong situation, or a bad rule applied correctly. Knowledge-based mistakes - a novel situation reasoned through wrongly under pressure. Violations are NOT errors: they are deliberate, and are classed routine, situational or exceptional. A routine violation is a statement about the procedure, not about the person.
retrieval_cards.why: Conflating violations with errors is the discrimination the limb tests, and each type needs a different remedy.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the human element about seafarers?
retrieval_cards.answer: No, and this is the commonest misunderstanding of the term. IMO frames it as a complex, multi-dimensional issue involving the entire spectrum of human activity in shipping - ships' crews, shore-based management, regulators, recognized organizations, shipyards, designers and legislators. Confining it to the crew reproduces exactly the error that limb (a) exposes.
retrieval_cards.why: The scope of the term is where the mark is, and getting it wrong contradicts the first limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Read one incident through all three terms.
retrieval_cards.answer: A fatigued engineer opens the wrong valve and floods a space. The error is the act - a skill-based slip. The factors are the conditions - two identical unlabelled valves, poor lighting, and a watch pattern that put him there after eighteen hours. The element is the territory - manning, training, the budget that left the labels off, and a reporting culture in which nobody had raised the valves. Each implies a different response: a warning, a redesign, or a change of manning.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for examples, and one incident read three ways demonstrates the distinction instead of asserting it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does the Casualty Investigation Code separate the safety investigation from blame?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because they cannot be done together. The Code, adopted by resolution MSC.255(84) on 16 May 2008 and mandatory from 1 January 2010, directs a marine safety investigation at the circumstances and causes of a casualty so that safety may be enhanced. An enquiry conducted to apportion fault stops at the last human act, and an enquiry conducted to prevent recurrence has to go past it - and people only tell the truth to the second kind.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the point at which limb (a)'s argument becomes international law rather than opinion.

blocks.h: 1. Where the power comes from, and what an inspection is before clear grounds exist

blocks.p: The phrase clear grounds cannot be explained without first saying what it is a threshold between, and the marks in the first half of limb a depend on getting that structure right.

The power to inspect at all comes from the conventions, each of which carries its own control article - SOLAS regulation I/19, MARPOL articles 5 and 6, Load Lines 1966 article 21, STCW article X and regulation I/4, and MLC 2006 Title 5.2. IMO's consolidated Procedures for Port State Control tell an officer how to exercise that power and supply the common vocabulary; they do not create it, because the resolution adopting them merely invites Governments to implement them. That distinction is worth a sentence in the answer, and it is why the substance below does not depend on which edition of the Procedures happens to be current.
The initial inspection is deliberately limited. On boarding, the officer is entitled to look at:

ul: the certificates and documents required by the conventions, checking that they are present, valid and issued by or on behalf of the flag State;
the general condition of the ship, including the engine room, the deck, the accommodation and hygiene - what an experienced eye takes in while walking through.

blocks.p: If the certificates are in order and nothing seen contradicts them, that is where the inspection ends. The officer has no general licence to take the ship apart. What entitles him to go further is precisely the existence of clear grounds - and that is why the term matters commercially as much as legally: it is the boundary between an hour's visit and a day alongside.

blocks.h: 2. 'Clear grounds' - the definition, and the two words that carry it

blocks.p: Clear grounds are evidence that the ship, her equipment or her crew does not correspond substantially with the requirements of the relevant conventions, or that the master or crew are not familiar with essential shipboard procedures relating to the safety of ships or the prevention of pollution.
Two words in that formulation do all the work, and a candidate who identifies them has essentially answered the limb:

rows: EVIDENCE
Suspicion, reputation, rumour, the flag she flies, and the officer's general feeling about the ship
There must be something observed. Clear grounds are found, not assumed
SUBSTANTIALLY
The trivial, the cosmetic and the isolated minor defect
A ship is not opened up because of one burnt-out lamp. The discrepancy must go to compliance, not to tidiness

blocks.p: There is a third element that is easy to miss and is genuinely different in kind: the crew's unfamiliarity with essential procedures is itself clear grounds, independently of the condition of any equipment. A ship may be in perfect material order and still be opened up because the watchkeepers cannot demonstrate how they would use what they have.

blocks.h: 3. The circumstances that create clear grounds - with examples

blocks.p: The stem asks for examples in terms, and the most useful way to give them is to group them by what the officer was looking at when the clear grounds arose.

rows: Documents and certificates

A certificate absent, expired or invalid; a certificate that does not match the ship or her particulars; apparent falsification; an Oil Record Book with gaps, or entries that do not reconcile with the sludge and bilge quantities actually on board; a garbage or ballast record that has plainly been written up in one sitting
Equipment

Principal equipment or arrangements required by the conventions and simply not there; equipment present but visibly unmaintained, corroded, blanked, disconnected or bypassed; an oily water separator whose 15 ppm alarm and stopping arrangement cannot be demonstrated; lifeboat or fire-fighting equipment obviously not exercised
Condition of the ship

Serious deterioration or heavy corrosion of the hull, hatch covers or structure; plainly unsafe conditions in the machinery spaces - accumulated oil, defeated guards, leaking fuel lines; obviously unsanitary accommodation or galley; a report from the pilot, the terminal or another authority that the ship is deficient
People and procedures

The crew unable to demonstrate familiarity with essential operations - starting the emergency generator, changing over the steering gear, operating the fixed fire-fighting system, mustering for abandonment; the master unable to explain his authority under the safety management system; watchkeepers whose certification or rest hours plainly do not support the watch pattern being worked

blocks.p: One class of clear grounds deserves separate treatment because of what it implies. Where the deficiency points at the safety management system rather than at an item - a Safety Management Certificate or Document of Compliance missing, invalid or not matching the ship; system documentation that is uncontrolled, superseded, or in a language the crew cannot read; the master unaware of the review he is required to make - the officer is entitled to conclude that nothing else on board can be relied upon either, because the system that was supposed to be maintaining all of it is not working. That is why an ISM-related finding tends to widen an inspection rather than narrow it.

blocks.h: 4. What follows once clear grounds exist

ol: A more detailed inspection, and it is directed at the areas in which the clear grounds arose. It is not a general re-survey of the ship - the clear grounds define its scope as well as authorising it.
Rectification. Deficiencies are recorded, and most are cleared before departure or within a stated period.

Detention, but only on a defined test: where the deficiencies are clearly hazardous to safety, health or the environment, or where they are so numerous that together they show the safety management system has failed. Detention is not the ordinary outcome of a detailed inspection.

Notification. The flag State is informed in sufficient detail for it to assess the severity, and so is the recognized organization that issued the certificates - which is the point at which this question meets the RO question on this same paper.
Proceeding to a repair port where the deficiency cannot be remedied where she lies, on conditions, with the next port and the flag State notified.

blocks.p: And two limits run through all of it. First, every convention carrying a control article also carries a duty that all possible efforts shall be made to avoid a ship being unduly detained or delayed, with compensation for loss where she is - MARPOL article 7(2) being the clearest expression of it. Second, the whole system is operated regionally: port States coordinate through memoranda of understanding, India being a member of the Indian Ocean MOU, with inspections in Indian ports carried out by surveyors of DG Shipping under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. A memorandum of understanding is an administrative agreement between authorities and not a convention, and it is worth saying so.

blocks.h: 5. The three terms that must be separated

blocks.p: Limb b asks for a difference between two terms, and the reliable way to establish it is to introduce a third term that is habitually confused with both. All three are defined by what they act upon:

rows: Correction (or immediate remedial action)
The non-conformity itself
Now
Fix the thing that is wrong
Corrective action
The CAUSE of a DETECTED non-conformity
After it has happened
Stop it happening again
Preventive action
The CAUSE of a POTENTIAL non-conformity
Before it has happened
Stop it happening at all

blocks.p: So the difference the stem asks for reduces to one word: DETECTED against POTENTIAL. Corrective action responds to something that has actually occurred and removes the cause so that it does not recur. Preventive action responds to something that has not occurred - a risk, a weakness, a trend, a near miss - and removes the cause so that it never does.
Two consequences follow immediately, and both carry marks:

ul: Correction is not corrective action, and confusing them is the commonest failure in the whole subject. Replacing a failed component is a correction. It leaves the cause exactly where it was, and the same component will fail again. A great many safety management systems are full of closed non-conformities that were only ever corrected.
The two are not different degrees of the same thing. They are distinguished by whether an event has occurred, not by how thorough the response was.

blocks.h: 6. Corrective action - what it actually involves

blocks.p: Corrective action is a process and not a decision, and the ISM Code requires the company to have procedures for it - the safety management system must provide for non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences to be reported to the company, investigated and analysed with the object of improving safety and pollution prevention, and for corrective action to be implemented. The steps are:

ol: Contain, and correct. Make the situation safe and deal with the immediate defect. This is the correction, and it is where the process is not allowed to stop.
Establish what actually happened, from records and from the people involved, before forming a view about why.

Find the cause - and go past the first plausible one. 'The engineer opened the wrong valve' is not a cause; it is where the enquiry stopped. Why were two identical valves unlabelled? Why had nobody reported it? Why did the procedure not match the plant?

Decide the action, and decide it against the cause found rather than against the event. That may be a change to a procedure, to the planned maintenance system, to labelling or layout, to training, or to manning.
Assign it, with an owner and a date. An action without either is a note.
Implement, and record.

VERIFY EFFECTIVENESS. This is the step most often omitted and the one an auditor will test: not was the action done, but did it work - has the non-conformity stopped recurring? An action closed without verification has not been closed.
Feed it back, through the management review and to the rest of the fleet.

blocks.p: The inputs to corrective action are, by definition, things that have already gone wrong: internal and external audit non-conformities, port State control deficiencies and detentions, class conditions and recommendations, accidents, hazardous occurrences, equipment failures and defect reports.

blocks.h: 7. Preventive action - where it comes from

blocks.p: Preventive action uses the same machinery but is fed by a completely different set of inputs - things that have not happened, or that have happened somewhere else:

ul: Near misses and hazardous occurrences. The most valuable input there is, and the one that depends entirely on people being willing to report - which is why a blame culture destroys preventive action before it destroys anything else.
Risk assessment of a job, a modification or an unusual operation, carried out before the work rather than after the injury.
Audit observations - findings that are not non-conformities but point at a weakness.
Trend analysis. Rising alarm counts, creeping defect backlogs, repeated minor findings in the same area, deteriorating oil analysis results. A trend is a non-conformity that has not arrived yet.

Fleet and industry experience. A casualty on a sister ship, a flag State or class circular, an engine builder's service letter, a published investigation report. Somebody else has already had the accident, which is the cheapest possible way to learn.
The port State control record of other ships. A deficiency recurring across the fleet is a warning to every ship that has not yet been inspected.

blocks.p: Preventive action is the harder discipline, for two reasons worth stating. First, it competes for resources against work that is visibly urgent, and nothing visibly bad is happening. Second, when it succeeds, nothing happens - which is very difficult to point at. It survives only where it is deliberately planned, resourced and reviewed, and it is the first thing to disappear on a ship that is behind on everything else.

blocks.h: 8. The two worked through one defect, and how the limbs connect

blocks.p: Take a single, ordinary engine-room event: a sea water cooler tube fails and floods the lubricating oil system.

rows: Correction
Plug or renew the tube, clean and renew the oil charge, return the plant to service
The ship works again. The cause is untouched and the next tube will go
Corrective action

Establish why it failed - erosion at the inlet, exhausted cathodic protection, a cooling water treatment regime not being followed, an inspection interval that had quietly been extended. Then change the thing that allowed it: revise the PMS interval, restore and monitor the protection, re-train on water treatment, and verify at the next opening that the wastage has stopped
That cooler will not fail the same way again
Preventive action

Ask which other coolers on this ship - and on her sisters - share the material, the duty and the treatment regime, and inspect or re-interval them before any of them leaks. Issue the finding to the fleet
The failure does not happen on the other units at all

blocks.p: And that example shows why the examiner has put these two limbs on the same question, which is worth a closing sentence. A port State control deficiency is an input to corrective action: something was found, on this ship, and the cause must be removed so that it is not found again. The same deficiency, read across the fleet, is an input to preventive action: the ships that have not yet been inspected can be put right before anyone looks. A company that only ever responds to what inspectors find is running its safety management system on corrective action alone - and it will be inspected, and detained, at exactly the rate its worst ship deserves.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Eight and eight, both printed - one of only two questions on this paper that print a complete sixteen. The two limbs are unrelated at first sight: limb a is enforcement law, limb b is safety-management vocabulary. Answer them separately and properly, then join them in one closing sentence, which is where the extra mark lives.

Limb a asks with examples and limb b asks for a difference. Both of those instructions are marking schemes in miniature: a definition of clear grounds without examples is half an answer, and two descriptions without a stated point of difference is not a comparison.

blocks.h: Set up limb a with the threshold

blocks.p: Clear grounds is a boundary, so say what lies on each side of it. Before: the officer may look at certificates and documents and the general condition of the ship, and no more. After: he may carry out a more detailed inspection, directed at the areas the clear grounds arose in. Stating the boundary first makes the definition mean something.

blocks.h: The definition, and the two words in it

blocks.p: Evidence that the ship, her equipment or her crew does not correspond SUBSTANTIALLY with the requirements of the conventions, or that master or crew are not familiar with essential shipboard procedures relating to safety or pollution prevention.

ul: EVIDENCE - excludes suspicion, reputation and the flag. Something must have been observed.
SUBSTANTIALLY - excludes the trivial. One failed lamp is not clear grounds.
And the third element people forget: unfamiliarity of the crew is itself clear grounds, whatever the state of the equipment.

blocks.h: Examples - group them, do not list them

blocks.p: Documents, equipment, condition, people. Four headings, two or three examples each, and the answer looks organised rather than remembered: certificates absent or expired and an Oil Record Book that will not reconcile; equipment missing, bypassed or plainly unmaintained; heavy corrosion and unsafe machinery spaces; and a crew who cannot start the emergency generator or change over the steering gear.

blocks.h: The ISM-related class, and why it widens everything

blocks.p: Where the finding points at the system rather than at an item - certificates missing or not matching, uncontrolled or superseded documentation, documentation in a language the crew cannot read, a master who cannot explain his authority - the officer is entitled to conclude that nothing else on board can be relied on either. That is why an ISM finding widens an inspection instead of narrowing it, and saying so shows you understand what the officer is actually reasoning about.

blocks.h: Limb b - introduce a third term to define the two

rows: Correction
The non-conformity itself
Fix the thing that is wrong
Corrective action
The cause of a DETECTED non-conformity
Stop it happening again
Preventive action
The cause of a POTENTIAL non-conformity
Stop it happening at all

blocks.p: The difference reduces to one word: DETECTED against POTENTIAL. Both attack a cause; they differ in whether the event has already happened. And correction is not corrective action - that is the confusion the limb is really testing, and a safety management system full of closed non-conformities that were only corrected is the practical proof of it.

blocks.h: The step everyone omits

blocks.p: Verification of effectiveness. Not was the action taken, but did it work - has the non-conformity stopped recurring? An action closed without verification has not been closed, and an auditor will go straight to it. Write the word 'effectiveness' into the answer.

blocks.h: Where each one's inputs come from

ul: Corrective - audit non-conformities, PSC deficiencies and detentions, class conditions, accidents, hazardous occurrences, defect reports. Things that went wrong here.

Preventive - near misses, risk assessments, audit observations, trend analysis, fleet and industry experience, circulars and service letters, other ships' PSC records. Things that went wrong elsewhere, or have not gone wrong yet.

blocks.h: One example, three responses

blocks.p: A cooler tube fails and floods the lubricating oil. Correction: plug the tube, renew the oil. Corrective action: find why it wasted - erosion, exhausted cathodic protection, water treatment not followed, an interval quietly extended - change that, and verify at the next opening. Preventive action: check every other cooler of the same material and duty on this ship and her sisters before one of them leaks. One example, three answers, and the distinction is demonstrated rather than asserted.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Defining clear grounds as 'anything that looks wrong'. It is evidence of a substantial departure.
Omitting the crew unfamiliarity element, which is a free-standing head of clear grounds.
Giving the definition and no examples, when the stem asks for them in terms.
Saying the port State's power comes from the IMO Procedures. It comes from the conventions; the Procedures are guidance.
Treating the detailed inspection as a general re-survey. Its scope is set by the clear grounds.
Saying every deficiency leads to detention. Detention needs deficiencies clearly hazardous to safety, health or the environment, or so numerous as to show systemic failure.
Confusing correction with corrective action - the central error of limb b.
Saying preventive action is 'more thorough' corrective action. The difference is detected against potential, not degree.
Omitting verification of effectiveness.
Never joining the two limbs, when the examiner has plainly put them together for a reason.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "What may the officer look at before he has clear grounds?" Certificates and documents, and the general condition of the ship. Nothing more.
"Is a dirty engine room clear grounds?" Only if it evidences a substantial departure - accumulated oil, defeated guards, leaking fuel lines. Untidiness alone is not.
"Your crew cannot start the emergency generator, but everything is certificated. Clear grounds?" Yes - unfamiliarity with essential procedures stands on its own.
"Where does the port State's power come from?" The control article of each convention - SOLAS I/19, MARPOL 5 and 6, Load Lines 21, STCW X.
"You replaced the failed pump. Is that corrective action?" No - that is a correction. Corrective action removes the cause.
"Give me a preventive action you took this month." It must be something that had not gone wrong here - a near miss, a trend, a service letter, a sister ship's casualty.
"How do you know your corrective action worked?" Verification of effectiveness - the non-conformity has stopped recurring, and there is a record saying so.
"A PSC deficiency - corrective or preventive?" Corrective for this ship; preventive for the rest of the fleet. That answer wins the question.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Show me your last PSC report and take me through what you did about each item.
Who raises a non-conformity on your ship, and what happens to it after you sign it off?
How many near misses were reported on your last voyage, and what came of them?
What did your company do after the last detention anywhere in the fleet?
How would you demonstrate to a PSCO that your crew are familiar with the steering gear changeover?
What is the difference between a non-conformity and a major non-conformity?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb a - before, trigger, after. BEFORE (1): the power is in the conventions; the initial inspection is certificates and general condition. TRIGGER (2): evidence of a substantial departure, or crew unfamiliarity. EXAMPLES (3): documents, equipment, condition, people - and ISM findings widen everything. AFTER (4): detailed inspection scoped by the grounds, rectify, detain only if clearly hazardous, notify flag and RO. Limb b - three terms, one word. Correction fixes the thing (5); corrective action removes the cause of a DETECTED one (6); preventive action removes the cause of a POTENTIAL one (7); and one cooler tube shows all three (8).

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: The edition of IMO's consolidated Procedures for Port State Control in circulation at this sitting is not held by MIW, and that limitation is stated rather than worked around. The only edition available for this answer is the set adopted by the 33rd Assembly on 6 December 2023 - nine months after this examination, and whose document was not even issued until the following January. Those resolutions are future for this paper and appear nowhere in this answer. The Procedures are therefore cited by identity and by concept only: no paragraph number is asserted anywhere, and no wording is quoted from any edition.

That limitation costs this answer very little, and the reason is worth understanding rather than merely accepting. The consolidated Procedures are recommendatory - the resolution adopting them merely invites Governments to implement them - so they are not the source of the port State's power. The power is in the conventions, whose control articles are held, and which did not move between this sitting and any later one. Limb a is anchored there, and the Procedures supply vocabulary rather than authority. An answer that named a resolution as the source of the legal power would be both wrong in principle and fragile in date.

No numeric threshold is asserted anywhere in this answer - not for steering gear, not for emergency power, not for any equipment. Equipment requirements are stated in function rather than by value, because the main and the auxiliary steering-gear requirements are widely conflated in secondary material and a value carried from the wrong one is a confident mistake. Nor is any detention statistic, deficiency code or targeting-factor value given: these are regional administrative data, they change continuously, and none is needed.

Limb b rests on the ISM Code as it stood at this sitting, on a held official chain, and it is cited at the level of its functional requirements - reporting, investigating and analysing non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences; implementing corrective action; and verifying through internal audit and management review. No provision is quoted and no element number is asserted. The three defined terms are carried as established quality-management vocabulary and are not attributed to any standard by number, because MIW holds no quality-management standard - they are defined by what each acts upon, which is the distinction the printed limb asks for and which is stable across the systems in use.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: TWO LIMBS OF EQUAL WEIGHT THAT LOOK UNRELATED AND ARE NOT. Limb a is enforcement law: what CLEAR GROUNDS are, which is a threshold question - the boundary between an initial inspection limited to certificates and general condition, and a more detailed inspection - and the stem asks for it WITH EXAMPLES. Limb b is safety-management vocabulary: the difference between corrective and preventive action, which turns on a single word. The connection, which the examiner has presumably intended, is that a port State deficiency is an input to corrective action for the ship inspected and to preventive action for every ship that has not been.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 8 and 8, BOTH PRINTED. This is one of only two questions on the paper printing a complete sixteen. Limb a needs the definition, the two qualifying words, examples grouped rather than listed, and what follows the trigger. Limb b needs three terms rather than two, the one-word distinction, and a worked example.

For limb b: that CORRECTION is separated from CORRECTIVE ACTION; that the difference between corrective and preventive turns on DETECTED against POTENTIAL rather than on thoroughness; that verification of effectiveness is named; and that the two are illustrated rather than merely defined.

Resolved by anchoring on the conventions, which did not move, and by citing the Procedures for vocabulary rather than authority. Limb b carries no freshness risk at all.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MEDIUM - the Indian layer must be stated at its March 2023 position: Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, DG Shipping, Indian Ocean MOU. The 2025 Act is three years future and the DGMA rename later still.
technical_ambiguities: Whether IMO's Procedures are a source of legal power. They are not - the adopting resolution only invites Governments to implement them - and saying so is what makes limb a robust against the unheld edition.
Whether crew unfamiliarity is a free-standing head of clear grounds or merely evidence of poor condition. It is free-standing: a materially perfect ship can be opened up on it alone.
Whether a more detailed inspection is a general re-survey. It is not; its scope is set by the areas in which the clear grounds arose.
Whether correction and corrective action are the same. They are not, and the confusion is the substance of what limb b tests.

Whether preventive action is simply thorough corrective action. It is not - the two are distinguished by whether the non-conformity has been DETECTED or is only POTENTIAL, which is a difference in kind and not in degree.

steps.title: Where the power comes from, and what an inspection is before clear grounds exist
points: The power is in the conventions - SOLAS I/19, MARPOL 5 and 6, Load Lines 21, STCW X and I/4, MLC Title 5.2
IMO's Procedures tell an officer how to exercise it and supply the vocabulary - they do not create it
The adopting resolution only invites Governments to implement them
The initial inspection is limited: certificates and documents, and the general condition of the ship
If the certificates are in order and nothing contradicts them, the inspection ends there
Clear grounds is therefore the boundary between an hour's visit and a day alongside

steps.title: 'Clear grounds' - the definition, and the two words that carry it
points: Evidence that ship, equipment or crew does not correspond substantially with convention requirements
OR that master or crew are not familiar with essential shipboard procedures for safety or pollution prevention
EVIDENCE excludes suspicion, reputation, rumour and the flag - something must be observed
SUBSTANTIALLY excludes the trivial, the cosmetic and the isolated minor defect
Crew unfamiliarity is a free-standing head - a materially perfect ship can be opened up on it alone

steps.title: The circumstances that create clear grounds - with examples
points: Documents - certificates absent, expired, invalid, mismatched or apparently falsified; an Oil Record Book that will not reconcile
Equipment - required equipment absent, or present but bypassed, blanked, corroded or plainly unmaintained
Condition - heavy corrosion, unsafe machinery spaces, unsanitary accommodation; a report from a pilot or terminal
People - crew unable to start the emergency generator or change over the steering gear; rest hours inconsistent with the watch pattern
ISM-related findings are a class apart - certificates missing or mismatched, uncontrolled or superseded documentation, a master who cannot explain his authority
They point at the system, so nothing else on board can be relied on - which widens the inspection

steps.title: What follows once clear grounds exist
points: A more detailed inspection, scoped by the grounds - not a general re-survey
Rectification, mostly before departure or within a stated period
Detention only on the test: clearly hazardous to safety, health or the environment, or so numerous as to show systemic failure
Notification to the flag State in sufficient detail, and to the recognized organization that issued the certificates
Proceeding to a repair port on conditions where the defect cannot be remedied where she lies
The standing limits: avoid undue detention or delay, with compensation under MARPOL article 7(2)
Operated regionally - the Indian Ocean MOU, DG Shipping, and the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958

steps.title: The three terms that must be separated
points: Define all three by what they act upon
Correction acts on the non-conformity itself - fix the thing that is wrong
Corrective action acts on the cause of a DETECTED non-conformity - stop it happening again
Preventive action acts on the cause of a POTENTIAL non-conformity - stop it happening at all
The difference reduces to one word: DETECTED against POTENTIAL
Correction is NOT corrective action - the commonest failure in the subject
They are not degrees of the same thing

steps.title: Corrective action - what it actually involves
points: The ISM safety management system must provide for reporting, investigation and analysis, and for corrective action
Contain and correct - and do not stop there
Establish what happened before forming a view about why
Find the cause and go past the first plausible one - 'he opened the wrong valve' is where the enquiry stopped
Decide the action against the cause, not against the event; assign an owner and a date
VERIFY EFFECTIVENESS - not was it done, but did it work. The step most often omitted
Feed it back through management review and to the fleet
Inputs: audit non-conformities, PSC deficiencies and detentions, class conditions, accidents, defect reports

steps.title: Preventive action - where it comes from
points: Near misses and hazardous occurrences - the most valuable input, and the first casualty of a blame culture
Risk assessment before a job, a modification or an unusual operation
Audit observations that are not non-conformities but point at a weakness
Trend analysis - alarm counts, defect backlogs, repeated minor findings, deteriorating oil analysis
Fleet and industry experience - a sister ship's casualty, a circular, a service letter, a published report
Other ships' PSC records - a fleet-wide deficiency is a warning to the uninspected
It is the harder discipline: it competes against visibly urgent work, and when it succeeds nothing happens

steps.title: The two worked through one defect, and how the limbs connect
points: A sea water cooler tube fails and floods the lubricating oil system
Correction - plug or renew the tube, renew the oil. The cause is untouched
Corrective action - find why it wasted, change the interval, protection or treatment, and verify at the next opening
Preventive action - inspect every other cooler of the same material and duty, here and on the sisters, before one leaks
A PSC deficiency is corrective action for this ship
and preventive action for every ship not yet inspected
A company running on corrective action alone will be detained at the rate its worst ship deserves

questions.memory_cue: Limb a - before, trigger, examples, after. BEFORE (1): power in the conventions; initial inspection is certificates and general condition. TRIGGER (2): EVIDENCE of a SUBSTANTIAL departure, or crew unfamiliarity. EXAMPLES (3): documents, equipment, condition, people - ISM findings widen everything. AFTER (4): scoped detailed inspection, detain only if clearly hazardous, notify flag and RO. Limb b - three terms, one word. Correction fixes the thing (5); corrective action removes the cause of a DETECTED one and must be verified (6); preventive action removes the cause of a POTENTIAL one (7); one cooler tube shows all three (8).
questions.understand_first: Both halves of this question are really about the same instinct, which is why the examiner has put them together. Start with the port State officer. He has not come aboard to survey your ship - he has come to check that the certificates somebody else issued are being lived up to. So he looks at the paperwork, walks through the engine room and the accommodation, and forms an impression. If nothing he sees contradicts the certificates, that is the end of it, and he leaves. What lets him go further is clear grounds, and the two words that define it are worth holding on to: he needs evidence - something actually observed, not a feeling about the flag or the owner - and the discrepancy has to be substantial, going to whether the ship complies rather than to whether she is tidy. And here is the part engineers underestimate: he does not need to find a single broken thing. If your watchkeeper cannot show him how the steering gear changeover works, that is clear grounds on its own, because a ship's equipment is only worth what the people using it know about it. Now the second half. When something does go wrong, there are three quite different things you can do about it and they get muddled constantly. You can fix the broken thing - that is a correction, and it is where most safety management systems quietly stop. You can find out why it broke and change that, so it does not break again - that is corrective action, and it only counts if you go back later and check it worked. Or you can look at everything else that could break the same way, and get to it first - that is preventive action. One word separates the last two: corrective action follows something that has happened; preventive action forestalls something that has not. And the connection back to the first limb is exact. The deficiency the officer wrote on your report is corrective action for your ship - and preventive action for every other ship in the fleet that he has not visited yet.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Limb a. The power to inspect is in the conventions - SOLAS I/19 with IX/6, XI-1/4, XI-2/9; MARPOL articles 5 and 6; Load Lines article 21; STCW article X and regulation I/4; MLC Title 5.2. IMO's Procedures are guidance and only invite implementation. The initial inspection is limited to certificates and documents and the general condition of the ship. CLEAR GROUNDS = EVIDENCE that the ship, her equipment or her crew does not correspond SUBSTANTIALLY with convention requirements, OR that master or crew are not familiar with essential shipboard procedures. Evidence excludes suspicion and reputation; substantially excludes the trivial; crew unfamiliarity stands on its own. Examples by group: documents (certificates absent, expired, mismatched, falsified; Oil Record Book not reconciling); equipment (missing, bypassed, blanked, unmaintained); condition (heavy corrosion, unsafe machinery spaces, unsanitary accommodation); people (cannot start the emergency generator or change over the steering gear). ISM-related findings point at the SYSTEM, so nothing else can be relied on - they widen the inspection. Then: detailed inspection scoped by the grounds, rectification, detention only if clearly hazardous or so numerous as to show systemic failure, notification to flag State and RO, repair port on conditions - and always avoid undue detention or delay. Limb b. CORRECTION acts on the non-conformity itself - fix the thing. CORRECTIVE ACTION acts on the cause of a DETECTED non-conformity - stop recurrence. PREVENTIVE ACTION acts on the cause of a POTENTIAL non-conformity - stop occurrence. The difference is DETECTED against POTENTIAL. Corrective process: contain and correct, establish what happened, find the cause and go past the first one, act on the cause, assign owner and date, implement, VERIFY EFFECTIVENESS, feed back. Preventive inputs: near misses, risk assessment, audit observations, trends, fleet and industry experience, other ships' PSC records.
critical_numbers: Clear grounds has TWO qualifying words - EVIDENCE and SUBSTANTIALLY - plus a free-standing head of crew unfamiliarity
FOUR groups of examples: documents, equipment, condition, people
THREE terms in limb b - correction, corrective action, preventive action - distinguished by what each acts upon
The whole of limb b's difference is ONE word: DETECTED against POTENTIAL
NO numeric equipment threshold is asserted anywhere in this answer, and no paragraph of the Procedures is cited
quick_revision.critical_regulation: SOLAS regulation I/19, control: a ship in a port of another Contracting Government is subject to control by officers duly authorised to verify that the certificates are valid; and where there are clear grounds for believing that the condition of the ship or of her equipment does not correspond substantially with the particulars of those certificates, steps shall be taken to ensure that the ship shall not sail until she can proceed to sea without danger to the ship or persons on board - every effort being made to avoid a ship being unduly detained or delayed. The corresponding control provisions are MARPOL articles 5 and 6, Load Lines 1966 article 21, STCW article X and regulation I/4, and MLC 2006 Title 5.2. IMO's consolidated Procedures supply the vocabulary and the sequence; they are recommendatory and confer no power, and the edition in circulation at this sitting is not held by MIW, so no paragraph is cited.
quick_revision.major_trap: Treating clear grounds as anything that looks wrong. It is evidence of a substantial departure, and both words exclude something. Second trap: forgetting that crew unfamiliarity is a free-standing head - a materially perfect ship can be opened up on it alone. Third: saying the power comes from the IMO Procedures; it comes from the conventions, and the Procedures only invite Governments to implement them. Fourth: treating the detailed inspection as a general re-survey, when its scope is set by the grounds that triggered it. Fifth, and the whole of limb b's trap: confusing correction with corrective action - replacing the failed part is a correction and leaves the cause exactly where it was. Sixth: describing preventive action as more thorough corrective action, when the difference is detected against potential - a difference in kind, not degree. Seventh: omitting verification of effectiveness, which is the step an auditor goes to first.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define clear grounds, and identify the two words that do the work.
retrieval_cards.answer: Evidence that the ship, her equipment or her crew does not correspond substantially with the requirements of the conventions, or that master or crew are not familiar with essential shipboard procedures relating to safety or the prevention of pollution. EVIDENCE excludes suspicion, reputation and the flag - something must be observed. SUBSTANTIALLY excludes the trivial and the cosmetic.
retrieval_cards.why: The two qualifying words are the definition; without them 'clear grounds' means whatever the officer feels.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship is materially perfect and fully certificated, but a watchkeeper cannot demonstrate the steering gear changeover. Clear grounds?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. Unfamiliarity of the master or crew with essential shipboard procedures relating to safety or pollution prevention is a free-standing head of clear grounds, independent of the condition of any equipment. Equipment is worth only what the people operating it know about it.
retrieval_cards.why: The element candidates most often omit, and a standard oral question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give examples of clear grounds, grouped.
retrieval_cards.answer: Documents - certificates absent, expired, invalid, not matching the ship or apparently falsified; an Oil Record Book that will not reconcile with what is on board. Equipment - required equipment missing, or present but bypassed, blanked, corroded or plainly unmaintained. Condition - heavy corrosion, unsafe machinery spaces, unsanitary accommodation. People - inability to start the emergency generator or operate the fixed fire-fighting system; rest hours inconsistent with the watch pattern.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for examples in terms, and grouping them shows organisation rather than recall.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does IMO's guidance give the port State its power, and how far can a detailed inspection go?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The power is in the convention control articles - SOLAS I/19, MARPOL 5 and 6, Load Lines 21, STCW X and I/4, MLC Title 5.2. IMO's consolidated Procedures are recommendatory; the adopting resolution only invites Governments to implement them. And the detailed inspection is directed at the areas in which the clear grounds arose - it is not a general re-survey of the ship.
retrieval_cards.why: Both halves are commonly got wrong, and the first is what makes the answer independent of which edition is current.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish correction, corrective action and preventive action.
retrieval_cards.answer: Correction acts on the non-conformity itself - fix the thing that is wrong. Corrective action acts on the cause of a DETECTED non-conformity, so it does not recur. Preventive action acts on the cause of a POTENTIAL non-conformity, so it never occurs. The difference the question asks about reduces to one word: DETECTED against POTENTIAL.
retrieval_cards.why: Introducing the third term is what makes the difference between the other two precise rather than approximate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You replaced the failed pump and closed the non-conformity. Was that corrective action?
retrieval_cards.answer: No - that was a correction. It dealt with the non-conformity itself and left the cause exactly where it was, so the same failure will return. Corrective action requires the cause to be found and removed, and it is not complete until effectiveness has been verified - not 'was the action taken' but 'did it stop recurring'.
retrieval_cards.why: The central confusion of limb b, and the reason so many safety management systems are full of closed but unresolved findings.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does preventive action get its inputs, and why is it the harder discipline?
retrieval_cards.answer: From near misses and hazardous occurrences, risk assessments, audit observations that fall short of non-conformities, trend analysis - alarm counts, defect backlogs, deteriorating oil analysis - and fleet and industry experience: a sister ship's casualty, a circular, a service letter, another ship's PSC record. It is harder because it competes against visibly urgent work, and because when it succeeds nothing happens, which is impossible to point at.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming real inputs proves the concept is understood operationally rather than as a definition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A cooler tube fails and floods the LO system. Give the correction, the corrective action and the preventive action.
retrieval_cards.answer: Correction: plug or renew the tube, renew the oil charge, return the plant to service. Corrective action: establish why it wasted - erosion, exhausted cathodic protection, water treatment not followed, an interval quietly extended - change that, and verify at the next opening that the wastage has stopped. Preventive action: inspect or re-interval every other cooler of the same material and duty on this ship and her sisters before one of them leaks.
retrieval_cards.why: One event answered three ways demonstrates the distinction instead of asserting it, which is what the stem's 'difference' is asking for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A port State control deficiency - is it an input to corrective or to preventive action?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both, depending on which ship you are talking about. For the ship inspected it is a detected non-conformity and therefore an input to corrective action. For every other ship in the fleet it is a potential one, and therefore an input to preventive action. A company that responds only to what inspectors find is running on corrective action alone, and will be detained at the rate its worst ship deserves.
retrieval_cards.why: It joins the two limbs, which is almost certainly why the examiner set them on the same question.
