blocks.h: 1. What IACS is and how it is organised

blocks.p: The International Association of Classification Societies is a non-governmental association of classification societies holding consultative status at IMO. The first thing to say about it is what it is not: it is not a regulator, it makes no law, and it issues no certificate. Its output reaches a ship in one of only two ways - through a Member society's own Rules, or because an Administration chooses to rely on it. Getting that clear at the outset is worth a mark on its own, because most weak answers treat IACS as though it were a branch of IMO.

rows: Council
The governing body, with one Representative from each Member. Sets strategy, approves the budget, decides admission and withdrawal of Members, and adopts IACS Resolutions
General Policy Group
The executive deputy to Council, made up of the Members' Permanent Representatives. Runs the work programme and approves the technical output for adoption
Panels and Expert Groups
The technical bodies. They draft and revise the Resolutions, each covering a subject area such as hull, machinery, survey or statutory matters
Permanent Secretariat
Based in London. Administers the association and carries its representation at IMO
Quality oversight function
Oversees Members' quality management systems and the periodic independent verification on which continued membership depends

blocks.p: No membership figure and no panel count is given here, deliberately. Both have changed more than once, and neither is needed to answer the question. A candidate who quotes a number risks being wrong for the year in question and gains nothing if he is right.

blocks.h: 2. UR, UI and PR - what each one acts upon

blocks.p: All three are IACS Resolutions. They are not three grades of the same thing - they differ in what they act upon, and that is the whole of the distinction:

headers: What it is, and how it reaches a ship
rows: UR - Unified Requirement
The society's own Rules

A minimum technical requirement which every Member must build into its Rules, normally within a period set when the Resolution is approved. How it reaches a ship: Never directly. Only through the classification rules of the society that classes the ship
UI - Unified Interpretation
An IMO convention

A common interpretation of a convention provision that is vague, or expressly left to the Administration's satisfaction. How it reaches a ship: through the surveyor applying the convention - and only where the Administration accepts the interpretation
PR - Procedural Requirement
The society itself

A requirement about how the society works - conduct of surveys, transfer of class, reporting, and the handling of outstanding conditions. How it reaches a ship: through the society's own procedures, and it binds the society rather than the ship

blocks.p: The three-word test for holding them apart under examination pressure: ship, convention, society. A UR is about the ship. A UI is about a convention. A PR is about the society.

blocks.h: 3. Does it signify to owners and operators - and why

blocks.p: The stem asks a yes-or-no question, but the marks are entirely in the reasons. The answer is yes, substantially, and it signifies in four distinct ways:

ul: A UR is a floor. It gives the owner a predictable minimum technical standard whichever IACS Member classes the ship, so a newbuilding specification does not have to be re-argued society by society. The corollary is commercial and unwelcome: a new UR applied to existing ships can be an unbudgeted fleet cost.

It removes rule-shopping. An owner cannot move between IACS Members in search of a materially softer technical rule, because the floor is common. That is a discipline on competitors as much as on the owner himself.

A UI reduces regulatory risk, which for an operator means reduced delay. The real cost of a disputed convention interpretation is not the argument - it is the ship alongside while the argument is had at a port State control inspection.

A PR has direct commercial bite. The Procedural Requirements on transfer of class mean that changing society does not shed outstanding conditions of class or overdue surveys; the gaining society takes them over. Transfer is not an escape route, and an owner who plans one on that assumption is planning badly.

blocks.p: And the limit must be stated, because it is the discriminating point. IACS Resolutions bind Members, not owners and not flag States. They have no statutory force of their own. A society outside IACS is not bound by any of them, and a ship classed with such a society is outside the system altogether - which is a matter the owner, the charterer and the underwriter each have their own reasons to care about.

blocks.h: 4. What a Recognized Organization is

blocks.p: This opens limb b. A Recognized Organization is an organization to which a flag Administration has delegated statutory survey and certification work - surveys and certificates required by the conventions, issued on the Administration's behalf. It is most commonly, but not necessarily, a classification society.
Three distinctions carry the marks here, and all three are regularly missed:

ul: The delegation is of function, not of responsibility. The Administration remains answerable for the ship's compliance and for the conduct of the organization it authorized. It has handed over the work, not the duty.

Classification society and RO are not synonyms. They are two capacities. Class is a private contractual arrangement between the society and the owner, against the society's own Rules. RO work is public, statutory and done for a flag State. The same surveyor may act in both capacities in a single attendance, and the two must not be confused when a dispute arises about what was surveyed and on whose authority.

A society is an RO only for the flag that delegated to it, and only to the extent of that delegation. The same society may hold quite different scopes from different Administrations - authorized for load line but not for ISM, or for one ship type and not another. There is no such thing as being an RO in general.

blocks.p: It follows that recognition and authorization are two separate acts. Recognition is the Administration's assessment of the organization against the mandatory requirements. Authorization is the later, specific delegation of named functions for named conventions. An organization may be recognized and still not authorized for a particular ship type or a particular convention, and an Administration is required not to authorize functions beyond what the organization can actually do.

blocks.h: 5. The RO Code and its salient features

blocks.p: How it came about, and how a code becomes binding. Before 2013 the criteria for recognising organizations were scattered across several Assembly resolutions and were applied unevenly. The Code for Recognized Organizations replaced them with a single harmonised, transparent and independent international standard. It was adopted by resolution MSC.349(92) on 21 June 2013 and by resolution MEPC.237(65), and it was made mandatory from 1 January 2015 by MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92) and MEPC.238(65), which amended SOLAS, MARPOL Annexes I and II and the 1988 Load Line Protocol to refer to it - with SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 as the hook. Recognise the technique, because IMO uses it repeatedly: a code is written as a free-standing document and then made binding by amending the conventions that point at it.
Salient feature one - three parts, and only two of them bind. This is the most examinable structural fact in the whole subject:

rows: Part 1
General provisions - purpose, definitions, application, the power to delegate, and notification to the Secretary-General
Mandatory
Part 2
Mandatory requirements - what the organization must satisfy, and what the flag State must do when it authorizes
Mandatory - it says shall
Part 3
Guidelines for flag State oversight of Recognized Organizations
Recommendatory - it says should

blocks.p: The adopting resolution recommends that Governments apply Part 3 unless their own national arrangements provide at least equivalent safety - which is what makes Part 3 guidance with teeth rather than guidance that can simply be ignored.
Salient feature two - what the organization itself must satisfy. Demonstration is the organization's burden; confirmation is the flag State's:

ul: General requirements - legal personality, demonstrated competence and experience, ethical conduct, and independence.
Management and organization - a documented structure, defined responsibilities, and control over its exclusive surveyors and its offices worldwide.
Resources - qualified surveyors and auditors, training and qualification against defined standards, and technical and research capability.
Processes - including the control of subcontracting, and defined handling of complaints and appeals.
Performance measurement - internal audit, vertical contract audit of a complete certification history, and control of statutory deficiencies.
A quality management system no less effective than the recognised international quality standard, certified by an accredited body that is independent of the organizations and of their associations.

blocks.p: Independence is the head the Code is really defending. An organization that surveys a ship, classes the same ship, and depends commercially on the owner it is surveying has a conflict that the entire structure above is designed to contain.

Salient feature three - what the flag State must do when it authorizes. It must rest the delegation on its conventional basis and use it only for its own ships; it must specify the functions - function by function and convention by convention, including the conditions for withdrawal and cancellation; it must reduce the delegation to a formal written agreement covering the legal basis, reporting, national interpretations and information exchange; and it must notify the Secretary-General of its list of Recognized Organizations and of the conditions of the authority delegated to each.

blocks.h: 6. How Administrations monitor Recognized Organizations

blocks.p: The third sentence of the limb, and it divides cleanly into what happens before delegation, what happens during it, and what happens to the Administration itself.

Before delegation: assess the organization against Part 2, determine its technical, managerial and research capability, confirm it can actually perform the functions contemplated, and reduce the delegation to a written agreement stating scope, limits, national requirements and interpretations, the instructions to be followed where a ship is found unfit to proceed, and the records to be kept.
During delegation, the oversight programme runs on four mechanisms:

ol: Access. The Administration must be able to reach into the organization - its quality management system, its internal instructions and circulars, its fleet documentation, and its casualty statistics.

A system to ensure adequacy. Reporting from the organization, additional flag State inspections of ships it has certified, and consultation between the several organizations authorized by the same flag.

Auditing. The Administration audits, and is permitted to rely on audits by an accredited independent body - conducted with ethical conduct, fair presentation and due professional care. In practice this includes vertical contract audits and witnessed surveys, which test the actual attendance rather than the paperwork about it.
Programme management. The whole of the above is run as a managed programme with stated objectives, allocated resources, records, and periodic review - not as a set of occasional interventions.

blocks.p: The performance indicators on which the review turns are: port State control detention performance of the ships the organization has certified, the results of its internal audits, the results of the third-party quality system audit, the findings of previous monitoring, and the condition of the ships certified. Casualties attributable to the delegation belong here too.

The sanctions are graduated, and the graduation is the point. Because the authorization is specified function by function, it can be narrowed as readily as it can be suspended or withdrawn - an Administration dissatisfied with an organization's handling of one convention need not, and usually will not, terminate the whole relationship. And a failure by the organization to report as agreed is a compliance failure, not poor service: it goes to the authorization itself.

Finally, the Administration is itself monitored. Under the IMO Member State Audit Scheme it is audited against the III Code - resolution A.1070(28), mandatory from 1 January 2016 - whose Part 2 expressly requires an oversight programme for delegated authority. The obligations against which it is measured are those in the non-exhaustive list at resolution A.1157(32), adopted by the 32nd Assembly and the instrument in force at this sitting.
Which closes the limb on the sentence that the whole of it exists to establish: a flag State may delegate the work, but it cannot delegate the responsibility.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Two limbs, sixteen marks, and they are about two entirely different things that candidates routinely merge. Limb a is about IACS - a private industry association that makes no law. Limb b is about the RO Code - a mandatory IMO instrument about flag States delegating statutory work. The overlap is only that the same societies appear in both. An answer that treats IACS as a regulator, or the RO Code as an IACS document, has lost the discrimination the question is built on.

Note also that limb b is three questions in one sentence: what an RO is, the salient features of the Code, and how Administrations monitor. Answer all three explicitly. Candidates who write at length on the first two and give monitoring a sentence lose a third of the limb.

blocks.h: The three-word test for UR, UI and PR

blocks.p: Ship, convention, society. A UR acts on the society's Rules and therefore on the ship. A UI acts on an IMO convention, giving a common reading of a vague or discretionary provision. A PR acts on the society itself - how it surveys, how it transfers class, how it reports. If those three words are written down first, the rest of limb a's first half writes itself.

blocks.h: The sentence that shows limb a is understood

blocks.p: IACS makes no law. Its Resolutions bind its Members, not owners and not flag States, and they reach a ship only through class Rules or because an Administration chooses to rely on them. State that, and then the significance limb has something to argue about; omit it, and everything else reads as though IACS were a regulator.

blocks.h: Significance - four reasons and a limit

ul: A UR is a floor - a predictable minimum whichever Member classes the ship. But a new UR on existing ships is an unbudgeted cost.
No rule-shopping between Members for a softer technical standard.
A UI cuts delay, because the real cost of a disputed interpretation is the ship alongside at a port State control inspection.
A PR has commercial bite - transfer of class does not shed outstanding conditions or overdue surveys.
The limit: IACS Resolutions bind Members only. A non-IACS society is outside the system entirely.

blocks.h: Class against RO - the distinction the examiner is hunting

blocks.p: Class is private and contractual, against the society's own Rules. RO work is public and statutory, done on behalf of a flag State. The same society, and often the same surveyor on the same day, acts in both capacities. And a society is an RO only for the flag that delegated, and only to the extent of that delegation - there is no such thing as being an RO in general. Add that delegation is of function, not of responsibility, and the definitional part of limb b is complete.

blocks.h: The single most examinable fact about the RO Code

blocks.p: Three parts, two of which bind. Part 1 general and Part 2 mandatory requirements are mandatory; Part 3, the flag State oversight guidelines, is recommendatory - and the adopting resolution recommends applying it unless national arrangements give at least equivalent safety. Part 2 says shall; Part 3 says should. If you remember one thing about the Code, remember this.

blocks.h: How a code becomes binding - a pattern worth carrying

blocks.p: The RO Code was adopted by MSC.349(92) of 21 June 2013 and MEPC.237(65), then made mandatory from 1 January 2015 by MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92) and MEPC.238(65), which amended SOLAS, MARPOL Annexes I and II and the 1988 Load Line Protocol - SOLAS XI-1/1 being the hook. The same technique makes the ISM Code, the ISPS Code and the III Code binding. Recognising the pattern is worth more than memorising this one instance.

blocks.h: Monitoring - before, during, and above

blocks.p: BEFORE: assess against Part 2, confirm capability, and put the delegation into a written agreement with stated scope and limits. DURING: access to the system, a mechanism to ensure adequacy, auditing including vertical contract audits and witnessed surveys, and the whole run as a managed programme. ABOVE: the Administration is itself audited under the Member State Audit Scheme against the III Code, A.1070(28), measured against the obligations listed in A.1157(32). Then close on the sentence: the work can be delegated, the responsibility cannot.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Treating IACS as a regulator or as a part of IMO. It is a private association with consultative status and no legal authority.
Saying the RO Code is an IACS document. It is an IMO instrument, adopted by MSC and MEPC resolutions.
Confusing classification with statutory work, or treating 'classification society' and 'Recognized Organization' as synonyms.
Saying Part 3 is mandatory. It is guidance - though guidance the adopting resolution presses hard.
Answering the significance limb with a bare yes. The marks are entirely in the reasons.
Giving a membership figure or a panel count. Both have changed, and neither is needed.
Answering the definition and the salient features and then giving monitoring one line, when it is a third of the limb.
Forgetting that the authorization is function-specific, and therefore that it can be narrowed rather than only withdrawn.
Saying the flag State transfers responsibility along with the work. It does not.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Does IACS issue certificates?" No. Its Members do, in their own right or as ROs for a flag State. IACS itself issues none.
"What is the difference between a UR and a UI?" A UR changes the society's Rules; a UI interprets an IMO convention. Different targets entirely.
"Your ship transfers class. Do the outstanding conditions go away?" No - the Procedural Requirements on transfer of class carry them across to the gaining society.
"Is your classification society your Recognized Organization?" Only for the flags that have delegated to it, and only for the functions delegated. Ask which hat the surveyor is wearing today.
"Which parts of the RO Code are mandatory?" Parts 1 and 2. Part 3 is recommendatory.
"Who is responsible if the RO gets it wrong?" The Administration. Function is delegated; responsibility is not.

"How would a flag State find out that an RO was performing badly?" Port State control detentions on the ships it certifies, audit results, vertical contract audits, witnessed surveys, and casualty statistics.
"Who audits the flag State?" IMO, under the Member State Audit Scheme, against the III Code.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Who classes your ship, and which flags has that society been authorized by?
Your surveyor attends for a class survey and a statutory survey on the same day. What changes between the two?
What is a condition of class, and what happens to it if the owner changes society?
Give me an example of something in your ship's construction that came from a Unified Requirement.
If you disagree with a surveyor's interpretation of a convention, who decides?
What could cause a flag State to withdraw part of an RO's authorization?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb a: what it is, the three letters, and why you care. IACS makes no law (1); ship, convention, society for UR, UI, PR (2); floor, no rule-shopping, less delay, transfer bites - and Resolutions bind Members only (3). Limb b: is, Code, monitor. An RO is a delegate of a flag State, function not responsibility (4); the Code is three parts, two mandatory, made binding through the conventions (5); monitoring is before, during and above, closing on the work delegated but not the duty (6).

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: One date on this question moves, and it is the obligations list. The non-exhaustive list of IMO instrument obligations against which a flag State is audited was carried by resolution A.1157(32) at this sitting. The 33rd Assembly replaced it with A.1187(33) on 6 December 2023 - nine months after this examination - and a later answer on this same question naturally cites the newer resolution. It must not be read back into this sitting. The correction was made here from the dates and not inherited. MIW holds no copy of A.1157(32); it is cited by identity, adopting session and revocation date only, and no clause of it is quoted.

Everything else on this question is temporally stable. The RO Code was adopted in 2013 and became mandatory on 1 January 2015; the III Code became mandatory on 1 January 2016. Neither moved before this sitting or in the period examined afterwards, and the December 2023 Assembly change replaced the obligations list, not the Code. The Indian frame is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and DG Shipping; the 2025 Act is three years after this sitting and is not cited.

No provision of the RO Code is quoted anywhere, and that is a limitation rather than a stylistic choice. The copy available for this answer is an image-only scan of unconfirmed edition, so no sentence of the Code could be read at source. The Code's parts, the mandatory and recommendatory split and the salient features are carried at the level MIW's own verification records establish them, and no sentence of the Code appears in quotation marks.

MIW holds no IACS procedural document at all - only its own class and survey notes - so the whole of limb a is graded industry guidance rather than primary, and is presented as such. No membership count and no panel count is asserted, and no technical panel constituted after this sitting is named: the panel structure changed in January 2024, so a settled figure taken from later material would be wrong for this date. The period for incorporating a Unified Requirement into Members' Rules is given as the normal position rather than as an invariable rule.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: TWO LIMBS ABOUT TWO DIFFERENT SYSTEMS THAT SHARE THE SAME ACTORS, and the intent is to see whether the candidate keeps them apart. Limb a is about IACS - a private, non-governmental association that makes no law - and specifically about the difference between its three instrument classes and whether any of it matters commercially. Limb b is about a mandatory IMO instrument governing the delegation of statutory work by flag States. The discriminators are: that IACS Resolutions bind Members and not owners; that UR, UI and PR act on the ship, the convention and the society respectively; that classification and RO work are different capacities; and that only Parts 1 and 2 of the RO Code are mandatory.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 by rubric, no marks printed against either limb. The derivation is recorded rather than concealed: instruction 2 states all questions carry equal marks, six answered questions are required, and the paper prints Total Marks - 100. The two limbs are taken as roughly equal. LIMB b IS THE COMPRESSION PROBLEM ON THIS QUESTION: its three sentences are set as a WHOLE sixteen-mark question at QP2309-Q2, and here they are worth about half that, so the material is re-cut rather than reproduced.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For limb a: the character of IACS as a non-governmental association with no legal authority; its principal organs; the UR/UI/PR distinction stated by what each acts upon; and reasons rather than a bare yes on significance, including the limit that Resolutions bind Members only. For limb b: the definition of an RO with delegation of function but not responsibility; the separation of class from statutory work; the Code's adoption and the technique by which it was made mandatory; the three parts and which of them bind; the requirements on the organization and on the flag State; and the oversight programme, ending on the Administration's own audit.

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - not because the subject moves, but because the single dated element on it MOVED NINE MONTHS AFTER THIS SITTING. The obligations list was replaced by the 33rd Assembly on 6 December 2023, so every later treatment of this question cites a resolution that is prohibited here. The IACS panel structure is a second, quieter trap of the same kind, closed by asserting no panel and no membership figure.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW - the instruments are international and the Indian layer is thin. Where it appears, the statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and the administration is DG Shipping; the 2025 Act and the DGMA rename are years future and neither appears.
technical_ambiguities: Whether 'structure of IACS' means its governance organs or its instrument hierarchy. The stem answers itself by going on to ask about UI, UR and PR, so the answer gives the governance structure and then treats the instruments separately.

Whether a Unified Requirement must be incorporated within a fixed period. The normal position is stated; the period for a given Resolution is set when it is approved, so no invariable rule is asserted.

Whether the oversight methods are a closed statutory list. They are not - Part 3 is recommendatory, and an Administration may satisfy the obligation by other means of at least equivalent effect. The answer says so.
Whether recognition and authorization are the same act. They are not, and the distinction explains why an authorization can be narrowed function by function rather than only withdrawn entirely.

Sections 1 to 3 are limb a: what IACS is and its organs in a table; UR, UI and PR distinguished in a table by what each acts upon, with the ship/convention/society test; then significance as four reasons plus the limit. steps.title: What IACS is and how it is organised
points: A non-governmental association of classification societies with consultative status at IMO
It makes no law and issues no certificate - its output reaches ships through Members' Rules or through Administrations relying on it
Council - governing body, one Representative per Member; strategy, budget, admission, adopts Resolutions
General Policy Group - executive deputy to Council, the Members' Permanent Representatives, runs the work programme
Panels and Expert Groups - the technical bodies that draft and revise the Resolutions
Permanent Secretariat in London; a quality oversight function over Members' quality systems
No membership figure and no panel count is stated - both have changed and neither is needed

steps.title: UR, UI and PR - what each one acts upon
points: All three are IACS Resolutions; they differ in what they act upon
UR acts on the society's own Rules - a minimum technical requirement each Member builds in
A UR reaches a ship through class rules, never directly
UI acts on an IMO convention - a common interpretation where a provision is vague or left to the Administration
A UI interprets; it does not create a class requirement
PR acts on the society itself - survey conduct, transfer of class, reporting, outstanding conditions
The test: ship, convention, society

steps.title: Does it signify to owners and operators - and why
points: Yes, substantially - and the question wants reasons, not a yes
A UR is a floor - a predictable standard whichever Member classes the ship
But a new UR applied to existing ships is an unbudgeted fleet cost
No rule-shopping between Members for a materially softer technical rule
A UI reduces delay - the cost of a disputed interpretation is the ship alongside at port State control
A PR has commercial bite - transfer of class does not shed outstanding conditions or overdue surveys
The limit: IACS Resolutions bind Members, not owners, and a non-IACS society is outside the system

steps.title: What a Recognized Organization is
points: An organization to which a flag Administration has delegated statutory survey and certification work
Most commonly, but not necessarily, a classification society
The delegation is of function, not of responsibility - the Administration remains answerable
Class and RO are different capacities - private and contractual against public and statutory
A society is an RO only for the flag that delegated, and only to the extent delegated
The same surveyor may act in both capacities in one attendance
Recognition and authorization are two separate acts - assessment, then specified delegation

steps.title: The RO Code and its salient features
points: Adopted by MSC.349(92) of 21 June 2013 and by MEPC.237(65)
A harmonised, transparent and independent standard replacing scattered Assembly criteria
Mandatory from 1 January 2015 by MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92) and MEPC.238(65)
Amending SOLAS, MARPOL Annexes I and II and the 1988 Load Line Protocol; SOLAS XI-1/1 is the hook
Part 1 general, Part 2 mandatory requirements, Part 3 oversight guidelines
Parts 1 and 2 bind; Part 3 is recommendatory - the most examinable structural fact

On the organization: legal personality, competence, ethics, independence, resources, subcontracting control, complaints and appeals, vertical contract audit, and a quality system certified by an accredited independent body
On the flag State: rest it on its conventional basis, SPECIFY the functions, make a formal written agreement, and notify the Secretary-General

steps.title: How Administrations monitor Recognized Organizations
points: Before: assess against Part 2, confirm capability, and reduce the delegation to a written agreement with scope and limits
During, mechanism one - ACCESS to the quality system, internal instructions, fleet documentation and casualty statistics
Mechanism two - a system to ensure adequacy: reporting, additional flag State inspections, consultation between the authorized organizations
Mechanism three - auditing, including vertical contract audits and witnessed surveys, with reliance permitted on accredited independent audits
Mechanism four - a managed programme with objectives, resources, records and periodic review
Performance indicators: port State detentions, internal audits, third-party quality audits, previous monitoring, and the condition of the ships certified
The authorization is function-specific, so it can be narrowed as readily as withdrawn; failure to report is a compliance failure
The Administration is itself audited under the Member State Audit Scheme against the III Code, A.1070(28), and the obligations at A.1157(32)
The work may be delegated; the responsibility cannot

questions.memory_cue: Limb a - what it is, three letters, why you care. IACS makes no law (1); ship, convention, society for UR, UI, PR (2); floor, no shopping, less delay, transfer bites, and Resolutions bind Members only (3). Limb b - is, Code, monitor. Delegation of function, not responsibility (4); three parts, two mandatory, made binding through the conventions (5); before, during and above, closing on the duty that cannot be delegated (6).
questions.understand_first: Two different things wear the same face in this question, and the whole of it is about telling them apart. A classification society is a private business. You pay it, it writes its own rules about how a ship should be built and maintained, and it surveys your ship against those rules. Nothing about that is law. IACS is the club those societies formed among themselves, so that their private rules would not drift apart and so that they could speak with one voice at IMO - and it too makes no law. When IACS agrees a Unified Requirement, nothing happens to your ship until each Member writes it into its own rules; that is the mechanism by which a private agreement between companies eventually reaches steel. The second thing is quite different. Every flag State has statutory duties under the conventions - to survey ships and to issue certificates - and almost none of them has the surveyors to do it worldwide. So they delegate, usually to the same societies, which then act in an entirely separate capacity as Recognized Organizations. That is public work done on a government's behalf. IMO eventually wrote a Code setting out what an organization must be like before a flag State may use it, and what the flag State must do to keep an eye on it afterwards - and the reason the Code exists at all is the obvious conflict in the arrangement, since the organization is being paid by the owner whose ship it is certifying on the government's behalf. Hold on to one sentence and the rest arranges itself around it: the flag State can hand over the work, but it can never hand over the responsibility.

quick_revision.recall_15s: IACS = a non-governmental association of classification societies, consultative status at IMO, makes no law and issues no certificate. Organs: Council (one Representative per Member, adopts Resolutions), General Policy Group (Permanent Representatives, runs the work programme), Panels and Expert Groups (draft the technical Resolutions), Permanent Secretariat, quality oversight of Members. UR acts on the society's RULES - a minimum technical requirement reaching the ship only through class rules. UI acts on an IMO CONVENTION - a common interpretation of a vague or discretionary provision. PR acts on the SOCIETY - survey conduct, transfer of class, reporting. Test: ship, convention, society. Significance: a UR is a floor and stops rule-shopping but can cost an existing fleet; a UI cuts delay at port State control; a PR means transfer of class does not shed outstanding conditions; limit - Resolutions bind Members, not owners. RO = an organization to which a flag Administration has delegated statutory survey and certification - function delegated, responsibility not; class and RO are different capacities; an RO only for the flag that delegated and only to the extent delegated. RO Code: adopted MSC.349(92) 21 June 2013 and MEPC.237(65); mandatory 1 January 2015 by MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92), MEPC.238(65) amending SOLAS, MARPOL I and II and the 1988 Load Line Protocol, hooked at SOLAS XI-1/1. Part 1 general and Part 2 mandatory bind; Part 3 oversight guidelines are recommendatory. Monitoring: assess and agree in writing before; then access, adequacy, auditing and a managed programme; indicators are detentions, audits and the condition of the ships certified. The Administration is itself audited under IMSAS against the III Code A.1070(28) and the obligations at A.1157(32).

Parts 1 and 2 are mandatory; Part 3, the flag State oversight guidelines, is recommendatory, and the adopting resolution recommends applying it unless national arrangements provide at least equivalent safety.
quick_revision.major_trap: Merging the two limbs - treating IACS as a regulator, or the RO Code as an IACS document. IACS is a private association that makes no law; the RO Code is an IMO instrument adopted by MSC and MEPC resolutions. Second trap: saying Part 3 is mandatory. Parts 1 and 2 bind; Part 3 is guidance. Third: answering the significance limb with a bare yes, when the marks are entirely in the reasons. Fourth: treating 'classification society' and 'Recognized Organization' as synonyms - they are two capacities, and a society is an RO only for the flag that delegated and only to the extent delegated. Fifth: saying the flag State transfers responsibility with the work. It does not. Sixth, and specific to this sitting: citing the obligations list at A.1187(33), which was adopted nine months after this examination. The operative instrument here is A.1157(32).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the IACS and RO Code question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb a: 1 what IACS is and its organs. 2 UR, UI and PR by what each acts upon. 3 significance to owners, with the limit. Limb b: 4 what a Recognized Organization is. 5 the RO Code, how it became binding, and its three parts. 6 how Administrations monitor, closing on the duty that cannot be delegated.
retrieval_cards.why: The two limbs are about two different systems that share the same actors, and the structure is what keeps them apart.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish a UR, a UI and a PR.
retrieval_cards.answer: A Unified Requirement acts on the society's own Rules - a minimum technical requirement each Member must build in, reaching a ship only through class rules. A Unified Interpretation acts on an IMO convention, giving a common reading where a provision is vague or left to the Administration. A Procedural Requirement acts on the society itself - survey conduct, transfer of class, reporting. The test: ship, convention, society.
retrieval_cards.why: They are not three grades of the same thing; they differ in what they act upon, and that is the whole distinction.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does IACS make law or issue certificates?
retrieval_cards.answer: No to both. It is a non-governmental association of classification societies with consultative status at IMO. Its Resolutions bind its Members, not owners and not flag States, and they reach a ship only through a Member's Rules or because an Administration chooses to rely on them. A society outside IACS is not bound by any of them.
retrieval_cards.why: Treating IACS as a regulator is the commonest way to lose the whole of limb a.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a Recognized Organization, and how does it differ from a classification society?
retrieval_cards.answer: An organization to which a flag Administration has delegated statutory survey and certification work - usually but not necessarily a classification society. Class is private and contractual, against the society's own Rules; RO work is public and statutory, done for a flag State. The delegation is of function, not of responsibility, and a society is an RO only for the flag that delegated and only to the extent of that delegation.
retrieval_cards.why: The two capacities are the substance of the definition, and the same surveyor may hold both in one attendance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How did the RO Code become mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: It was adopted by resolution MSC.349(92) of 21 June 2013 and by MEPC.237(65), then made mandatory from 1 January 2015 by MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92) and MEPC.238(65), which amended SOLAS, MARPOL Annexes I and II and the 1988 Load Line Protocol to refer to it. SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 is the hook. This is IMO's standard technique for making a code binding.
retrieval_cards.why: Adoption and entry into force are separate steps, and recognising the pattern is worth more than memorising this one instance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which parts of the RO Code are mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: Parts 1 and 2. Part 1 is general provisions and Part 2 is the mandatory requirements on the organization and on the flag State - Part 2 says shall. Part 3, the flag State oversight guidelines, is recommendatory and says should, though the adopting resolution recommends applying it unless national arrangements provide at least equivalent safety.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most examinable structural fact in the subject, and a very common error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does an Administration monitor a Recognized Organization?
retrieval_cards.answer: Before: assess against Part 2, confirm capability, and put the delegation into a written agreement with stated scope and limits. During: access to the quality system, instructions, fleet documentation and casualty statistics; a system to ensure adequacy through reporting and additional flag inspections; auditing, including vertical contract audits and witnessed surveys; and a managed programme with objectives and periodic review.
retrieval_cards.why: Monitoring is a third of limb b and is the part candidates most often reduce to a single line.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship transfers class. What happens to outstanding conditions of class?
retrieval_cards.answer: They go with the ship. The IACS Procedural Requirements on transfer of class require the gaining society to take over outstanding conditions of class and overdue surveys. Transfer is not a way of shedding them, which is the clearest commercial illustration of why a Procedural Requirement matters to an owner.
retrieval_cards.why: The significance limb asks why any of this matters commercially, and this is the sharpest single example.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who audits the flag State, and against what?
retrieval_cards.answer: IMO, under the Member State Audit Scheme, against the III Code - resolution A.1070(28), mandatory from 1 January 2016 - whose Part 2 expressly requires an oversight programme for delegated authority. The obligations against which it is measured are the non-exhaustive list at resolution A.1157(32), the instrument in force at this sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: It closes the limb on the point the whole of it exists to make: the work may be delegated, the responsibility may not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between recognition and authorization?
retrieval_cards.answer: Recognition is the Administration's assessment of an organization against the mandatory requirements of the Code. Authorization is the later, specific delegation of named functions for named conventions. An organization may be recognized and still not authorized for a particular ship type or convention - and because the authorization is specified function by function, it can be narrowed as readily as suspended or withdrawn.
retrieval_cards.why: The distinction explains why enforcement is graduated rather than all-or-nothing, which is how it actually works in practice.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the operative non-exhaustive list of obligations at this sitting is resolution A.1157(32), and NOT A.1187(33).
reverify_before_publication.why: TRUE AS AT MARCH 2023 and established from the adoption dates directly. A.1187(33) was adopted on 6 December 2023, nine months after this examination, and it revoked A.1157(32). It is not the position today, and a reviewer reading this after December 2023 must NOT 'correct' it to the newer resolution number. MIW holds no copy of A.1157(32) and no clause of it is quoted; it is cited by identity, adopting session and revocation date only.

reverify_before_publication.why: The corpus copy of the RO Code carries review-queue item RQ-25, which leaves its edition and completeness unverified, and it has no readable text layer. No provision could be read verbatim in this session, and no sentence of the Code appears in quotation marks anywhere. reverify_before_publication.why: MIW holds no IACS procedural document - only its own class and survey notes - so the whole of limb a is graded industry guidance rather than primary and is presented as such. No IACS Resolution number, no membership count and no panel count is asserted, and no technical panel constituted after March 2023 is named.

blocks.h: 1. Why the oil is analysed, and what the four techniques are for

blocks.p: A running machine is a sealed box. The one thing that comes out of it continuously, and that has been in contact with every working surface inside it, is the oil. Whatever wears, whatever leaks in and whatever the oil itself becomes is carried in that sample. This is why used-oil analysis is the foundation of condition-based maintenance and not an accessory to it.

The four techniques named in this question are not four ways of doing the same job. Between them they answer three different questions, and setting that out before describing any instrument is what turns the rest of the answer into an argument rather than a list:

rows: Is the machine wearing?
Elemental spectrometry and particle count
Is the oil still fit to remain in service?
FTIR, and Base Number with Acid Number
Is anything getting in that should not be there?
All four, each from a different direction

blocks.p: One rule governs the use of all of them, and it is worth stating at the outset because every later section depends on it: the trend against that machine's own history is worth more than any single value. An absolute figure means very little until you know where that particular machine normally sits.

blocks.h: 2. A) Elemental (spectrometric) analysis

blocks.p: Principle. A measured quantity of oil is excited - in a plasma, or across the arc of a rotating-disc electrode. The atoms of each element present emit light at wavelengths characteristic of that element, and the intensity at each of those wavelengths is proportional to how much of the element is there. The instrument reads many elements at once and reports each in parts per million.
What the results mean. The elements sort into three families, and reading them as families rather than as a column of numbers is the difference between a report and a diagnosis:

rows: Wear metals
Iron; copper, lead, tin; chromium; aluminium; silver; nickel

Iron from liners, rings, gears and shafting. Copper, lead and tin from bearings and bushes. Chromium from rings and plated surfaces. Aluminium from pistons and some bearing materials. Each element points at a different part of the machine, which is what makes the technique diagnostic rather than merely alarming
Contaminants
Silicon; sodium and boron; vanadium and nickel

Silicon from airborne dirt through a defective filter, seal or breather - and silicon is abrasive. Sodium and boron from coolant leakage. Vanadium and nickel are carried in residual fuel, so their appearance in a crankcase oil indicates fuel finding its way in
Additive elements
Calcium and magnesium; zinc and phosphorus; barium

Calcium and magnesium from detergent and dispersant additives; zinc and phosphorus from anti-wear additives. A falling trend is additive depletion and marks the end of the oil's useful life. A rising trend almost always means the wrong oil has been put in

blocks.p: Silicon needs a sentence of its own, because it reads two ways. A rising silicon trend in normal service is dirt ingress, and it is serious, because silica is harder than the metal it is circulating between. A single high silicon result immediately after an overhaul is usually silicone sealant or antifoam residue and is not. Knowing which of the two you are looking at requires the maintenance history, not the report.

blocks.h: 3. What spectrometry cannot see, and why that governs its use

blocks.p: This is the most important qualification in the whole question and it is the one most often left out. The method depends on the particle being completely atomised in the excitation source. Coarse particles are not, so the response falls away progressively as particle size increases. In practice the technique reports essentially the fine fraction only.

The consequence has to be stated plainly, because it changes how the result may be used. Normal rubbing wear generates fine debris and is seen very well. Bearing fatigue, spalling, scuffing and gear pitting generate coarse debris and may not register at all. So a satisfactory spectrometric report is not evidence that the machine is in good order; it is evidence that the fine fraction is normal, which is a very much weaker statement and is sometimes a dangerously reassuring one. This limitation is the entire reason that particle count, ferrography and magnetic plug inspection belong alongside spectrometry rather than as alternatives to it.

blocks.h: 4. B) Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy

blocks.p: Principle. Infrared energy is passed through a thin film of the oil. Molecular bonds absorb infrared at wavenumbers characteristic of the bond, so the pattern of absorption is a fingerprint of what molecules are present. Instead of scanning one wavelength at a time, the instrument collects all wavelengths simultaneously as an interferogram and applies a Fourier transform to convert it into a spectrum - which is what the name describes and why the technique is fast.

It is a differential measurement, and this is the point candidates lose. The spectrum of the used oil is compared against the spectrum of the same oil unused, and what is reported is the difference. Without a new-oil reference the result is very much weaker. That is a technical fact with a direct practical instruction attached: retain a sealed sample of every oil delivery taken aboard.
What it detects, each in its own characteristic absorption region:

ul: Oxidation - the principal measure of the oil's thermal and chemical ageing.
Nitration - from combustion products, and prominent in gas and dual-fuel engines.
Sulphation - from sulphur oxides, and therefore directly related to the sulphur of the fuel being burned.
Water, and glycol where coolant is finding its way in.
Soot - which appears as a broad rise in the baseline rather than as a discrete peak, because soot scatters rather than absorbing selectively.
Fuel dilution and additive depletion.

blocks.p: Strengths and limits. It is quick, needs a very small sample, uses no reagents and returns several parameters at once, which makes it the natural routine screen. But it is semi-quantitative - very good on trend, weaker on absolute value - and it is completely blind to wear metals and to particles. It describes the oil. It says nothing about the machine.

blocks.h: 5. C) Particle count

blocks.p: Principle. The solid particles suspended in the oil are counted and sized. The usual method is automatic optical light obscuration: the oil passes through a cell across a light beam, and each particle casts a shadow whose magnitude gives its size. Where the oil is too dark or too heavily sooted for light to pass, pore-blockage methods are used instead, and microscopic counting remains the referee method.

Reporting. Results are given as counts per millilitre in cumulative size bands - the number of particles larger than each of several sizes - and those bands are condensed into a cleanliness code for trending and for specification. No code or band table is reproduced here, because MIW does not hold the standard and because in service the target code is set by the equipment manufacturer for that system.

Why it matters. It is decisive for hydraulic, servo and control systems, where clearances are measured in microns and a particle population that would be harmless in a crankcase will destroy a servo valve. It is the direct measure of filtration and centrifuge performance and of ingress through seals and breathers - a rising count with unchanged wear metals usually means the cleaning has failed, not that the machine has. And crucially it sees the coarse particles that spectrometry misses, which is what makes the two complementary.

Limits. Optical counters count water droplets and air bubbles as particles, so a wet or aerated sample reads falsely high and must be settled, with water measured separately where necessary. And the technique reports how many and how big, never what: it cannot tell steel from sand from soot.

blocks.h: 6. D) Base Number against Acid Number

blocks.p: These two are confused more often than any other pair in oil analysis, and there is a good reason for it: both are titrations, and both are reported in the same units - milligrammes of potassium hydroxide per gramme of oil. They are nonetheless measurements of opposite things.

rows: What is measured
The alkaline reserve conferred by overbased detergent additives
The quantity of acidic constituents present in the oil
Where it comes from
Deliberately formulated into the oil by the blender
Combustion acids, and oxidation of the oil itself
Direction in service
FALLS as acid is neutralised and additive is consumed
RISES as acidic species accumulate
Units
mg KOH per gramme
mg KOH per gramme - the same units, which is the source of the confusion
What an adverse value means
The alkaline reserve is exhausted and the oil can no longer protect the metal against acid attack
Acid is present and attacking, or the oil is heavily oxidised

blocks.p: Three points separate a good answer from an adequate one:

ul: An oil can carry a significant Base Number and a significant Acid Number at the same time. They are separate titrations of separate species, and weak organic acids can coexist with an alkaline reserve. A candidate who treats them as two ends of one scale misreads every report of this kind.

Two standard titration methods for Base Number are in general use - one using a strongly acidic titrant, one a weaker one - and they return systematically different values on the same oil, the stronger method giving the higher figure. Results from the two must never be trended together: a change of laboratory or method then looks exactly like a change in the oil.

Which of the two numbers governs depends on the oil. Cylinder oils and trunk-piston engine oils carry a deliberate alkaline reserve to neutralise combustion acid, so BN is the controlling parameter. Turbine, hydraulic, gear and stern tube oils carry no alkaline reserve at all, so BN is meaningless for them and AN is the governing parameter - a rising AN being the direct measure of oxidative degradation.

blocks.p: On cylinder oils in particular, the relationship with the fuel changed when the 0.50 per cent m/m limit on the sulphur content of fuel oil used outside emission control areas took effect on 1 January 2020. Less sulphur means less acid formed and, in principle, a lower base number required. But over-alkalinity is not a safe error in the other direction: detergent that finds no acid to neutralise deposits as hard calcium ash, which is abrasive and polishes the liner. Base number is therefore matched to the fuel actually being burned and reviewed at every changeover.

blocks.h: 7. Correct interpretation - reading the four results together

blocks.p: This is what the stem's opening sentence is demanding, and it is the point at which the four techniques stop being a list. The governing rule is that no single result diagnoses anything. Pairs and trends do.

rows: Iron rising, residual Base Number falling toward exhaustion
Corrosive wear - alkaline reserve is being consumed faster than it is being supplied. In a cylinder this is cold corrosion
High - the clearest signature in the subject
Iron rising, Base Number still healthy
Not corrosion. Look for abrasive ingress, scuffing or a mechanical cause - and note that raising the feed rate will make matters worse, not better
High
Wear metals normal, particle count climbing
Filtration or centrifuge failure, or ingress. The machine is not necessarily wearing faster; the oil is simply not being cleaned
High
Particle count climbing while spectrometry stays clean
Suspect coarse debris that spectrometry cannot see - bearing fatigue or spalling. Confirm physically at once
Medium - and the most dangerous case on the list, because the spectrometric report looks reassuring
Silicon rising together with iron and chromium
Abrasive dirt ingress through a defective air filter, seal or breather, producing three-body abrasive wear
High
Silicon high alone, shortly after an overhaul
Silicone sealant or antifoam residue rather than dirt. Re-sample before acting on it
High
Sodium and boron rising with glycol and water on FTIR
Coolant leak. Find it before the bearings do - glycol is far more damaging to bearing metal than water alone
High
Vanadium and nickel present, fuel dilution on FTIR, viscosity falling
Fuel dilution from leaking injection equipment or poor combustion
High
Oxidation and Acid Number both rising, wear metals normal
The oil is degrading and the machine is not - overheating, air entrainment, or an over-extended drain interval
High
Copper, lead or tin rising alone
Bearing distress. Copper alone can also come from cooler-tube corrosion, so identify the source before condemning a bearing
Medium

High
Additive elements rising
The wrong oil has been added. Check the topping-up records before anything else
High

blocks.p: Two disciplines govern the whole of it. First, trend rather than spot-read: a value has meaning only against that machine's own history, taken the same way from the same point. Second, rate of change matters more than level - a moderate iron figure that has doubled in a month is far more serious than a higher figure that has been flat for a year.

blocks.h: 8. Corrective measures - what is actually done

blocks.p: The stem asks for corrective measures, so the answer has to say what the Chief Engineer does. The general sequence on any adverse result is: verify the result, confirm it physically, correct the cause, and only then correct the oil.

ol: Verify before acting. Re-sample properly - same point, same method, machine at operating temperature with the oil circulating - and re-test. A large share of alarming results are sampling artefacts, and taking a machine out of service on a bad sample is an expensive way to learn that.

Confirm physically. Where wear is indicated, go and look: magnetic plugs and chip detectors, filter elements cut open and examined, centrifuge sludge, ferrography for the shape of the debris, and direct inspection where it is accessible - scavenge ports, crankcase, gear teeth, bearing clearances. Ferrography is the technique that reveals the morphology of the debris and therefore the wear mechanism, which no elemental figure can.

Deal with abrasive ingress at the entry path - air filters, seals, breathers, hatch and cover joints - and not by adding filtration alone. Filtration removes the consequence and leaves the cause running.

Deal with a coolant leak immediately. Locate it by pressure-testing coolers, jackets and covers. Glycol attacks bearing metal and forms sludge, and a coolant leak left in service will ruin bearings long before the wear metals reach any alarm value.
Deal with fuel dilution at the injection equipment, timing and combustion, and by checking for leakage past pumps and pipework. Then renew the oil, because diluted oil cannot be recovered.

Deal with water by finding the source - cooler leaks, condensation, steam coils, stern tube ingress - and by running the purifier correctly: correct gravity disc, correct throughput, correct temperature. Water is the one contaminant the ship can usually remove for itself.

Deal with a rising particle count by checking and renewing filters, verifying filter differential pressure and bypass operation, and reviewing purifier throughput, temperature and discharge interval. Then look for the ingress path.

Deal with a low residual Base Number in a cylinder oil by raising the feed rate or moving to a higher-BN oil, matched to the sulphur of the fuel actually burned - and confirm the change worked by scrape-down analysis rather than assuming it. Do the reverse where residual BN is running high, because over-alkalinity deposits abrasive calcium ash.

Deal with high Acid Number and high oxidation in a system oil by investigating the cause first - overheating, air entrainment, contamination, an over-extended drain interval - then by partial or complete renewal, cleaning the system before recharging so that the new charge is not contaminated on the first day.
Deal with additive depletion by renewal. Additives cannot be topped up in service, and attempting it usually produces an incompatibility rather than a recovery.

Record the action and close the loop. Every action taken, and the analysis result that follows it, goes into that machine's history under the planned maintenance system. Unrecorded corrective action is indistinguishable from no corrective action, and it destroys the trend on which the next diagnosis depends.

blocks.p: And the standing caution, which belongs in the answer explicitly: every condemning limit and target value comes from the engine builder and the oil supplier for that specific installation. None is quoted here and none should be carried from one ship to another - the same figure on a different engine, oil or duty can be entirely wrong.

blocks.h: 9. Sampling and trending - without which none of it means anything

ul: Sample from the same point, in the same way, at the same interval, with the machine at operating temperature and the oil circulating. Oil drawn from a settled sump is not the fluid that is in service.
Take the sample from a live line or a dedicated sampling point, upstream of the filter, and never from the drain or the bottom of a tank.
Flush the sampling point first and use clean, dedicated bottles. A contaminated bottle will produce a particle count that condemns a healthy machine.
Keep a retained sample of every new oil delivered - FTIR is a differential measurement and is much weaker without its reference.
Label completely: ship, machine, sampling point, running hours since the last change and since overhaul, oil grade, and any top-up made.
Trend the results, and read the rate of change rather than the absolute value.
Plan the sampling in the planned maintenance system under the ISM maintenance regime at chapter 10, so that it happens whether or not anyone remembers it.

blocks.p: The closing point is the one the stem's preamble is really driving at: analysis does not maintain machinery. It tells you where to look. Its whole value is realised in the interpretation and the corrective action that follow, and a programme that generates reports nobody reads and acts on is a cost with no benefit attached.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks, four named sub-items - and a preamble that quietly adds two more tasks. The stem's first sentence says that periodical oil analysis, its correct interpretation and corrective measures, are of critical significance, and the command verb is "discuss", not "briefly discuss". That is an instruction, not scene-setting. So the shape is roughly half the answer across the four techniques and half on reading and acting on the results. A candidate who describes the four instruments beautifully and stops has answered a different and much easier question.

blocks.h: Open with the three questions

blocks.p: Is the machine wearing? Is the oil still fit? Is anything getting in? Spectrometry and particle count answer the first; FTIR with BN and AN answer the second; all four answer the third from different directions. Two sentences, and the four techniques become a system instead of a list - which is exactly what "discuss" is asking for.

blocks.h: The qualification most candidates omit

blocks.p: Spectrometry reports the fine fraction only. The method needs the particle to be completely atomised in the excitation source, and coarse particles are not - so the response falls away as size increases. Normal rubbing wear is fine and is seen well; bearing fatigue, spalling, scuffing and gear pitting are coarse and may be invisible. A clean spectrometric report is therefore not evidence of a healthy machine. Write that sentence down: it is the single most valuable thing in the question, and it is the reason particle count exists alongside spectrometry rather than instead of it.

blocks.h: FTIR - two words to get right

blocks.p: Interferogram and differential. The instrument gathers all wavelengths at once as an interferogram and Fourier transforms it into a spectrum - that is what the name means and why it is fast. And it works by subtracting the spectrum of the same oil unused, so without a new-oil reference the result is much weaker. That carries a practical instruction with it: retain a sealed sample of every oil delivery.

blocks.h: The four techniques in one table

rows: Spectrometry
The machine

blocks.p: The pairing to carry into the hall: spectrometry says WHAT, particle count says HOW MUCH and HOW BIG. Neither is sufficient alone, and that is the practical point of the entire question.

blocks.h: BN and AN - the three things that score

ol: Same units, opposite directions. Both in mg KOH per gramme - which is why they are confused. BN falls, AN rises.
An oil can show both at once. Separate titrations of separate species; not two ends of one scale.

Which one governs depends on the oil. Cylinder and trunk-piston oils carry an alkaline reserve, so BN governs. Turbine, hydraulic, gear and stern tube oils have no reserve, so AN governs and measures oxidative degradation.

blocks.p: And the trap inside the trap: two standard BN titration methods are in use and they give systematically different values on the same oil, the stronger titrant returning the higher figure. Never trend them together - a change of laboratory can look exactly like a change in the oil.

blocks.h: Interpretation - learn the pairs, not the values

blocks.p: An examiner asking for "correct interpretation" wants diagnostic pairs:

ul: Iron up + residual BN near exhaustion = corrosive wear. In a cylinder, cold corrosion.
Iron up + BN healthy = not corrosion. More oil will make it worse.
Particle count up + wear metals normal = filtration or centrifuge failure, or ingress.
Particle count up + spectrometry clean = coarse debris spectrometry cannot see. The most dangerous case, because the report looks reassuring.
Silicon up + iron and chromium up = abrasive dirt ingress.
Sodium and boron up + glycol and water on FTIR = coolant leak.
Vanadium and nickel + fuel dilution on FTIR + viscosity down = fuel dilution.
Oxidation up + AN up + no wear metals = the oil is degrading and the machine is fine.
Additive elements up = somebody has added the wrong oil.

blocks.h: Corrective measures - the sequence

blocks.p: Verify - confirm physically - correct the cause - then correct the oil. Re-sample before acting, because a large share of alarming results are sampling artefacts. Then go and look: magnetic plugs, filters cut open, centrifuge sludge, ferrography - ferrography being the one that gives you the shape of the debris and therefore the wear mechanism. Then attack the cause - the leaking seal, the failing cooler, the injection equipment - and only after that renew or adjust the oil. Adding filtration to deal with dirt ingress treats the consequence and leaves the cause running.

blocks.h: Quote no numbers - and say why

blocks.p: No condemning limit, alarm level, ppm value, cleanliness code, base number or wear rate should be offered as a general rule. Every one is engine-builder, oil, application and service specific, and a figure carried from one installation to another is a genuine hazard as well as an examination risk. Writing "the limit comes from the engine builder's service letter and the oil supplier's recommendation for this installation" scores better than a half-remembered figure that may belong to a different machine - and it is the answer a Chief Engineer is supposed to give.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Describing the four techniques and never answering the stem's express demand for interpretation and corrective measures - roughly half the marks.
Omitting the particle-size limitation of spectrometry, and so implying that a clean report means a healthy machine.
Treating spectrometry and particle count as alternatives rather than as complements.
Saying FTIR measures wear metals. It is blind to them entirely.
Forgetting that FTIR is a differential measurement requiring a new-oil reference.
Assuming BN and AN cannot both be significant in the same sample.
Applying BN to a turbine or hydraulic oil, which carries no alkaline reserve.
Quoting condemning limits, ppm values or cleanliness codes as though they were general rules.
Ignoring sampling technique, without which every number in the report is unreliable.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Your spectrometric report is clean. Is the engine healthy?" No - it says the fine fraction is normal. Coarse debris from fatigue or spalling may not appear at all.
"What does FTIR see that spectrometry cannot, and the reverse?" FTIR sees the chemical condition of the oil; spectrometry sees the elements. Neither sees the other's subject.
"Why is water a problem for a particle counter?" Optical counters count droplets and air bubbles as particles, so a wet or aerated sample reads falsely high.
"Can an oil show a healthy Base Number and a significant Acid Number together?" Yes - separate titrations of separate species.
"Would you trend Base Number results from two different laboratories?" No - two standard methods exist and give systematically different values.
"Iron is up. Do you increase the cylinder oil feed rate?" Only if the residual BN is low. If BN is healthy the cause is not corrosion and more oil will make it worse.
"What tells you the shape of the wear debris?" Ferrography - and the shape identifies the wear mechanism.
"Where do your condemning limits come from?" The engine builder's service letters and the oil supplier for this installation. Not from a textbook, and not from the last ship.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Show me where you take your main engine system oil sample, and talk me through doing it.
Your last report shows sodium and boron rising. What is your first action?
What is a scrape-down analysis, and how does it differ from a system oil analysis?
How does your purifier remove water, and how would you know that it was working?
Which of your oils has no base number at all, and what do you monitor on it instead?
You get an alarming result on a Sunday at sea. What do you do before you do anything else?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Three questions, four techniques, two pairs, one sequence. THREE QUESTIONS: is it wearing, is the oil fit, is anything getting in. FOUR TECHNIQUES: spectrometry says WHAT, particle count says HOW MUCH and HOW BIG, FTIR says what the OIL has become, BN and AN say how much fight is LEFT. TWO PAIRS for diagnosis: iron with residual BN, and particle count with spectrometry. ONE SEQUENCE for action: verify - confirm physically - correct the cause - then correct the oil.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: NO IMO INSTRUMENT, INDIAN STATUTE OR CLASS RULE PRESCRIBES A LUBRICATING OIL ANALYSIS PROGRAMME. None is named here, because naming one would give the answer an authority it does not have.

MARPOL Annex VI - the 0.50 per cent m/m limit on the sulphur content of fuel oil used outside emission control areas, in force since 1 January 2020 and therefore three years old at this sitting. Used only to explain cylinder oil base number selection; no provision is quoted and no regulation number is asserted.

ISM Code chapter 10 - maintenance of the ship and equipment, the regime under which sampling and analysis are planned and recorded. The held chain runs A.741(18) as amended through MSC.353(92), which is the text in force at this sitting.
The cleanliness code used for reporting particle counts - named as the reporting convention only. NOT HELD by MIW; no code, band or table reproduced.
The two standard titration methods for Base Number - described by chemistry and by the direction of the discrepancy. NOT HELD by MIW and no standard number asserted.

Engine builder service letters and the oil supplier's recommendation for the specific installation - the only correct sources for condemning limits, alarm levels and target values. Not held; none reproduced.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: This question carries no statutory content, and the answer says so expressly rather than borrowing authority from an unrelated instrument. Atomic emission spectrometry, infrared spectroscopy, particle counting and acid-base titration are not dated law and carry no amendment boundary, so the reversal problem that governs the rest of this paper does not touch it. The answer would read the same at any sitting in this period.

The no-figures rule is absolute here and is the most important evidential feature of the answer. No condemning limit, alarm level, ppm value, cleanliness code, base number figure or wear rate appears as a general rule anywhere. Every one is engine-builder, oil, application and service specific, and a figure carried between installations is a genuine hazard as well as an evidential defect. The engine builder's service letters and the oil supplier's recommendation for the specific installation are the governing sources, and MIW holds neither. A deliberate consequence of that discipline is that nothing in this answer can go stale through a re-issued service letter or a revised standard.

The infrared absorption regions are named by what they indicate and not by wavenumber, because the positions shift with chemical environment and the integration windows are instrument and method specific. The two standard Base Number titration methods are not identified by standard number; they are distinguished by their chemistry and by the direction of the discrepancy between them. The cleanliness code is named as a reporting convention only. No oil company, analyser manufacturer, engine builder, laboratory or proprietary condition-monitoring programme is named anywhere.

The interpretation, corrective-measures and sampling material is engineering judgement, reasoned from the properties of the four techniques. It answers what the printed preamble expressly demands. It is not a manufacturer's recommendation and is not presented as one, and a diagnosis is never asserted from numbers alone - each pairing carries a stated confidence and directs the reader to physical confirmation.
