steps.title: Why the oil is analysed, and what the four techniques are for
points: A running machine is a sealed box; the oil is the only thing that comes out of it
It has been in contact with every working surface inside
Is the machine wearing? - spectrometry and particle count
Is the oil still fit? - FTIR, and BN with AN
Is anything getting in? - all four, from different directions
The governing rule: trend against that machine's own history, not the absolute value

steps.title: A) Elemental (spectrometric) analysis
points: Sample excited in a plasma or across a rotating-disc electrode arc
Each element emits at characteristic wavelengths; intensity gives concentration in ppm
Wear metals - iron from liners, rings, gears, shafting; copper, lead, tin from bearings; chromium from rings and plating; aluminium from pistons
Contaminants - silicon from dirt and abrasive; sodium and boron from coolant; vanadium and nickel from residual fuel
Additive elements - calcium and magnesium (detergent), zinc and phosphorus (anti-wear)
Additives falling = depletion; rising = the wrong oil was added
Silicon reads two ways - dirt ingress in service, or sealant and antifoam residue right after an overhaul

steps.title: What spectrometry cannot see, and why that governs its use
points: The method needs complete atomisation of the particle in the excitation source
Coarse particles are not fully atomised, so response falls away with increasing size
It therefore reports essentially the fine fraction only
Normal rubbing wear is fine and is seen well
Bearing fatigue, spalling, scuffing and gear pitting are coarse and may not be seen
So a clean spectrometric report is NOT evidence of a healthy machine
Which is exactly why particle count, ferrography and plug inspection sit alongside it

steps.title: B) Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy
points: Infrared through a thin film; molecular bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers
All wavelengths gathered at once as an interferogram and Fourier transformed to a spectrum
A DIFFERENTIAL measurement - compared against the spectrum of the same oil unused
Practical consequence: retain a sealed sample of every oil delivery
Detects oxidation, nitration, sulphation, water and glycol
Soot appears as a broad baseline rise, not a discrete peak
Also fuel dilution and additive depletion
Fast, small sample, no reagents - but semi-quantitative and blind to wear metals and particles

steps.title: C) Particle count
points: Solid particles counted and sized, usually by optical light obscuration
Pore blockage where the oil is too dark; microscopy is the referee method
Reported as counts per millilitre in cumulative size bands, condensed to a cleanliness code
Decisive for hydraulic, servo and control systems where clearances are microns
The direct measure of filtration and centrifuge performance and of ingress
It sees the coarse particles spectrometry misses - the two are complementary
Limits: counts water droplets and air bubbles as particles; never says what they are

steps.title: D) Base Number against Acid Number
points: Both titrations, both in mg KOH per gramme - which is why they are confused
BN = alkaline reserve from overbased detergent additives; it FALLS in service
AN = acidic constituents from combustion and oxidation; it RISES
An oil can carry both at once - separate titrations of separate species
Two standard BN methods give systematically different values - never trend them together
BN governs cylinder and trunk-piston oils, matched to the sulphur actually burned
AN governs turbine, hydraulic, gear and stern tube oils, which carry no reserve
Since the 0.50 per cent limit of 1 January 2020, BN is matched to the fuel in use - and over-alkalinity deposits abrasive calcium ash

steps.title: Correct interpretation - reading the four results together
points: No single result diagnoses anything; pairs and trends do
Iron up + residual BN near exhaustion = corrosive wear (in a cylinder, cold corrosion)
Iron up + BN healthy = NOT corrosion; more oil will make it worse
Particle count up + wear metals normal = filtration or centrifuge failure, or ingress
Particle count up + spectrometry clean = coarse debris - the most dangerous case
Silicon up + iron and chromium up = abrasive dirt ingress
Sodium and boron up + glycol and water on FTIR = coolant leak
Vanadium and nickel + fuel on FTIR + viscosity down = fuel dilution
Oxidation up + AN up + no wear metals = the oil is degrading, the machine is fine
Additive elements up = the wrong oil was added
Two disciplines: trend, do not spot-read; and rate of change beats level

steps.title: Corrective measures - what is actually done
points: The sequence: verify - confirm physically - correct the cause - then correct the oil
Re-sample before acting - a large share of alarming results are sampling artefacts
Confirm physically - magnetic plugs, filters cut open, centrifuge sludge, ferrography for debris shape, direct inspection
Abrasive ingress - find the entry path (filters, seals, breathers), not just more filtration
Coolant leak - pressure-test coolers, jackets, covers; glycol destroys bearing metal
Fuel dilution - injection equipment, timing, combustion; then renew, because diluted oil cannot be recovered
Water - find the source and run the purifier correctly (gravity disc, throughput, temperature)
Rising particle count - filters, differential pressure, bypass, purifier operation; then the ingress path
Low residual BN in cylinder oil - raise feed rate or move to a higher-BN oil matched to fuel sulphur, and confirm by scrape-down
High AN and oxidation - find the cause, then renew, cleaning the system before recharging
Additive depletion - renew; additives cannot be topped up
Record and close the loop in the PMS - unrecorded action destroys the trend
Standing caution: every limit comes from the builder and the oil supplier for THAT installation

steps.title: Sampling and trending - without which none of it means anything
points: Same point, same way, same interval; machine at temperature and oil circulating
From a live line upstream of the filter, never the drain or the tank bottom
Flush the point; use clean dedicated bottles - a dirty bottle condemns a healthy machine
Retain a sample of every new oil - FTIR needs its reference
Label fully: ship, machine, point, hours since change and since overhaul, grade, top-ups
Trend, and read the rate of change rather than the level
Plan it in the PMS under the ISM maintenance regime at chapter 10
Close: analysis does not maintain machinery - it tells you where to look

questions.memory_cue: Three questions, four techniques, two pairs, one sequence. QUESTIONS: is it wearing, is the oil fit, is anything getting in (1). TECHNIQUES: spectrometry says WHAT (2, and its limitation is step 3), particle count says HOW MUCH and HOW BIG (5), FTIR says what the OIL has become (4), BN and AN say how much FIGHT is left (6). PAIRS: iron with residual BN, and particle count with spectrometry (7). SEQUENCE: verify, confirm physically, correct the cause, then correct the oil (8), on samples taken properly (9).
questions.understand_first: Every machine on the ship is sealed, and you cannot look inside it while it runs. The oil can - it touches every working surface continuously and carries away a sample of everything that happens in there. Oil analysis is nothing more than the business of reading that sample. The reason there are four techniques rather than one is that they are answering different questions and each is blind to the others' subjects. Two of them look at the machine: spectrometry tells you what the debris is made of, and particle count tells you how much of it there is and how big it is - and you need both, because spectrometry physically cannot see coarse particles, so a clean spectrometric report on a spalling bearing is a false reassurance rather than good news. The other two look at the oil: FTIR tells you what the oil has chemically become, and Base and Acid Number tell you how much fight it has left. Once you see it that way, the interpretation the question demands stops being a feat of memory. You are not reading numbers, you are reading pairs. Iron rising tells you very little on its own; iron rising with the base number gone tells you the oil stopped protecting the metal, while iron rising with the base number healthy tells you something entirely different and warns you that adding more oil will make it worse. And then the last idea, which is what the stem's opening sentence is really driving at: the analysis does not maintain anything. It tells you where to look. A programme that produces reports nobody reads is a cost with no benefit.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Four techniques answering three questions. Elemental spectrometry - the sample is excited in a plasma or rotating-disc arc, each element emits at characteristic wavelengths and intensity gives ppm; reads wear metals (iron, copper, lead, tin, chromium, aluminium), contaminants (silicon from dirt, sodium and boron from coolant, vanadium and nickel from residual fuel) and additive elements (calcium, magnesium, zinc, phosphorus). Its critical limitation: coarse particles are not fully atomised, so it reports the fine fraction only - fatigue, spalling and scuffing debris may be invisible, so a clean report is not a healthy machine. FTIR - bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers, all gathered as an interferogram and Fourier transformed; a differential measurement against the same oil unused; detects oxidation, nitration, sulphation, water, glycol, soot (a baseline rise), fuel dilution and additive depletion; fast but semi-quantitative and blind to wear metals. Particle count - light obscuration, pore blockage on dark oil, microscopy as referee; counts per millilitre in cumulative bands condensed to a cleanliness code; decisive for hydraulics, the measure of filtration performance, and it sees what spectrometry misses - but counts water and air as particles and never says what they are. BN and AN - both mg KOH/g, BN falls, AN rises, and both can be present at once; two standard BN methods differ systematically so never trend them together; BN governs cylinder and trunk-piston oils, AN governs turbine, hydraulic, gear and stern tube oils. Interpret by pairs: iron up with BN gone = corrosion; iron up with BN healthy = not corrosion; count up with metals normal = filtration failure; count up with spectrometry clean = coarse debris, the dangerous case. Then verify, confirm physically, correct the cause, correct the oil, on properly taken samples that are trended.
critical_numbers: 0.50 per cent m/m limit on the sulphur content of fuel oil used outside emission control areas, in force 1 January 2020 - three years and two months before this sitting, and the only figure quoted in this answer
NO condemning limit, alarm level, ppm value, cleanliness code, base number figure or wear rate is quoted as a general rule
Both BN and AN are expressed in milligrammes of potassium hydroxide per gramme of oil - the same units, opposite meanings
The governing sources for every limit: the engine builder's service letters and the oil supplier's recommendation for that specific installation
quick_revision.critical_regulation: None. No IMO instrument, Indian statute or classification rule prescribes a lubricating oil analysis programme, and saying so expressly is correct rather than evasive. MARPOL Annex VI is named only for the 0.50 per cent sulphur limit that changed how cylinder oil base number is selected. Sampling and analysis are planned and recorded under ISM Code chapter 10 as part of the maintenance regime, on the held chain A.741(18) as amended through MSC.353(92).
quick_revision.major_trap: Describing the four techniques and never answering the stem's express demand for correct interpretation and corrective measures - which the opening sentence states and which 'discuss' rather than 'briefly discuss' reinforces. That is roughly half the marks. Second trap: omitting the particle-size limitation of spectrometry, and so implying that a clean spectrometric report means a healthy machine. It does not - coarse debris from bearing fatigue, spalling and scuffing may not be seen at all. Third: assuming BN and AN cannot both be significant in the same sample, or applying BN to a turbine or hydraulic oil that carries no alkaline reserve. Fourth: trending base numbers across two different laboratories or methods, when the two standard methods give systematically different values on the same oil. Fifth: quoting condemning limits, ppm values or cleanliness codes as general rules - every one is engine-builder, oil and application specific, and a figure carried between installations is a genuine hazard.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the lubricating oil analysis question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Why analyse, and the three questions. 2 Elemental spectrometry. 3 Its particle-size limitation. 4 FTIR. 5 Particle count. 6 BN against AN - steps 2 to 6 being the four printed sub-items. 7 Correct interpretation, by diagnostic pairs. 8 Corrective measures. 9 Sampling and trending.
retrieval_cards.why: The printed preamble expressly demands interpretation and corrective measures, and the verb is 'discuss', not 'briefly discuss'. Sections 7 and 8 are roughly half the marks and are what most candidates never write.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is each of the four techniques actually for?
retrieval_cards.answer: Is the machine wearing? - elemental spectrometry and particle count. Is the oil still fit? - FTIR, and Base and Acid Number. Is anything getting in? - all four, from different directions. The pairing to remember: spectrometry says WHAT the debris is; particle count says HOW MUCH and HOW BIG. FTIR and BN/AN say nothing about the machine at all - they describe the oil.
retrieval_cards.why: Framing them as a system rather than a list is what 'discuss' is asking for, and it makes the interpretation section reconstructable from first principles.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your spectrometric report is clean. Is the engine healthy?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The method needs the particle to be completely atomised in the excitation source, and coarse particles are not - so the response falls away as size increases and the technique reports essentially the fine fraction only. Normal rubbing wear is seen well; bearing fatigue, spalling, scuffing and gear pitting are coarse and may not be seen at all. That is exactly why particle count, ferrography and magnetic plug inspection sit alongside it.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most valuable point in the question, the one most often omitted, and the standard oral trap.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain FTIR, and why it needs a reference sample.
retrieval_cards.answer: Infrared passes through a thin film of oil and molecular bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers. All wavelengths are gathered at once as an interferogram and Fourier transformed into a spectrum, which is what makes it fast. It is a differential measurement against the same oil unused, so without a new-oil reference it is much weaker. It detects oxidation, nitration, sulphation, water, glycol, soot as a baseline rise, and fuel dilution - and is blind to wear metals.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Differential' is the word candidates miss, and it carries a standing instruction: retain a sealed sample of every oil delivery.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does particle counting work, and what is it blind to?
retrieval_cards.answer: Solid particles are counted and sized, usually by optical light obscuration. Pore-blockage methods are used where the oil is too dark, and microscopy is the referee method. Results are counts per millilitre in cumulative size bands, condensed to a cleanliness code. It is decisive for hydraulic and servo systems, measures filtration performance, and sees the coarse particles spectrometry misses. Blind spots: it counts water and air as particles, and never says what they are.
retrieval_cards.why: Complementary to spectrometry rather than an alternative to it - and the water-and-air limitation explains a great many false alarms.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish Base Number from Acid Number.
retrieval_cards.answer: Both are titrations reported in mg KOH per gramme of oil, which is why they are confused. BN is the alkaline reserve from overbased detergent additives and it FALLS in service. AN is the acidic constituents present and it RISES. An oil can carry both at once - separate titrations of separate species. BN governs cylinder and trunk-piston oils; AN governs turbine, hydraulic, gear and stern tube oils, which carry no reserve at all.
retrieval_cards.why: Three separate marks live here: same units, opposite directions, and which one governs which oil.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Would you trend Base Number results from two different laboratories?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Two distinct standard titration methods for Base Number are in use - one with a strongly acidic titrant, one with a weaker one - and they return systematically different results on the same oil, the stronger method giving the higher figure. Trending them together makes a change of laboratory or method look exactly like a change in the oil.
retrieval_cards.why: A quiet trap that catches experienced engineers as often as candidates, because the report looks identical either way.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the diagnostic pairs for interpreting an oil analysis report.
retrieval_cards.answer: Iron up + residual BN near exhaustion = corrosive wear; in a cylinder, cold corrosion. Iron up + BN healthy = not corrosion, and more oil will worsen it. Particle count up + wear metals normal = filtration failure or ingress. Particle count up + spectrometry clean = coarse debris, the most dangerous case. Silicon with iron and chromium = dirt ingress. Sodium and boron with glycol = coolant leak. Oxidation and AN up with no wear metals = the oil is degrading, not the machine.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem demands 'correct interpretation'. No single result diagnoses anything - pairs and trends do, and rate of change beats absolute level.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the corrective sequence on an adverse result?
retrieval_cards.answer: Verify - confirm physically - correct the cause - then correct the oil. Re-sample and re-test first, because many alarming results are sampling artefacts. Then go and look: magnetic plugs, filters cut open, centrifuge sludge, ferrography for debris shape. Then attack the cause - the leaking seal, the failing cooler, the injection equipment - because filtration removes the consequence and leaves the cause running. Only then renew or adjust the oil, and record every action, or the trend is destroyed.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the second half of what the stem asks for, and 'correct the cause before the oil' is the sentence that shows it has been understood.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where do condemning limits come from?
retrieval_cards.answer: From the engine builder's service letters and the oil supplier's recommendation for that specific installation - never from a textbook and never from the last ship. Every condemning limit, alarm level, ppm value, cleanliness code and base number target is engine, oil, application and service specific, and a figure carried between installations is a genuine hazard as well as an examination risk.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying this scores better than a remembered number, and it is the answer a Chief Engineer is supposed to give.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That two distinct standard titration methods for Base Number are in general use and return systematically different results on the same oil, the stronger titrant giving the higher value.
reverify_before_publication.why: Carried as authoritative secondary. MIW holds no test-method standard, and neither method is identified by standard number here. Only the chemistry and the direction of the discrepancy are stated. Confirm against the test-method standards before publication.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The infrared absorption regions attributed to oxidation, nitration, sulphation, water, glycol and soot.
reverify_before_publication.why: Named by what they indicate and NOT by wavenumber, because the positions are properties of the molecular bonds, shift with chemical environment, and the integration windows are instrument and method specific. No wavenumber value is asserted anywhere. Confirm against an analytical reference before publication.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the 0.50 per cent m/m limit on the sulphur content of fuel oil used outside emission control areas was in force at this sitting.
reverify_before_publication.why: In force since 1 January 2020, three years and two months before March 2023, and used only to explain how cylinder oil base number is matched to the fuel burned. Date-driven by construction, checked backwards against this sitting rather than inherited from the June 2024 donor, and to be re-checked before publication.
